name: Mississippi Today
title: Hattiesburg songwriter explains why local music matters
description: The Saenger Theater in downtown Hattiesburg on Nov. 13, 2026.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.  

You can live in a town for years and still feel like you’re visiting. You know the streets, where to buy groceries, which restaurant you like. Belonging takes something more.
For me, local music has often been how that happens.
You start going to a room. You recognize a few faces. You hear someone play a song they wrote, and something in it stays with you. You come back. Eventually, you have people to say hello to, a favorite song to ask for and a friend you want to bring along.
You have a place in what’s happening.
When I talk about local music, I’m thinking particularly about original music: people writing songs and making records in the communities where they live. Hearing a song from its writer offers a connection you can follow. You might hear an early version, then watch it become a record. The song becomes part of your history with a place.
I grew up in Doraville, Georgia, outside Atlanta. We had a local band, the Atlanta Rhythm Section, that became nationally known. They even wrote a song called “Doraville.” People elsewhere were hearing a band from our backyard sing about our home. It gave us something to claim.
Later, at the University of Georgia in Athens, I found that feeling again, this time playing in a band myself. The work being made around us mattered. You didn’t have to leave town before people took you seriously.
There’s an attitude I still run into: “If you’re so good, why are you still here?” That’s a strange thing to ask someone whose work might be one of the reasons a place is worth living in.
Drew Yiung performs at the Keg & Barrel in Hattiesburg in 2025. Credit: Courtesy photo by Rob Walker
I recently spoke with producer and engineer John Keane, who recorded my band’s first album in Athens. We talked about musicians and visual artists moving through the same circles. Bands grew out of an art community where trying something unfamiliar was part of the point. The audience expected to be surprised, too.
John remembered people arriving for school and staying because of the friends they made in music and art. Others moved away and came back. Athens offered a life they wanted, with people they wanted to be around.
That matters when communities talk about attracting and retaining people. A job may bring someone to town. What happens after work can help them decide whether to stay.
Mississippi has spent years making sure the world remembers the musicians who came from here. We’ve built museums, marked highways and put considerable effort into telling those stories. That’s work worth doing.
But I wonder whether we’re giving the same attention to the people writing songs and making records here today. We ought to be able to celebrate our musical history while making it possible for the next generation to earn a living creating it.
I came to Hattiesburg for an artist-in-residence position and apparently forgot to leave. Getting to know the musicians here had something to do with that.
My master’s in economic development at the University of Southern Mississippi and my work with Greater New Orleans Inc. and Visit Mississippi gave me another way to think about what surrounds a song.
Shows involve sound engineers, venue staff and promoters. Recording brings work to studios, producers, designers and photographers. A musician’s ability to keep working affects people beyond the band.
Touring musicians also carry their hometowns with them. We tell audiences where we’re from, talk about the people we play with and recommend places to hear music. Someone who has never visited Hattiesburg can leave our show knowing a little more about it.
Music tourism can begin with a drive from the next town. Staff at the historic Saenger Theater in downtown Hattiesburg say the theater’s audiences regularly include visitors from Mobile, the Mississippi Gulf Coast, Jackson and New Orleans, with some traveling from Texas, Florida and Tennessee.
The staff says multiple downtown restaurants have reported additional customers when the theater has a show. Some visiting patrons ask for hotel recommendations, and touring artists and production crews also need overnight accommodations.
The theater does not have figures measuring the restaurant spending or hotel stays its events generate. Those accounts give us a place to start asking how music supports downtown businesses, and what more we could learn by tracking it.
Residents benefit, too. Young people should be able to imagine an interesting life in their hometown. Retirees still need places to meet people or hear a good band on a Tuesday.
Hattiesburg already offers several ways in. I recently played a Thursday lunchtime concert in the Brown Bag series. Live at Five and programming at Midtown Green give people other places to gather. FestivalSouth brings performances into the city’s calendar across several art forms.
Museum shows can put songwriters in front of listeners who might never hear them in a club.
Hattiesburg is hardly alone in this. Across Mississippi, communities are finding different ways to bring people together through music. The challenge is making sure musicians have places to play, audiences willing to listen and opportunities to keep doing the work.
When and where we present music matters. Bringing music into parks, museums, libraries and other public spaces introduces it to people who might never walk into a nightclub. Some people work early. Some have children or someone at home who needs them. Others simply prefer an afternoon concert to a late night out. These performances widen the audience and make music a more natural part of everyday community life.
That’s particularly important in a place like Hattiesburg, which has been positioning itself as an attractive place to retire. Access to music, art and culture is part of what makes a community appealing at any age. People aren’t just looking for somewhere affordable to live. They’re looking for somewhere interesting to live, with opportunities to get out, meet people and feel connected.
The musicians need a workable life, too. Can they afford somewhere to live and rehearse? Are there rooms where they can develop an audience? Are publicly supported events paying them fairly? Can younger players find a place to start?
On Nov. 20, I’ll be part of the Hattiesburg Music Showcase at the Saenger, alongside Blue Mountain, Jacob Arnold & The Bird Dogs and Grits & Greens. Four acts offer only a glimpse of the music being made here, but they give listeners a chance to hear different approaches to writing and playing original songs.
The Saenger opened in 1929 and underwent a major interior renovation in 2000. Preserving a theater gives us a stage. What we put on it, and whether we show up, helps determine what that investment makes possible.
Come for someone you know. Take a chance on someone you don’t. Then find another show, bring a friend and come back when something catches your ear.
Eventually, a song reminds you of a room, the people and a particular time in your life.
You remember being there. You remember belonging.

Drew Young is a Hattiesburg-based songwriter, educator and cultural producer. He has worked with Visit Mississippi and Greater New Orleans Inc. and writes about music, culture and community for “TIDAL” and on his Substack. He is the creator of “Back Roads & Back Stories” and holds a master’s degree in economic development from the University of Southern Mississippi.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Weddle makes unusual legal move to try again to move his contributions case to Franklin County
description: Former London Mayor Randall Weddle is asking a second time to move his trial for allegedly making excess campaign contributions to Gov. Andy Beshear from Laurel County to Franklin County. On Monday, Weddle’s attorney Guthrie True filed an unusual petition with the Kentucky Court of Appeals asking it to reverse a ruling by Laurel Circuit […]
text:
Randall Weddle, mayor of London, Kentucky, speaking at Gov. Andy Beshear's press conference on May 18, 2023.(Screen grab from Gov. Andy Beshear's YouTube Channel)Former London Mayor Randall Weddle is asking a second time to move his trial for allegedly making excess campaign contributions to Gov. Andy Beshear from Laurel County to Franklin County.
On Monday, Weddle’s attorney Guthrie True filed an unusual petition with the Kentucky Court of Appeals asking it to reverse a ruling by Laurel Circuit Judge Michael Caperton which would keep the case in Laurel County.
In a case being prosecuted by Attorney General Russell Coleman, the Laurel grand jury indicted Weddle last spring on four counts of intentionally exceeding the legal limits on campaign contributions. The indictment alleges that Weddle did so by giving $18,000 too much to Beshear’s 2023 campaign for governor and as much as $205,000 too much to the Kentucky Democratic Party in late 2022 by donating the money in the names of his family members, friends and employees. 
Those amounts are far above the limits set by law at the time of the donations – $2,000 to a candidate’s campaign per election, and $15,000 per year to a state political party.
Weddle pleaded not guilty, and True immediately asked for a change of venue to Franklin County – the motion Caperton denied last month.
True is now taking an extraordinary step in filing what in effect is a pre-trial appeal – petitioning for a “writ of mandamus” from the appeals court that would say Caperton was wrong and order that he transfer the case to Franklin. 
The 28-page petition says that by bringing the indictment in Laurel County Coleman “engaged in forum shopping – plain and simple – in the hopes of some strategic advantage.”
True argues that Kentucky law clearly allows any case alleging illegal campaign contributions can be brought to Franklin because that is the county where all state political campaigns and committees file their reports. Otherwise, he argues the law requires that such cases be brought in the county in which the contributions were “solicited, made or accepted.”
In this case, True says all parties in the case agree the contributions were solicited from Franklin County, accepted in Franklin County, and made by Weddle on his credit card while he was on a family vacation in the Bahamas.
The petition states that Weddle “will suffer great injustice and irreparable harm if he is compelled to go through trial in the wrong venue and risk conviction followed by a retrial in the correct venue.”
Last month Caperton rejected True’s arguments and agreed with attorneys on Coleman’s staff that Laurel is a proper venue – primarily because Weddle has a Laurel County address on his credit card and Laurel County is where Weddle lives. “A donation is ultimately ‘made’ from the place where the card is registered, not where the Defendant physically happens to be at the particular time he is using his phone and pushes the ‘donation’ button,” Caperton said in his order.
A spokesman for Coleman’s office told the Lantern they could not comment on “an open investigation.”
In a footnote of Monday’s petition, True repeated his basic case for Weddle – a case True previously gave to the Kentucky Registry of Election Finance while that body was initially investigating the matter. “When Mr. Weddle learned of a problem with the contributions … he reported the problem – ultimately to the candidate himself, Governor Beshear – and the contributions were refunded. In the end, there were no contributions at all,” True stated in the footnote.
The election registry later deferred its investigation when Coleman’s office began looking into the matter.

The purchase, announced in July by Northrim, marks the first time that Northrim has expanded outside the state of Alaska. People’s Bank of Commerce has 11 branches in […]
text:
U.S. currency is seen in a close-up photo. (Getty Images)The Alaska Division of Banking and Securities is planning to approve Northrim Bank’s takeover of Oregon’s People’s Bank of Commerce, it said in a public notice Thursday.
The purchase, announced in July by Northrim, marks the first time that Northrim has expanded outside the state of Alaska. People’s Bank of Commerce has 11 branches in southern Oregon and the Willamette Valley. Northrim, based in Alaska, has 21 branches spread across the state.
Under the terms of the purchase, Northrim will give stock in Northrim to the owners of People’s Bank, who will own more than 22% of the enlarged company.
People’s Bank shareholders approved the deal in October, and the companies expect the arrangement to become final on Jan. 1.
The Knoll Bond Rating Agency, which analyzed the deal this summer, concluded that it would strengthen Northrim and is aligned with the bank’s efforts to expand outside Alaska.

title: California sues OpenAI over hacking that stoked AI fears

That recognition belongs to Dolores Huerta, the labor leader who inspired legions of Californians with her decades of activism. text:
Attendees gather at the OpenAI DevDay 2026 conference in San Francisco on Sept. 29, 2026. Photo by Jeff Chiu, AP Photo




The first woman to lie in state in the California Capitol wasn’t a lawmaker. That recognition belongs to Dolores Huerta, the labor leader who inspired legions of Californians with her decades of activism. Our visual editor Miguel Gutierrez Jr. spent Monday at her memorial, and you’ll want to make time for the images he captured. 
It was a big day in legal news: California sued OpenAI; the Trump administration lost once again in its attempt to cancel already-awarded university grants; and a group of district attorneys filed an appeal asking the state Supreme Court to block Gov. Gavin Newsom’s death penalty commutations. We have more on all of those stories in today’s newsletter. 
California is suing artificial intelligence giant OpenAI over an AI-driven cybersecurity incident that the state claims was the result of the company prioritizing “growth and rapid model development over safety and accountability.”
As CalMatters’ Colin Lecher explains, OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, was evaluating internal research models when it discovered that its AI agents had hacked their way into Hugging Face, an online platform where users can submit tools and data related to AI.
The high-profile breach underscored the dangers of AI, and intensified concerns that so-called “rogue” AI agents could damage critical infrastructure or compromise military weapon systems.
In September California Attorney General Rob Bonta said his office would investigate the incident, but according to the lawsuit — filed Monday in San Francisco Superior Court — OpenAI has failed to comply with the probe.

The lawsuit: “The company has responded to … subpoenas with just a smattering of publicly available information, self-serving blog posts, and redacted copies of a few dozen external communications containing highlevel descriptions of select security incidents.”

OpenAI also knowingly tested a risky AI model without sufficient oversight, while misleading and endangering the public, Bonta said at a press conference announcing the lawsuit. 
An OpenAI spokesperson told NPR that the company has “engaged — and will continue to engage — constructively with the Attorney General’s office to share information and advance, strong, practical safety standards for the entire industry.”
In its latest funding round earlier this month, OpenAI raised about $11 billion, and is estimated to reach a valuation of $1.25 trillion. 
Read more.



CalMatters Ideas Festival: 2027 Ideas Festival will expand to Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Francisco. One full day of candid conversations in each, with the leaders, innovators and changemakers shaping California’s future. Learn more.

Other Stories You Should Know


‘The power of ordinary people’


Dolores Huerta’s casket lies in honor at the state Capitol in Sacramento on Nov. 16, 2026. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




Hundreds of people gathered in Sacramento Monday to honor the late Dolores Huerta. The civil and labor rights leader is the first civilian and woman to lie in honor at the state Capitol. She passed away on Oct. 28 at the age of 96 after a battle with cancer.
A late morning procession of lowrider cars and marchers walked behind a white hearse carrying Huerta. Some were holding the red United Farm Workers flag while the crowd chanted, “Sí se puede” — the famous “Yes we can” rallying cry that Huerta coined as an advocate for farmworkers. 
In a private ceremony, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, U.S. House Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi and leaders for the state Senate and Assembly gave joint remarks, describing Huerta as “the heart and soul” of America’s Latino community.

Becerra: “Huerta taught a nation that there is a power greater than wealth and stronger than fear: The power of ordinary people who stand together to tear down the walls of injustice. Because she lived, California is more just and America is more free.”

Services honoring Huerta are expected to move to Bakersfield, where a vigil will be held Thursday, followed by a memorial the day after.
See more photos from the service from CalMatters visuals editor Miguel Gutierrez Jr.:
Hundreds of mourners, with some chanting “Sí se puede!,” march down Third Street towards Capitol Mall to commemorate Huerta. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters

Huerta’s hearse, with “Sí Se Puede” flags at the front, sits at Crocker Park in Sacramento. Mourners cried and waved as the procession made its way to the state Capitol. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters

Members of Kalpulli Itzkuauhtli and Xiuhcoatl Danza Azteca perform a ceremony in honor of Huerta at the state Capitol. The scent from the burning copal was heavy in the air as the dancers readied to perform their ceremony. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters



UC wins again against Trump


Tré Willingham works inside a lab in Rowland Hall at UC Irvine on June 15, 2026. Photos by Ariana Drehsler for CalMatters




The Trump administration lost its last attempt to cancel research grants from the University of California after the Supreme Court rejected its request to review rulings that ordered it to continue funding those projects, reports CalMatters’ Mikhail Zinshteyn.
Trump last year issued a series of executive orders to defund so-called diversity, equity and inclusion efforts, including research grants. Between January and July 2025, federal agencies terminated more than $900 million in grants to UC researchers. 
Lawyers for the U.S. Department of Justice argued that agencies had the right to cut the grants because they did not comply with Trump’s executive orders, even though the UC researchers broke no rules in how they used the money. But attorneys for the UC researchers, in a legal brief to the high court, said the move is “a quintessential First Amendment violation.” 
Read more.



And lastly: DAs sue to block Newsom’s death row clemency


An officer opens the gate for an incarcerated person leaving the exercise yard at San Quentin State Prison’s death row in San Quentin on Aug. 15, 2016. Photo by Justin Sullivan, Getty Images




Dozens of California district attorneys filed a lawsuit Monday to stop Newsom’s commutations of over 500 people on death row. The lawsuit claims that the governor abused his power and acted unlawfully by granting prisoners clemency without allowing victims of their crimes the “opportunity to be heard.” Read more from CalMattes’ Nigel Duara.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Kobach’s opinion on phone ban for Kansas schools: Backpacks and lockers aren’t secure enough
description: LAWRENCE — Students and teachers in Kansas public schools have adapted to the new bell-to-bell cellphone ban since the start of the school year. But now, Attorney General Kris Kobach says storing phones in backpacks or lockers doesn’t comply with the ban. Kobach said in an attorney general opinion that backpacks and lockers that are accessible […]
text:
Kris Kobach speaks before President Donald Trump takes the stage at a Nov. 1, 2026, rally in Salina. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)LAWRENCE — Students and teachers in Kansas public schools have adapted to the new bell-to-bell cellphone ban since the start of the school year. But now, Attorney General Kris Kobach says storing phones in backpacks or lockers doesn’t comply with the ban.
Kobach said in an attorney general opinion that backpacks and lockers that are accessible to students during the school day don’t satisfy the bill’s definition of “secure storage” of personal electronic devices. 
“Students’ backpacks are generally accessible to students during the school day, so personal electronic devices would not be stored in an ‘inaccessible location,’ ” Kobach said in the opinion. “Assuming students carry their backpacks at some point during the school day, storage in backpacks is not away from the student’s person.”
Kansas is one of four states to have a bell-to-bell policy with inaccessible storage rules, following passage this year of bipartisan legislation. If backpacks and lockers are considered accessible to students, as Kobach determined, many districts likely aren’t complying with the law. 
Kim Whitman, leader of the Kansas Coalition of the Distraction-Free Schools Policy Project, said many districts are likely scrambling after the clarification from Kobach. 
“They weren’t given the best advice from the beginning and that has set them back,” Whitman said. “There seemed to be a focus on how to get around the law that doesn’t cause any disruption or confrontation with parents, instead of doing what’s best for students and for teachers. When in reality, what we know is students are better off without their phones.”
Sen. Kenny Titus, a Republican from Pottawatomie County, said he asked Kobach for an opinion on the matter after seeing the guidance given to schools by Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly’s administration and by the Kansas Association of School Boards. He said their guidance “seemed to contradict” the legislation.
The Kansas Association of School Boards’s guidance outlines storage solutions for personal devices, including locking personal devices in district-issued bags or pouches upon arrival, turnover of devices to a central location, devices being turned off and stored not on the student’s person and prohibiting students from bringing personal devices into school altogether. 
The KASB document provides pros and cons for each solution, with cons such as cost, burdens on staff and security of student devices. The guidance also says the bill doesn’t create any enforcement measures for districts that don’t comply.
“Fortunately, the legislation does not include enforcement mechanisms to penalize districts found not to be in compliance,” the KASB guidance said. “KASB does not endorse any particular storage solutions. However, our attorneys have fielded many questions over recent weeks concerning this topic and have some observations.”
Leah Fliter, assistant executive director of advocacy and governmental relations for KASB, said the organization opposed the legislation from the beginning and had its concerns about the bill’s language dismissed early on.
She said Kobach’s opinion isn’t binding and doesn’t change KASB’s opinion on the law.
“This opinion doesn’t really plow any new ground,” Fliter said. “We said all along that the way the bill was written, it was going to interfere with local control and that storage in a locker or backpack was probably not going to satisfy the statute.”
Will Lawrence, the governor’s chief of staff, listed in a letter to the Kansas State Department of Education and Kansas State Board of Education four potential storage solutions similar to KASB’s, but said it isn’t an “exhaustive list.”
“While we understand complying with this legislation will be a significant endeavor and require some level of trial and error, the benefits this bill will have for our students and their academic achievement is worth the hard work of implementation,” Lawrence said. “We must do all we can to protect our students and ensure their school days are defined by collaborative learning, not distracting screentime.”
United School Administrators of Kansas Executive Director G.A. Buie said in a video message to superintendents in May not to spend extra money buying storage solutions, adding there are “no consequences for this bill” if districts don’t follow the law. 
Whitman said Buie gave poor advice to districts from the get-go. 
“It was a video clip talking about the cellphone law and how there was no enforcement, so just get something on paper and don’t worry about it, just put those phones in backpacks and call it good,” Whitman said. 
Whitman said students’ phones being inaccessible would ideally place policing personal device usage on administrators rather than teachers, but that it has to start with students’ devices being completely inaccessible. 
“The system in place actually frees up the teachers and puts the burden on the administrators to enforce it,” Whitman said. “I’ve heard nothing but positives from teachers so far. I’ve even had a teacher tell me that he actually enjoys teaching again.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Past rulings, questions of experience dominate SC Supreme Court candidate screenings
description: SC Supreme Court hopefuls responded to criticisms and field questions about past rulings, including a high court case involving race.
text:
South Carolina Judicial Merit Selection Committee Chairman Luke Rankin, R-Myrtle Beach, questions candidates for the state Supreme Court Monday, June 16, 2026, in Columbia, as part of the judicial screening and election process. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — South Carolina Supreme Court hopefuls responded to criticisms ranging from a lack of experience to perceptions of arrogance and fielded questions about past rulings, including a high court case involving race.
The questioning came Monday as the five candidates seeking a 10-year term on the state’s highest court appeared before the panel tasked with screening them for the job.
Five judges so far file to run for SC Supreme Court seat

Those running include:

Administrative Law Court Chief Judge Ralph “Tripp” Anderson
S.C. Appeals Court Judge John Geathers
Judge Eugene “Bubba” Griffith Jr., a Circuit Court judge from Newberry
S.C. Appeals Court Judge Blake Hewitt
Judge Maite Murphy, a Circuit Court judge from Summerville

Each is seeking the opening created after former Justice John Few dropped his bid for re-election in March, a day before the Legislature was scheduled to vote.
Few had become the first sitting justice in more than 20 years to face a challenge to keep his seat. His three opponents included the former leader of the state House.
When it became clear that former Speaker Jay Lucas had sealed up enough votes from legislators to win, Few pulled out, triggering a clause in state law that restarted the process.
Monday’s screenings began with two candidates with the longest careers on South Carolina’s judicial bench. The Legislature first elected Anderson in 1994 and Geathers in 1995 to the Administrative Law Court, which handles public disputes with state agencies.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Race and what’s ‘reasonable’
During the questioning of Geathers, the panel appeared most interested in a dissent written by then-Chief Justice Don Beatty that he signed on to.
Geathers was filling in on the high court for State v. Spears. It was one of roughly a dozen times Geathers has served as a substitute justice.
The 2020 split ruling in question upheld a 30-year sentence for trafficking crack cocaine.
Before the original trial, the attorney for Eric Terrell Spears, a Black man, sought to suppress evidence of the drugs found in his waistband, arguing the 2012 frisking at a bus stop violated Spears’ Fourth Amendment rights against unreasonable search and seizure.
The high court agreed 3-2 with the trial judge, finding Spears voluntarily engaged with the agents and his actions “created a reasonable suspicion that he may have been armed and dangerous,” justifying the pat-down.
Retired SC chief justice tells Black teens diverse perspectives matter: ‘Never be intimidated’

In his dissent, Beatty argued courts should consider a person’s race in determining what’s reasonable.
A “reasonable Black person” would not have felt free to walk away, and Spears’ nervous reaction to officers was normal, he wrote: “An objective eye would acknowledge the fact that African-Americans are being reasonable when they respond in accordance with their collective experiences gained over two hundred years.” The drug evidence should have been suppressed from trial, he concluded.
The chief justice, who was the only Black justice on the high court, selects who fills in when there’s a temporary vacancy or absence for whatever reason.
Had he not chosen Geathers, the state’s lone Black Appeals Court judge, to sit in on that case, Beatty would have been the only racial minority weighing in. And Geathers agreed with Beatty.
Peter Protopapas, a Columbia personal injury lawyer appointed to the 12-member screening panel by Gov. Henry McMaster, asked Geathers whether he thought individual characteristics, such as race, should be taken into account in future cases.
South Carolina Appeals Court Judge John Geathers fields questions Monday, June 16, 2026, in Columbia, as part of the judicial screening and election process. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
Geathers said he remembered the argument being about whether the plainclothes officers had “reasonable suspicion” to follow and stop Spears in the first place, not about Spears’ race.
Asked again by Senate Judiciary Chairman Luke Rankin about the dissent and the studies cited in it, Geathers said he did not recall.
As part of his screening, Geathers received only positive comments from lawyers and citizens who weighed in.
And Christian Stegmaier, a retail and hospitality lawyer in Columbia, praised Geathers’ handling of a case from his Administrative Law Court days.
The 1998 case involved landowners from Newberry County, who were representing themselves in a septic tank permitting dispute with state environmental regulators. Geathers traveled to the property for an in-person explanation from permitters about the denial.
Candidates face criticism, questions of experience
Anderson, on the other hand, faced a rare series of criticisms.
Anonymous complaints from lawyers accused him of being sarcastic in the courtroom and comments submitted from a citizens’ panel claimed he was arrogant. Similar criticisms didn’t come up during his previous hearings before the panel.
Anderson, chief judge of the Administrative Law Court since 2009, has run for an opening on the high court several times.
Responding to the criticism, he said, “The one that really bothers me the most would be the arrogance. I’ve been before this screening committee for over 30 years, and that’s never been raised. I’m the same judge.”
He then went on to talk about his physical disability due to an accident a week before he graduated college and how learning to live as a quadriplegic instilled humility.
Staff also questioned him about what they saw as patterns of cases in which his decisions were reversed on appeal.
Those reversals involved times Anderson didn’t hear cases, believing it didn’t fall within the purview of the Administrative Law Court, as well as times he determined state law was ambiguous on a matter.
What didn’t come up, at least not during the public hearing, were Anderson’s decisions in the high-profile case of an illegal sea wall constructed by millionaire Rom Reddy to guard his Isle of Palms mansion from erosion — a case that led to Reddy’s unsuccessful run for governor earlier this year.
Anderson sided with environmentalists in ruling Reddy would have to take the wall down but dismissed the nearly $300,000 fine Reddy faced. And as the case goes through appeal, the wall can stay up.
South Carolina Circuit Court Judge Bubba Griffith fields questions Monday, June 16, 2026, in Columbia, as part of the judicial screening and election process. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
When it came time to hear from Griffith and Murphy, the panel asked the pair of Circuit Court judges whether they’d enjoy the slower-paced, academic side of the judiciary rather than the hustle and bustle of the lower court.
Griffith, a Circuit Court judge for 22 years, acknowledged he’d need to brush up on opinion writing. Outside of the Supreme Court, he wants to help educate local magistrates, who are appointed by senators and often aren’t lawyers.
“I want to help teach lawyers how to be better lawyers and teach magistrate judges how to be better judges,” he said.
The 62-year-old also acknowledged he wanted to seek the job before retirement. In South Carolina, judges must retire from full-time work the year they turn 72.
Murphy, a magistrate and master-in-equity before the Legislature elected her to the Circuit Court in 2013, said its “always important to evolve, to learn, to grow,” and thinks the Supreme Court would provide that opportunity.
The now 57-year-old previously ran for the Supreme Court to replace Justice Kaye Hearn, who retired after turning 72 in 2022.
South Carolina Circuit Court Judge Maite Murphy fields questions Monday, June 16, 2026, in Columbia, as part of the judicial screening and election process. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
Murphy dropped out in fall 2022, almost two months before screenings began, amid questions about whether electing her to the Supreme Court would put too much judicial power in one couple. At the time, her husband was House Judiciary Chairman Chris Murphy. They later divorced, and he died in July.
Hearn, who Murphy sought to replace, had ascended to the Supreme Court while her husband, state Rep. George Hearn, R-Conway, was in office and a member of the same committee.
On Monday, Murphy fended off anonymous allegations from lawyers that she has been impartial and unprepared for court.
And Hewitt, in his third run for the high court, continued to be dogged by criticisms that he lacks experience.
It’s something he’s faced his entire judicial career after he went straight from private practice to the state Appeals Court in 2020.
As long as the screening panel finds no reason to disqualify any of the candidates, all five will go on to run for election before the General Assembly on March 3, 2027.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: Lame duck ultimatum: Get kratom off Michigan’s store shelves
description: There is always a great deal of lip service about protecting our children. But when it comes down to it in Lansing, political clout and profit seems to  matter more. Children make up a small percentage of our state’s population, but they are 100 percent of our collective future. Eight months have passed since the […]
text:
Liquid kratom extracts and capsules containing 7-OH are displayed for sale at a smoke shop in Buffalo, N.Y. A growing market is prompting state lawmakers to reconsider how the substance should be regulated. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)There is always a great deal of lip service about protecting our children. But when it comes down to it in Lansing, political clout and profit seems to  matter more. Children make up a small percentage of our state’s population, but they are 100 percent of our collective future.
Eight months have passed since the Michigan House of Representatives voted to ban kratom. As the Legislature enters its final lame duck stretch of 2026, an addictive, unregulated substance remains as easy for a teenager to buy as a Snickers bar. Sold in brightly colored packaging — tonics, tablets, powders, gummies, even chocolate bars and honey sticks — at neighborhood gas stations, party stores and smoke shops, kratom and its concentrated cousins, colloquially known as “gas station heroin,” are hiding in plain sight.
Not a harmless herb with a dangerous cousin — one product line, one pathway
The kratom industry wants Michigan to believe there are two separate products: a gentle, centuries-old herbal leaf and a dangerous lab-made outlier. Ban the bad one, they say, and leave the leaf alone.
That is a distinction designed to protect a business model, not our kids.
Kratom-infused drinks are stacked in a refrigerator at a smoke shop in Howard County, Md. (Photo by Amanda Watford/Stateline)
Kratom comes from the Southeast Asian Mitragyna speciosa tree. Its leaf acts on the same brain receptors as opioids, and it is marketed as a pain reliever, an energy and mood booster, and a treatment for anxiety, depression and even withdrawal from heroin and fentanyl. It is habit-forming in its own right.
Manufacturers have also flooded the market with chemically manipulated, concentrated variants such as 7-hydroxymitragynine (7-OH) — a compound present only in trace amounts in the natural leaf but now sold in pills and shots far more potent than morphine. The pharmacological effects of these products, along with their withdrawal symptoms and overdose profiles, closely mirror those of prescription and illicit opioids.
The leaf and the concentrate are not separate worlds. They sit on the same shelves, sold by the same stores, often under the same brand names. The leaf is the on-ramp; the concentrate is where too many people end up. And because there is no state testing or regulatory oversight for any of these products, consumers — especially children — have no way of knowing the potency or chemical makeup of what they are swallowing.
The vulnerability of developing young brains and central nervous systems makes children and teenagers especially susceptible to acute toxicity, severe neurological side effects and rapid dependency.
Today, we are playing Russian roulette with the safety of our children, families and communities.
The data are stark: state lawmakers report that kratom was detected in 995 of nearly 2,000 overdose deaths in Michigan during 2024, alongside a reported 1,200 percent surge in national use driven by accessible, over-the-counter gummies and concentrates.
As a former state superintendent of Michigan’s schools, former state mental health director, and former president and CEO of Detroit Wayne Integrated Health Network (DWIHN), the largest community mental health agency in Michigan, I have had a front-row seat watching children and families devastated by the scourge of addictive drugs.
We are allowing companies to profit off the suffering of children and our fellow citizens.
A Michigan mother’s warning
This past Sunday night, 60 Minutes brought this crisis into living rooms across America, and the human face of the story was one of our own. Correspondent Jon Wertheim profiled Melanie Clark, a Michigan mother of three and trained opera singer. Struggling with postpartum depression and exhaustion, she was drawn in by Instagram ads for a kratom-based “tonic” sold at gas stations near her home.
Notice where her story starts: not with a lab-made 7-OH tablet, but with a kratom drink marketed as a wellness product. Within about three weeks, she felt addicted. After trying to quit, she relapsed and moved on to 7-OH tablets, which landed her in the hospital. Her withdrawal was so severe that her husband had to call the police. Thankfully, she says she is doing much better today.
Melanie’s story should stop every lawmaker in Lansing cold. If kratom can ensnare a grown woman with a supportive family, imagine what it can do to a 15-year-old with a few dollars in their pocket and a gas station on their walk home from school.
Why House Bill 5537 gets it right
In March 2026, the Michigan House passed House Bill 5537 by a vote of 56–48. The bill does what a partial approach cannot: it prohibits growing, synthesizing, distributing and selling kratom in every form — the plant, its leaves, its extracts, and its synthetic and concentrated derivatives — while exempting FDA-approved products. It carries misdemeanor penalties, with stiffer consequences for selling to minors.
Banning only 7-OH would invite a game of chemical whack-a-mole: outlaw one derivative and manufacturers will reformulate the next one, while the leaf products that start people down this road stay on the counter next to the candy.
Getty Images Plus
The bill was quickly sent to the Senate Committee on Government Operations — known around the Capitol as a place for bills to die — and has sat there ever since.
Lansing insiders say there has been heavy pushback from lobbyists for kratom manufacturers and from gas station and party store owners.
Because 2026 marks the end of Michigan’s two-year legislative term, inaction in lame duck is not a harmless pause; it is a fatal reset. If the Senate adjourns without acting, HB 5537 dies, forcing lawmakers to start over in 2027 while another class of middle and high school students is exposed.
Washington is moving backward
Nor can Michigan wait for Washington. As 60 Minutes reported, the federal government announced plans in July to schedule 7-OH as a controlled substance. Then last month, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services reversed course and raised the amount of 7-OH allowed in products roughly twentyfold. Former FDA Commissioner Dr. Marty Makary and former HHS senior adviser Calley Means both told the program they resigned in part because kratom policy was being shaped by business interests rather than public health.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
HHS denies that outside pressure influenced its decision, but 60 Minutes also documented a decade of lobbying money, much of it from the American Kratom Association, aimed at the FDA, HHS, the White House and Congress.
Note what that lobbying protects: the industry’s preferred line is to sacrifice 7-OH and save the leaf. When federal protection is moving backward, states must lead.
A local patchwork is not enough
Communities have stepped up where the state has not. To its credit, Sterling Heights in May became the first city in Michigan to ban the sale and distribution of all kratom products — not just the synthetics — threatening to revoke the licenses of businesses that don’t comply. Plymouth Township has followed with restrictions of its own.
But a municipal ban does little good when a teenager can drive five minutes across a city line to the nearest gas station. Only statewide action can close that loophole and hold predatory distributors accountable.
Michigan is also falling behind. A growing list of states, including Alabama, Arkansas, Indiana, Vermont and Wisconsin, ban kratom outright, and many more restrict sales to minors. Decades ago, Michigan watched the prescription opioid crisis spiral out of control because regulators hesitated while corporations profited from addiction. We cannot afford to repeat that tragedy.
The ask
The American Kratom Association and other opponents argue for age limits and labeling rules instead of prohibition. I understand that some adults say kratom helped them through pain or off other opioids, and their struggles are real. The answer for them is real treatment and FDA-approved medicine — which this bill exempts — not an unregulated product sold beside the Slurpee machine. Labels and age rules on a product no one tests will not keep it out of children’s hands.
Protecting Michigan’s youth is not a Republican or Democratic issue; it is a basic moral obligation.
Gov. Gretchen Whitmer has goodwill to spend and should spend some of it saving children, families and communities. House Speaker Matt Hall (R-Richland Township) and Senate Majority Leader Winnie Brinks (D-Grand Rapids) must rise above partisan gridlock, move HB 5537 across the finish line, and take kratom in all its forms off store shelves before the 2026 session closes.
Our children and families need more than political posturing or infighting. Without action, unnecessary misery, and even death, will be on the hands of our elected officials.

name: California
title: The soil scientist who revolutionized organic strawberry farming in California
description: Joji Muramoto redefined how farmers treated one of California's most chemically intensive crops. His work epitomizes the innovation at risk under hostile immigration policies.
text:
The sun was just starting to emerge through the fog at Hansen Agricultural Experiment Station as Joji Muramoto, 65, pulled two dozen soil sensors out of his SUV to set up his latest field trial. 
When Muramoto first came to this facility east of Oxnard some two decades ago, few people thought his organic method for controlling soilborne diseases in strawberry fields would work. Now, as the specialist for the University of California’s Cooperative Extension program lays out the final field trial before his retirement next summer, the elegant fermentation-based technique is used in at least 11 states and nine other countries — not just on strawberries but increasingly for vegetables and tree crops as well.
Muramoto knelt on the soil in well-worn jeans and dug a hole for one of the sensors, measuring to be sure the bottom was precisely 9½- inches deep. He worked with the sure-handed muscle memory of someone who’s done this thousands of times, and the urgency of someone who knew his work was not yet finished. 
On the drive over from his last experiment, in Coachella, he passed field after field of conventional strawberries, which are still treated with the powerful chemical fumigants that have caused hundreds of acute illnesses in agricultural workers and people living nearby. 
It’s a reminder of why he came to California 30 years ago, and why he started this research in the first place.

When Muramoto was 10 years old, growing up in suburban Tokyo in the early 1970s, he found his 6-year-old sister struggling with a nosebleed that wouldn’t stop. After a scary ambulance ride and a battery of tests, she was diagnosed with leukemia. She was transferred to a pediatric cancer center, but the doctors couldn’t save her. 
Devastated — and worried about how chemical exposure might have impacted her daughter’s health — Muramoto’s mother joined the burgeoning Japanese organic movement. The family became members of a consumer group that had convinced more than a dozen farmers to convert to organic methods by agreeing to purchase their produce. 
It was the beginning of community-supported agriculture and a learning experience for everyone: Muramoto remembers the first box they received contained a miniscule, rough-skinned mandarin orange. 
“It was delicious, but it was not pretty,” he recalled.
During his spring and summer breaks in middle school and high school, Muramoto stayed with the organic farming families to assist with chores. As he weeded and harvested, fed chickens and collected eggs, he saw that the produce was becoming more robust. The farmers had learned the secrets of growing food without chemicals, and as they repeated like a mantra, the key was properly caring for the soil. 
Muramoto was hooked and eager to pursue undergraduate studies in soil science.
Joji Muramoto at the Hansen Agricultural Research and Extension Center in Camarillo on Sept. 24, 2026. Photo by Julie Leopo-Bermudez for CalMatters



Joji Muramoto studies soil-growing practices for crops, such as strawberries, to reduce or eliminate the use of fumigants. Photos by Julie Leopo-Bermudez for CalMatters
He later spent more than a decade in the soil science laboratory at the Tokyo University of Agriculture, where he earned a doctoral degree and ultimately became an assistant professor. Using the new technology of the day — an inductively coupled plasma emission spectrometer — he helped develop a new method for testing soils and crops that could analyze multiple elements at once, so farmers could quickly get a sense for whether their fields might be low in calcium or high in phosphorus. 
He was delighted when these new testing methods proved helpful to the organic farmers who first taught him about the importance of soil health. 
But few other researchers in the soil science lab were collaborating with organic farmers. Housed within the department of agricultural chemistry, the lab’s primary function was to prescribe fertilizers. Many of the program’s graduates went to work in the industry, and farming without chemicals was not considered feasible by the influential senior faculty.
Drawn to UC Santa Cruz research
For Muramoto, constantly cutting against this grain took a toll. When he landed in the hospital with a stomach ulcer, he realized it was time for a change.
While Muramoto was recovering, a colleague tipped him off to the field of agroecology, which focused entirely on solving farmers’ problems with biological strategies rather than chemical ones. As Muramoto pored over the references his colleague shared, he became engrossed in a paper written by UC Santa Cruz professor Steve Gliessman, who was researching organic production methods for strawberries. 
Muramoto wrote to Gliessman, who agreed to sponsor him as a visiting scholar. He quit his faculty job in Japan, and in 1996, the whole Muramoto family arrived in Santa Cruz: Joji, his pregnant wife and their 2-year-old son.
Muramoto searched for research he could do to advance agroecology in the Santa Cruz area, working with Gliessman and local farmers. Initially, he focused on nutrient management, given his background in chemistry.
Meanwhile, Muramoto and his family tried to establish some stability. He had no idea how long his visa might be extended, and his position was not salaried. He had to support himself with whatever grants he and Gliessman could scrounge up and the savings and retirement he’d brought from Japan. 
A year into the job, his elder son was diagnosed with autism. To Muramoto’s amazement, Santa Cruz County enrolled his son in a specialized public preschool for children with autism, then provided a one-on-one aide once the child was ready for kindergarten. The family received state benefits to buy milk and bread. Overwhelmed and grateful for the support provided by their new community, Muramoto redoubled his efforts to give back through research that could support organic farmers.

The aha moment
In 2001, the leaves on some of the strawberries at the UC Santa Cruz organic farm started to brown and wilt. One by one, the plants shriveled up and died. The farm had been stricken with verticillium wilt, a fungal disease in the soil. The farm manager, Jim Leap, had been careful to rotate crops to try to starve out any disease outbreaks: After growing strawberries, he wouldn’t plant them again in the same field for seven years. 
But verticillium was wily. It could feed on more than 400 plants (including tomatoes, lettuce and potatoes) and survive in the soil for up to five years without a host plant. Leap asked the research team for help. 
A visiting Dutch plant pathologist suggested they try a new method that had recently been developed in the Netherlands: spreading carbon-rich material on the soil, saturating the ground with water, then covering it with a plastic tarp for several weeks. If they could create enough fermentation, the Dutch researchers had found, they could suppress disease. 
When Muramoto dug into the research, he was surprised to learn that a team in Japan had independently developed a similar process. He and professor Carol Shennan (who had succeeded Gliessman as director of the university’s Center for Agroecology) combined the most promising aspects of the Dutch and Japanese methods to see if they could curb the verticillium on the farm.
Muramoto threw himself into the details of the new method, which he and Shennan dubbed “anaerobic soil disinfestation,” or ASD. He had a ready carbon source: the remnants of the cover crop that the farm had used to recharge the soil. He worked with Leap to spread the cover crop residue on the trial field, then doused the field with water and covered it with plastic tarps. 
No luck. So he tried again. And again. Still, verticillium populations remained stubborn. 
Muramoto decided to try one last field trial, this time with a combination of cover crop residue and rice bran. When he took the tarp off and tested the soil, he could hardly believe it. The disease was almost completely gone. 

Joji Muramoto holds sensors used to measure soil conditions at the Hansen Agricultural Research and Extension Center in Camarillo on Sept. 24, 2026. Photo by Julie Leopo-Bermudez for CalMatters

As the late summer sun beamed down, Muramoto had an aha moment. The difference had been the soil temperature. With enough heat, they had a way to control verticillium, without applying any chemicals.
Confronting the ‘fumigants or nothing’ mantra
Just a few miles from the UC Santa Cruz farm, conventional strawberry farmers in the Salinas Valley had their own solution to verticillium — the powerful fumigant methyl bromide. Because this chemical was damaging the ozone layer, however, international protocols required it be phased out. Beset with complaints from the strawberry industry, the U.S. Department of Agriculture launched a grant program to encourage researchers to develop alternative fumigants. 
When Muramoto and Shennan decided to apply for the grant, they knew it would be a longshot. The reviewers were expecting research proposals focused on alternative chemicals, not an alternative to using any chemicals at all. 
“‘Fumigants or nothing’ was really the mantra at the time,” Shennan said, “and so to try something this different was really a challenge.” 
Their first proposal fell flat, but in 2007, they received three years of funding from the USDA, plus an additional three years of funding from the California Strawberry Commission. Now their ASD technique would be put to the test on commercial farms.
Convincing commercial strawberry growers in Salinas, Santa Maria and Oxnard — some of the most expensive farmland in the country — to try a method developed on the famously countercultural UC Santa Cruz organic farm was a tough sell. 
“(Muramoto) approached me at this meeting in Watsonville with this goofy technology, nobody knew what it was,” recalled Oleg Daugovish, an advisor for the UC Cooperative Extension program and one of Muramoto’s earliest collaborators. “But he’s a persistent guy.”
Muramoto knew he’d need to demonstrate the method on working farms, but that meant finding farmers willing to participate. He started with just a couple farms on the first grant, which yielded promising enough results to spur another round of funding. 
He expanded the study, with 10 replicated-field trials up and down the California coast. On average, marketable strawberry yields on the ASD-treated fields were nearly on par (99%) with yields on the fields treated with chemical fumigants. In addition to suppressing pathogens, it seemed the rice bran was acting as a slow release fertilizer to boost strawberry growth. 
Then Muramoto got a big break.
In 2013, Glen Hasegawa, a prominent strawberry grower in Oxnard, agreed to host a 5-acre trial of ASD, on a field so saturated with disease that he’d all but given up on it. Hasegawa’s problem wasn’t verticillium but charcoal rot, caused by another fungal pathogen that had been spreading across California. He told Muramoto he’d be happy if ASD could increase his strawberry yields by 20%. 
As a board member of the California Strawberry Commission, Hasegawa was known statewide, and all eyes were on this strange new alternative to fumigation. He spread rice bran, mixed it into the sandy soil, covered the beds with plastic mulch, and turned on the irrigation. After three weeks, Hasegawa punched holes in the tarps and planted strawberries. At harvest time, he could hardly believe it: his yields had doubled. He increased his ASD trial to 50 acres the following season, and the method took off around the state. 
“That was a big turning point,” Muramoto said. “Word of mouth spread, and a lot of growers started to use rice bran.”
Joji Muramoto at the Hansen Agricultural Research and Extension Center in Camarillo on Sept. 24, 2026. Photo by Julie Leopo-Bermudez for CalMatters
Over the course of the next decade, organic strawberry production in California increased from just over 3,000 acres to nearly 5,800 acres, almost 14% of the state’s total strawberry production. Nearly half of these acres were treated with rice bran.
Muramoto saw that the success of the new method had spurred the expansion of organic production across the strawberry sector, among the most chemically intensive crops in the state. He calculated that the method had removed 565,492 pounds of fumigants from agricultural fields, reducing health risks to workers and nearby residents.
“When my sister passed, these kinds of relationships (between agricultural chemicals and health risks) were not very clear scientifically,” Muramoto told me, “but these days we have more data showing the direct relationship, the causality. Now it’s known.” 
He pointed me to a host of epidemiological research linking pesticide exposure with health impacts to children and pregnant women, including a 2020 study conducted by researchers at UCLA and USC which found that exposure to certain pesticides during pregnancy may increase the risk of childhood leukemia. 

In 2019, the University of California created the first Cooperative Extension specialist position dedicated to organic agriculture. When the hire was announced in May, no one was surprised they’d chosen Muramoto. This was the work he had already been doing, now for more than two decades. After 23 years on soft money, relying on grants to support his immigrant family, he finally had a secure, permanent job.  
Muramoto has been busy the past seven years, visiting organic farmers across the state and designing research to address their challenges. Rice bran’s gotten pricy, so he’s been trialing variations of ASD that use wheat bran and dried food waste instead — with promising results. And he’s trying to stay one step ahead of the latest fungal pathogen, Fusarium oxysporum, which behaves differently than verticillium. 
Change that takes a lifetime of devotion
As Muramoto looks ahead to his retirement next July, I asked him what he hopes will be his legacy. 
He laughed. “I have no idea,” he said. 
But the next day, he sent me a quote from Kanzo Uchimura’s book, “The Greatest Legacy,” challenging the idea that a person’s key contributions could be captured in tangible accomplishments, like publications or resources.
“The greatest legacy that all of us can leave for future generations” Uchimura wrote, is “a person living their life with courage and integrity.” 
Reading these words brought me back to the summer of 2010 when I worked with Muramoto in his lab, as one of more than 150 students he mentored over the course of his career. As Muramoto patiently explained the research design and lab protocols, I remember being awestruck by the sheer volume of it all: the neatly organized sensors, the impeccable field data spreadsheets and the many, many soil samples. 
This project, I remember thinking, will take an entire lifetime.
Working with Muramoto showed me the best of what our public universities can produce when we invest in them: painstaking, long-term science that can make a real difference in people’s lives. It made me forever appreciate the way that California has always benefited from the innovative contributions of immigrants, and what we stand to lose if we make it harder for folks to come here. 
Muramoto’s devotion to developing fumigant alternatives introduced me to a form of change and social action that is underappreciated but so crucial in our current moment: a humble, quiet constancy that keeps chipping away at a problem and never gives up.
