name: National
title: States split over EPA’s proposal to drop greenhouse gas rules for power plants
description: States are divided over the Trump administration’s proposal to repeal remaining greenhouse gas standards for power plants, while medical groups warn of public health dangers. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency released a proposal that contends it doesn’t have the authority to regulate power plant greenhouse gas emissions to address global climate chang[...]
text:
A coal-fired power plant operates in Centralia, Washington. States are divided over the Trump administration’s proposal to repeal remaining greenhouse gas power plant standards. (Photo by the Washington Department of Ecology via Washington State Standard)States are divided over the Trump administration’s proposal to repeal remaining greenhouse gas standards for power plants, while medical groups warn of public health dangers.
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency released a proposal that contends it doesn’t have the authority to regulate power plant greenhouse gas emissions to address global climate change concerns. This would rescind the agency’s own findings in 2015 that it had the authority to do so under a section of the Clean Air Act. 
If finalized and upheld by courts, the move would repeal remaining power plant greenhouse-gas emissions regulations for fossil fuel-fired electric generating units. The agency said it aims to maintain affordability and reliability of energy supplies. 
It follows a final EPA rule that went into effect Monday that partially repeals 2024 emissions standards for fossil fuel-fired power plants as well as requirements that states develop related plans.
The proposed rule would go even further. A comment period for that measure closed earlier this month, generating over 165,000 comments, including from states, health and environmental groups, and private citizens. States, public health and environmental groups have also filed legal challenges to the EPA’s rollbacks. 
Some states said the EPA’s regulatory authority over fossil fuel emissions is overreach and would harm their economies, while others said such federal regulations are needed as states, tribes and local governments grapple with the health and costs of air pollution and climate change.
Trump is forcing coal plants to stay open. It could cost customers billions.

In a joint comment submitted last week, the attorneys general of 22 mostly Democratic-leaning states plus Washington, D.C., and officials from New York City, Denver, Chicago and California’s Bay Area wrote that climate change is costly to state and local governments and imposes public health dangers. 
In the over-160-page letter, the states pointed to a consensus study report from the National Academies of Science, Engineering, and Medicine last year that concluded that human activity-initiated greenhouse gas emissions will lead to more climate change, “with the severity of expected change increasing with every ton of greenhouse gases emitted.”
The attorneys general wrote that EPA is pushing its proposal despite such “unequivocal evidence, and the increasingly devastating climate harms” that state and local governments experience. They added that the proposal “has no basis in fact or law, would result in large-scale emission increases that will harm the States and Local Governments, and is an unlawful abdication of EPA’s responsibility under the Clean Air Act to protect public health and welfare.”
But the attorneys general of West Virginia and 24 other largely Republican-leaning states  contended that the proposal “properly reverses course on past EPA attempts to reshape the Nation’s electricity-generating sector.”
It would “allow States to secure affordable, reliable, and environmentally responsible energy for their residents,” they added.
North Dakota, which signed on to that letter, also submitted its own comment saying it strongly supports the supplemental proposal. The state noted that it has a specific interest in the issue, since it collects a coal conversion tax when power is generated from coal within the state, which then helps pay for school districts and other government services. 
Supreme Court takes up climate case testing local lawsuits against oil companies

The National Tribal Air Association, an organization of 162 tribes focused on air quality management policies and programs for American Indian and Alaska Native tribes, groups that have been disproportionately affected by emissions, submitted a comment opposing EPA’s actions.
“Many fossil fuel-fired electric generating units are located on or near American Indian and Alaska Native communities, and Tribes and Tribal members may disproportionately bear the public health and environmental consequences of the increased greenhouse gas and other emissions that this proposal would permit,” the association wrote.
Carrie Jenks, executive director of the Environmental & Energy Law Program at Harvard Law School, noted that some ongoing court cases may affect the EPA rules. Jenks also said that states that support EPA’s authority to regulate greenhouse gases are typically the ones that also support their own authority to regulate them within their own programs.
“Then there are groups of states that want EPA’s authority to be limited, if not eliminated,” adding that others argue that states can’t regulate their own sources of greenhouse gases.
Over 70 medical and public health organizations also submitted comments in opposition to the rollbacks. The groups included the American Medical Association, the American Lung Association, and several state American Academy of Pediatrics chapters, who argued the changes would harm the health of children and other vulnerable groups. 
“Children, older adults, people who work outside, individuals with preexisting health conditions or who are pregnant, low-wealth communities and communities of color often experience disproportionate health harms stemming from climate change and extreme weather events,” the groups wrote.
Stateline reporter Nada Hassanein can be reached at nhassanein@stateline.org.

name: Maryland Matters
title: State eyes restart of American Legion Bridge replacement, Capital Beltway widening
description: State transportation officials appear ready to test industry interest again on a joint venture to replace the American Legion Bridge and widen part of the Capital Beltway in Montgomery County that could be funded through a public-private partnership.
text:
Traffic congestion along Capital Beltway including the American Legion Bridge continued to be a concern. A memo obtained by Maryland Matters suggessts state officials are looking to restart a widening project proposed six years ago and possibly partner with a private contractor to build it. (File photo by Bruce DePuyt/Maryland Matters)State transportation officials appear ready to test industry interest again on a joint venture to replace the American Legion Bridge and widen a portion of the Capital Beltway in Montgomery County.
An internal Department of Transportation memo obtained by Maryland Matters says one option under consideration is seeking a partner for a new Public-Private Partnership — commonly known as a P3.
A P3 had been proposed for the project when Gov. Wes Moore (D) first entered office in 2023, but the deal fell through as the new administration questioned the benefit to the state. State transportation officials, who confirmed the authenticity of the memo, were quick to say that no decisions have been made, but that a P3 is one of the options actively under consideration.
“It’s just to get more information out into the public domain about what we expect in terms of delivering the project, and it sets the stage for us to begin to have conversations with developers … later this month into December about options for delivering this project in a way that’s going to meet Maryland’s needs and best serve the public interest,” Transportation Secretary Katie Thomson said on Monday.
The memo lays out a timeline with an industry forum and one-on-one meetings with potential contractors as the first stage, possibly by the end of the year. That would be followed by applications for P3 candidate concepts, possibly in the first part of 2027.
The Board of Public Works could be asked to designate the project a P3 in mid to late 2027, and the state could close on the financial agreement by early 2029, according to the draft memo.
As costs balloon, state officials pitch Key Bridge project to key federal lawmakers

The memo and transportation officials caution that there has been no decision “to deliver the project as a P3 or proceed with any solicitation.” But state officials acknowledge the fastest and most likely path would be to partner with a consortium that would build and profit from the project.
The project laid out in the memo is trimmed down from the $7.6 billion plan that was eyed when Moore took office, but officials say it will still be in the billions. Despite the expense, there is interest at the state and federal level to restart the project.
Thomson said she is optimistic about receiving federal grant money.
The state applied for a grant through the federal Bridge Infrastructure program, requesting $864 million to be put toward eight spans on Interstate 495, including the American Legion Bridge. The route coincides with the widening project.
“It is an important down payment on advancing the project itself, it allows us to to cover costs that would not be recoverable if we pursue a P3, like the right of way,” Thomson said.
The federal money would be coupled with state funds previously earmarked for the project
Congestion and safety issues
Replacing the aging American Legion Bridge is seen as a priority for easing congestion and improving safety.
The bridge, built in 1962, is considered to be at or near the end of its useful life. Nearly a quarter-million vehicles use the bridge each day. In all, state officials estimate there are 12 hours of congestion on the bridge daily.
“It is considered the worst bottleneck in the state for freight mobility,” said State Highway Administrator Will Pines. “All those Amazon trucks and the packages that people get every day are greatly impacted for this interstate corridor.”
Over a three-year period, the state recorded 1,000 crashes along the stretch of the proposed highway widening. One third of those involved an injury or fatality. Pines said transportation officials estimate they can reduce those injuries by as much as 28% if the project is completed.
The pre-solicitation memo restarts a conversation on a project that was essentially mothballed nearly four years ago. It also comes after Maryland officials have had a chance to talk with other states “to kind of learn how they’ve done innovative financing for large similar projects,” Pines said.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“The next step for us is to engage industry through market soundings to really understand the right structure” if a P3 were to be done, Pines said, “which again, as the secretary said, that’s not decided by this document.”
“I think the timeline in the document reflects the funding that we think could be available from a P3,” Pines said. “Certainly, if we brought public funding forward as fast as that assumption, then we would be able to meet a similar delivery schedule.”
Thomson agreed, calling a P3 “a more viable option, assuming we can get the terms and it it meets the needs that we described earlier. But if that does not appear to be the best approach, then we will work with the governor and the General Assembly to pursue public funding.”
Costs less but still ‘in the billions’
The widening of portions of the Capital Beltway in Maryland and replacement of the American Legion Bridge were first proposed roughly six years go by Republican Gov. Larry Hogan.
The original $7.6 billion plan called for construction of toll lanes to widen the Capital Beltway along a 15-mile stretch including the American Legion Bridge and Interstate 270. At the time, it was considered to be the largest public-private partnership project in the country.
A consortium led by Australia-based Transurban would have built and maintained the project and recouped costs from tolls over a 50-year period. The company has built similar toll lane facilities in Virginia. After 50 years, the entire project would have reverted to state government control.
“It was a really, really large program that frankly had a lot of challenges with it,” Pines said.
Moore entered office agreeing that congestion in the area was a problem, but his administration had questions about the proposed P3 deal. Transurban ultimately withdrew from the project. Moore later told reporters he did not oppose P3s, just “dumb P3s.”
Pines called the new vision for the project “a more truncated” version of the 2023 plan, The new plan calls for widening a 6.5-mile stretch to the I-270 spur.
“We did truncate the limits to the spur because previously the biggest controversy and sort of distaste for those lanes was really primarily in the Rockville area,” Pines said. “We worked with the mayor of Rockville and others to say, ‘This is something that may be there for the future, but for right now, we don’t need to jam a solution that you’re not looking for.'”
Proposed six-year transportation plan focuses on priorities, not new projects

Pines said a cost estimate at this stage on the truncated project is difficult, but he believes it would be less than the cost of the original project, even with the sharp increases in construction costs seen by MDOT over the last few years.
“I would say it’s definitely in the billions,” he said. “We’re not expecting it to be $7 billion because of the truncated limits, but it’s certainly a big project, and we will want to do updated cost estimates given today’s market conditions as we work towards making that delivery decision.”
Currently there is $60 million in the state’s annual transportation plan for early work on the project.
“We will continue to evaluate financing options for the bridge P3,” Thomson said last week. “As the governor has said, it’s one option as long as it’s an option that’s in the public interest. So we continue to evaluate that. But it’s really a decision for the governor and the General Assembly to make about how they want to fund these projects.”
A ‘bad rap’
But not everyone thinks P3s are a good deal for taxpayers.
Gary V. Hodge, a transportation advocate, said he worries that state officials will be seduced by P3 agreements in order to move big projects.
“I suspect that cutting deals … will mean that Maryland loses some of its autonomy and decision-making authority on transportation on our highways,” Hodge said. “So, there’s a difficult negotiation to be had there.”
Pines acknowledged the negative views some have on such agreements, but pointed to P3 agreements on projects including the Seagirt Marine Terminal and travel plazas along Interstat 95 as successes.
“Sometimes P3s can get a bad rap, but when they’re done well, done correctly, when risk is managed appropriately and the contracts are structured right, they can work and be really advantageous for the state. And we’ve seen that in several cases in Maryland,” he said.
Pines had previously said that similar projects in Georgia, Tennessee and Virginia were potential models. Those projects were based on fixed prices to build rather than a progressive model, where costs can increase as the project is built.
“We would say it’s a lesson learned that the progressive model that was attempted previously had a lot of risks that were left open,” Pines said. “I think that we want to resolve issues like right of way, utilities, and making sure that things like the design in Virginia are resolved that would allow us to move towards a fixed price rather than leaving a lot to be negotiated as an afterthought.”
Officials have also learned lessons from the Purple Line light rail project and its delays and major cost overruns.
‘The state is broke’
Thomson and Pines repeatedly stressed that a P3 is not the only financing option.
“The state could come up with additional revenues,” Thomson said when asked about the project last week.
Given the state’s financial position, that seems more difficult.
“The fundamental point … is that the state is broke. The state has no financing capacity in the transportation trust fund,” said Hodge. “So, anything that’s done capital-wise, and we’re talking a huge swath of projects — we’re talking about everything from the Red Line in Baltimore to my project in Southern Maryland, the Southern Maryland Rapid Transit Project, the Key Bridge, the American Legion Bridge, on and on — the state has absolutely no money for any of these projects in the capital fund.”
Thomson, in a letter to county officials last week, reiterated that her agency would focus on existing projects and maintenance over new projects.
“One of the things that we intend to work with the General Assembly on in this next session is sufficient, predictable, and sustainable funding for the transportation trust fund that would allow us to continue to invest in critical capital investment projects across the system,” Thomson said Monday.
Pines said relying on traditional public funding of the project based on current finances would force the state to reprioritize projects in its six-year program.
“There’s a lot of other competing needs,” Pines said. “It’s important to us that if a P3 is considered, that we actually make sure that it’s a smart decision, not just a hold your nose and take it. We want to make sure we get this thing right and that we make an intelligent, well informed, deliberative decision.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: A subtle shift for Moore, partisan crowing in nonpartisan races, more in political notes
authors: Bryan P. Sears, William J. Ford
description: Gov. Wes Moore makes a subtle change in his response to a possible presidential candidacy, partisan groups claim victory in supposedly nonpartisan school board races, and Hugo E. Cantu joins the Chamber of Commerce staff, in political notes.
text:
Gov. Wes Moore (D) speaks to reporters after his debate with Republican gubernatorial nominee Dan Cox on Oct. 6, 2026, at Maryland Public Television. He dodged questions then about whether he would serve a full four-year term as governor. (Photo by Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Gov. Wes Moore has gone from the prospective candidate who can’t say no, to the prospective candidate who won’t say yes — yet — as he continues to face questions about his political future.
Since he was first elected in 2022 as Maryland’s first Black governor, speculation has swirled over whether Moore would run for president. Moore has offered a variety of answers over the years, but never flat-out said no to a White House bid.
Over the weekend, there was a subtle shift in the answer.
He’s not saying he’s running.
He’s also not saying he’s not running.
“The honest answer is I don’t know. I’m still sorting it out,” Moore said during an interview with Chuck Todd Sunday on the online platform Noosphere.
Moore isn’t laying low while he works it out. The governor remains a regular on national news programs. He’s also traveled the country the last four years raising money for himself and helping other candidates. Last week, he announced he was releasing a book in March — the timing seen as the standard precursor for governors and others who are testing the waters.
He’s also faced the repeated local and national scrutiny of his resume and personal story that comes with a candidate on the rise politically.
The author Wes Moore: Book on ‘healing a divided nation’ set for March release

“Sometimes I think to myself, I’m a kid who, at 11 years old, had handcuffs on my wrists, right? I was raised by an immigrant single mother. She didn’t get her first job that gave her benefits after my dad died until I was 14 years old,” Moore told Todd during an interview recorded in Annapolis.
“I’m the only governor in this country who graduated from a from a two-year college, I joined the Army at 17 years old. Like this is not some predestined thing,” he said. “And in fact, five years ago, I was polling at 1% when I was running for governor, and I was just trying to figure out how can I get this state to care about child poverty. That was my goal. That’s what I wanted to accomplish, right?”
Moore told Todd the decision he has to make is personal and has to take into consideration the needs of his teenage daughter and son. Despite the traditional start of the presidential cycle soon after the midterm elections, Moore said he has no timeline for a decision.
“I don’t know if I put enough thought into what is … too early or too late or whatever like that. I’m sure other folks have,” he said.
Partisans claim victory in nonpartisan school board races
Although Maryland’s school board races are designated as nonpartisan, it doesn’t come across that way in many contests. And, as in other political contests, the two sides can look at the same event and come away with different interpretations.
Case in point: Both the Maryland State Education Association and the 1776 Project PAC were claiming victory in school board races this year.
The teachers union released a post-election analysis Monday that said 32 of the 47 candidates it endorsed won their general election races against “extremist” opponents.
For example, the teacher’s union endorsed Omar Lazo who defeated Brenda Diaz in Montgomery County. Diaz is a former public school teacher in the county who resigned four years ago, after refusing to follow mask mandates in 2021. She was supported by the county’s Republican Party.
Lazo garnered 51% of the total vote, compared to Diaz’s 48%, according to the state Board of Elections.
In Calvert County, Dona Cox Ostenso captured the second and final spot on the school board with 14,953 votes, 258 votes ahead of Board President Jana Post, who is listed among the leaders with the county’s Republican Party.
“Voters roundly rejected candidates who focused on politicizing classrooms and banning books,” MSEA President Paul Lemle said in a statement. “Our union supported candidates who focused on the things our students and educators really need, like making sure our schools are safe, welcoming, and properly funded —and voters overwhelmingly agreed.”

But the more conservative-leaning 1776 Project PAC also proclaimed success with endorsements of eight candidates – with three in Harford County, two in Talbot County and one each in Baltimore, Somerset and Worcester counties.
One of the endorsed candidates in Harford County was Melissa Hahn, who won her reelection by 3,085 votes. Talbot County candidate Mike Butler got 1,625 votes to 775 for school Board President Emily L. Jackson. The 1776 Project labeled Jackson “as woke.”
“The results mark a significant win for the 1776 Project PAC’s efforts to support conservative candidates in school board elections and shift the balance of power in local education,” the group said in a statement Thursday.
Chamber adds Cantu to government relations staff
The Maryland Chamber of Commerce announced Monday that it has added Hugo E. Cantu as its new director of government affairs ahead of the 2027 General Assembly.
Cantu had been director of government affairs for Apartment and Office Building Association, and had worked before that as senior staff to council members in Prince George’s and Montgomery counties. He also has experience in Annapolis, having worked with the Ways and Means and Economic Matters committees, according to a release from the chamber.
At the Chamber, Cantu will lead advocacy on key policy issues and work alongside Senior Vice President of Government Affairs Grason Wiggins. He succeeds Hannah Allen, who served most recently at the chamber’s senior director of government affairs.
“Hugo understands how state and local policy decisions affect businesses and the communities they serve,” Wiggins said in the announcement. “We’re excited to have him on the team as we prepare for the 2027 legislative session and the work ahead.”
Cantu said his parents came to Maryland from Chihuahua, Mexico, for the opportunities here. “That experience shapes why I care so deeply about Maryland’s economic future,” said Cantu, adding that he was honored to join the chamber.
Cantu earned a bachelor’s degree in public policy, with a minor in real estate development from the University of Maryland, College Park, and an associate’s degree in business administration from Montgomery College. He has served as president of the University of Maryland School of Public Policy Alumni Board and as a member of the school’s Board of Governors.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Georgia begins construction on new psychiatric hospital for prisoners
description: Georgia has officially broken ground on a new $409 million forensic psychiatric hospital — the first to be built in more than 50 years — aimed at serving the more than 800 Georgians who are currently housed in the state’s criminal justice system while awaiting critical mental health services.  Georgia is building first state psychiatric […]
text:
Hard hats, shovels and construction equipment  sit on the site of what will become a $409 million forensic psychiatric hospital. Maya Homan/Georgia RecorderGeorgia has officially broken ground on a new $409 million forensic psychiatric hospital — the first to be built in more than 50 years — aimed at serving the more than 800 Georgians who are currently housed in the state’s criminal justice system while awaiting critical mental health services. 
Georgia is building first state psychiatric hospital since landmark disability case

State lawmakers announced plans to construct the 300-bed hospital earlier this year, with proponents arguing that the facility will help relieve pressure on county jails across Georgia, where many people with severe mental health issues end up waiting for services. 
The hospital is intended to ensure that Georgians in the criminal justice system who need psychiatric treatment can be seen more quickly. It will serve those who are awaiting competency evaluations to see if they can stand trial, as well as those who are found not guilty of a crime by reason of insanity.
At a Monday groundbreaking ceremony in DeKalb County, Department of Behavioral Health and Developmental Disabilities Commissioner Kevin Tanner, called the project “one of the most significant investments in behavioral health infrastructure” in Georgia history.
“You may never know the family who spent years searching for answers, or the struggles that preceded a person’s involvement with the criminal justice system,” he said. “But I can tell you, every person has a story. And for some of the people who will one day walk through the doors of this hospital, the care they receive here may change how their story unfolds.” 
A mock-up shows what Georgia’s $409 million forensic psychiatric hospital will look like. Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
The new facility is expected to open in 2029.
Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle gathered to mark the occasion. Rep. Mary Margaret Oliver, a Decatur Democrat, said the new hospital was long overdue.
“Mental illness treatment isn’t best delivered in jails,” she said. “This is a big step forward, and as always, we have more important work to do.”
She added that elected officials should take additional steps to ensure that Georgians struggling with mental health issues have the support they need, including enforcing Georgia’s mental health parity laws.
Outgoing state Sen. Blake Tillery, a Vidalia Republican who helped secure funding for the project, emphasized that there is still more work to be done in upcoming legislative sessions to ensure that the facility serves its intended purpose.
State Sen. Blake Tillery, a Vidalia Republican, speaks at a groundbreaking ceremony for Georgia’s $409 million forensic psychiatric hospital . Maya Homan/Georgia Recorder
“The real work actually starts when the bricks are done being laid,” he said, addressing his fellow lawmakers.
“Let’s please make sure we’re pushing this forward, that we’re staffing it adequately. It will be a whole lot more than $409 million. And let’s make sure that we prioritize that when we’re prioritizing other things that will move forward in the next General Assembly.”
However, advocates for those with disabilities have expressed concerns about the use of institutionalization for people with severe mental health issues. The new facility was announced within a week of a federal judge releasing the state from a portion of the 2010 settlement known as the Olmstead agreement, which required the state to provide community-based care to people with disabilities. The agreement stemmed from a landmark 1999 Supreme Court ruling that declared unjustified institutionalization of those with disabilities to be a violation of the Americans with Disabilities Act.
D’Arcy Robb, executive director of the Georgia Council on Developmental Disabilities, said she understood the need for the new facility.
Brick and mortar reminders of Georgia’s mistreatment of psychiatric patients could be erased soon

“We are certainly not going to argue that folks experiencing a severe persistent mental illness belong in jail,” she said. 
But she worries about the potential for abuse and neglect of patients that can happen in large institutional facilities.
“I think that we just need to be really mindful as a state, knowing that there is a history right here in our state, of safety systems in these institutional settings really breaking down,” she said.
Robb also said she’d like to see lawmakers invest in more “upstream” solutions and early interventions that could prevent individuals and their families from having to navigate the criminal justice system.
“By the time you get to that point of needing that, I’d like to go five steps back and five years back and see what could we have done to have prevented that in the first place,” she said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: 5th, 6th District runoff candidates say they’ve seen surge in campaign donations
description: Candidates in Louisiana’s congressional runoff elections say they have seen a surge in campaign fundraising for the Dec. 12 runoff.
text:
State Rep. Pat Moore, D-Monroe, a candidate in the runoff for Louisiana's 5th Congressional District, speaks Monday, Nov. 16. 2026, during a candidates forum the Baton Rouge Press Club held at Drusilla's Restaurant. (Photo by Julie O'Donoghue/Louisiana Illuminator)Candidates in Louisiana’s congressional runoff elections say they have seen a surge in campaign fundraising for the Dec. 12 runoff. 

Chauna Banks, a Democrat and former East Baton Rouge Metropolitan Council member, and state Sen. Blake Miguez, R-New Iberia, will face each other in a runoff election for the 6th District. 
State Reps. Gabe Firment, R-Pollock, and Pat Moore, D-Monroe, are competing for the 5th District seat. 
Moore said her campaign had raised at least $1 million since the Nov. 3 election, when she and Firment emerged from a nine-person field. She received 59,000 donations over a weeklong period, according to her campaign. 

“It will help me get advertising out. It will help me get messages out to the people, let them know I’m in this race,” Moore said Monday at a Baton Rouge Press Club candidates’ forum. 
Banks joined Moore at the forum. Firment said he had a conflicting fundraising, and Miguez declined the invitation.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The campaigns for Banks and Firment also said they have seen large increases in fundraising since the general election, though they didn’t provide specific campaign cash estimates. 

“The fundraising has been the best of Gabe’s career by far,” Firment spokesman Bruce Harvie said in an interview. 
The Miguez campaign reported an “uptick” in donations as well, spokesman Chris Pack said.
All four candidates will have to share more information about their campaign fundraising and spending by Nov. 30, when their next round of campaign finance reports, covering the period from Oct. 15 to Nov. 22, will be due. 
A handful of congressional seats remain undecided in other states where votes are still being tabulated from the Nov. 3 election. The two Louisiana races are outliers because they require  runoffs. U.S. House candidates in all parties were placed on the Nov. 3 ballot after Gov. Jeff Landry rescheduled party primaries earlier in the year to allow legislators to redraw Louisiana’s congressional districts. 

The lack of competition for national political resources and donations is likely benefitting the Louisiana candidates who remain, according to Banks. 
“We are getting calls from all over the country,” she said at the forum. “We may be getting a little leftover money, but all money is good money in the case we’re in.” 
Banks and Moore struggled to raise money ahead of the Nov. 3 election. 

Banks said she hadn’t raised or spent more than $5,000 on her 6th District campaign as of Oct. 15. It was such a small sum that she wasn’t required to file a campaign finance disclosure report with the Federal Election Commission. By comparison, Miguez’s campaign collected a field-leading $7.7 million, including $3.5 million Miguez personally loaned to his campaign, according to his federal report.

Moore’s campaign raised only $23,000 in the same period, approximately $11,300 of which came from a series of personal loans, according to her federal campaign finance forms. Firment had raised $454,000 by the same deadline. Both runoff candidates were far behind the biggest spender in the 5th District field, state Rep. Michael Echols, who raised $3.9 million and put $2.3 million into his fourth-place finish.
The Republican candidates are heavily favored to win both seats, given that the 5th and 6th districts were drawn last spring to specifically favor GOP candidates. But the two Democrats won more votes than any other candidates in their respective primaries in spite of being short on campaign dollars. 

In the 5th District, Moore received 18% of the vote to Firment’s 17%. In the 6th District, Banks and Miguez each received 19% of the vote, with a little more than 600 votes separating them in a 10-person field. 
Moore likened her initial lack of campaign contributions before Nov. 3 to the story of Jesus finding a way to stretch a small amount of loaves and fishes to feed a large crowd of people. 

“When I looked and saw the amount of dollars I had, the first thing I said was, ‘Lord, what am I going to do?” Moore said. 
In Louisiana, Democratic candidates typically have to rely on small, out-of-state donations to fund the congressional campaigns. Almost 86% of Democratic Senate candidate Jamie Davis’ campaign donations came from outside Louisiana, according to an analysis by Open Secrets, a nonpartisan organization that tracks political spending. 

The Louisiana Democratic Party will also be providing Banks and Moore resources for the first time in the runoff. 
The state party endorsed two different Democrats in the 5th and 6th district races for the Nov. 3 election. But after Banks and Moore made it into the runoff, the Democratic State Central Committee pivoted to support their election efforts at the end of last week. 
Banks and Moore will now have help paying for text message campaigns and political mail if they want it, Louisiana Democratic Party chairman Randal Gaines said in an interview Monday. 

The Republican Party of Louisiana endorsed Miguez ahead of the Nov. 3 election and Firment on Nov. 4, once he became the Republican candidate in the Dec. 12 runoff.  The state GOP had backed Board of Regents chair Misti Cordell in the primary.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Mass. advocates pledge to fight new HUD rule on immigrant households
description: MASSACHUSETTS TENANT AND immigrant advocates are criticizing the Trump administration’s new rule requiring residents of federally funded public housing to show proof of citizenship or certain legal immigration status, a […]
text:
MASSACHUSETTS TENANT AND immigrant advocates are criticizing the Trump administration’s new rule requiring residents of federally funded public housing to show proof of citizenship or certain legal immigration status, a change researchers warn could disrupt 20,000 families nationwide whose members have different immigration statuses. 
The rule, published Thursday by the US Department of Housing and Urban Development and set to take effect next month, is the agency’s final word on a policy change it had sought since President Donald Trump’s first term in office. 
It makes a substantial change to HUD rules that have been in place since 1995. For the past three decades, so-called mixed-status households have been able to live together in federally funded housing so long as the amount of federal subsidy was prorated to cover only the family members who could prove citizenship.  
Under the new rule, set to take effect on December 14, every member of the household would need to be either a US citizen or a noncitizen whose immigration status makes them eligible to receive HUD housing assistance.  
Tenant advocates have decried the rule. In April, the Massachusetts Union of Public Housing Tenants and the Massachusetts Law Reform Institute wrote in a comment letter that it “will result in eligible families being ousted from their homes, cause family division, and cost housing providers and HUD millions of dollars to implement.” 
Legal challenges to the change are likely. Advocacy groups and Democratic attorneys general have successfully sued the administration over previous HUD policies. 
“We will not stand by while the Administration orchestrates a mass eviction of our immigrant neighbors,” the public housing tenant group said, after the rule’s publication. “We are closely reviewing the final rule with our members and exploring all available avenues with our allies to stop its implementation. You’ll hear more from us soon.” 
In their own opposition letter in April, a coalition of 22 attorneys general, including Massachusetts’s top prosecutor Andrea Campbell, argued the proposed change not only could displace tens of thousands of families but also violated federal law. 
Nearly 1,000 mixed-status households in Massachusetts could be affected, they said. 
The new federal rule, the attorneys general wrote, “would severely harm the States’ immigrant communities by forcing families to choose between evicting family members and losing their affordable housing, thus increasing the homelessness in our States.” It would also eliminate housing assistance for many additional state residents who are US citizens and eligible non-citizens, “because the verification systems are prone to error.” 
Federal rental assistance programs include Housing Choice vouchers, Section 8 vouchers, and public housing subsidies. While most public housing in the country is federally funded, Massachusetts is one of just four states that also provides state-funded public housing. Bay State local housing authorities manage about 30,000 federally-supported public housing units and 41,500 state-funded units. 
Every member of households living in federally-funded housing would need to prove their legal status, and the Citizens’ Housing and Planning Association warned that overseeing this expanded verification process will create “significant regulatory burdens” for public housing authorities and housing providers.
A late 2025 analysis of the proposed rule from the Center for Budget and Policy Priorities, a nonpartisan research and policy institute, estimated that nearly 80,000 people nationwide could be displaced, including about 37,000 children who are mostly US citizens. 
HUD proposed a similar change to the decades-old provision in late 2019 but after a lengthy public comment period withdrew it when Joe Biden became president in 2021. The agency reintroduced it in February. 
“President Trump warned that the days of illegal aliens and ineligible noncitizens exploiting government-funded welfare programs would be over,” HUD Secretary Scott Turner said in a statement last week. “American taxpayers will no longer foot the bill. Promises made, promises kept.”
Massachusetts advocacy groups, individuals, and elected officials criticized the change. 
In a letter opposing the proposed rule, a coalition of Massachusetts state senators pointed to the crippling housing shortage and already stretched resources for public housing supports. 
“Massachusetts is in the middle of a severe housing shortage, shelter systems here are operating well beyond capacity, and waitlists for subsidized housing in most cities and towns run for years,” they wrote. “In this environment, a federal housing subsidy is not supplemental income for most families who hold one; it is what keeps them housed. This rule would take that away from thousands of households in our state without any sound policy justification.” 
The change isn’t being made in a vacuum, they said.  
Turner in February announced a long-awaited proposed rule that encourages public housing authorities to limit assistance to no less than two years for non-disabled, non-elderly adults, and urges both housing authorities and landlords who rent to people using Section 8 vouchers to require that tenants have full-time employment. 
The public comment period for the work requirement rule has closed, but a final rule has not been promulgated.  
State officials estimate that the work requirement rule, if finalized, would put an additional 115,000 people Massachusetts at risk of losing rental assistance, including 51,100 children and 79,500 people in working families. 
In reviewing over 11,000 comments submitted on the proposed mixed-status rule, HUD notes a number of supportive and critical threads. Those in support tended to say that US government assistance should be limited only to people lawfully in the country and that the rule change would improve the integrity of the program. 
Commenters objecting to the rule argued that it contradicts the agency’s own regulatory impact analysis, which projects that the number of people eligible for assistance would fall by more than half, from roughly 55,100 to 24,100. They said the change would cost an additional $311 million to $385 million to serve the same number of households.  
Turner pointed to an audit of HUD-assisted households nationwide that identified nearly 200,000 tenants — just under 2 percent — whose eligibility verification was either incomplete or unknown. HUD-funded housing serves only a quarter of eligible households in need. 
“Because there are more individuals eligible for assistance than there is assistance available, the assistance relinquished by exiting mixed families would be provided to fully eligible households on waiting lists,” the department said in its rule announcement. “HUD acknowledges these transfer and cost implications.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Wisconsin hemp industry hopeful about Democrats’ plan to end cannabis prohibition
description: The Badger State has a chance to end nearly a century of cannabis prohibition when a new Democratic majority takes control of the Legislature in January. The incoming leaders of the Senate and Assembly, as well as newly Gov.-elect David Crowley, have said they favor legislation to make hemp and marijuana products legal.  “People across […]
text:
Hemp plant at a farm in Minnesota. (Photo by Baylor Spears)The Badger State has a chance to end nearly a century of cannabis prohibition when a new Democratic majority takes control of the Legislature in January. The incoming leaders of the Senate and Assembly, as well as newly Gov.-elect David Crowley, have said they favor legislation to make hemp and marijuana products legal. 
“People across the entire state have had these referendums saying they want to legalize marijuana,” incoming Senate Majority Leader Dianne Hesselbein said on WISN-TV’s UpFront on Sunday. “And we know that we’re losing money to our neighboring states. We need to get that done.” 
Gov.-elect David Crowley and Lt. Gov.-elect Sarah Godlewski alongside Sen. Dianne Hesselbein, Rep. Greta Neubauer and Democratic Party of Wisconsin Chair Devin Remiker celebrate after winning the 2026 election. (Photo by Isiah Holmes/Wisconsin Examiner)
Cannabis legalization, a policy supported by nearly 70% of Wisconsin voters, will be a top priority for the newly elected Democratic trifecta. After losing control of the state Senate and Assembly following the midterm elections, Republican lawmakers can no longer block legalization efforts. Meanwhile, for people whose livelihoods depend on Wisconsin’s hemp industry — thrown in limbo by new federal regulations — anxiety is high that a solution might not come quickly enough.
By Dec. 11, hemp-derived products must contain no more than 0.4 milligrams of THC per container under federal law. The ban stems from a last minute addition to an agricultural appropriations bill  passed by Congress last year which ended a government shutdown. It changed standards set by the 2018 Farm Bill requiring hemp products to contain no more than 0.3% of THC on dry weight basis, creating a new requirement that is out of sync with the natural THC content of  the cannabis plant. 
The vast majority of hemp products including smokable flower, vaporizers, edibles and creams will be affected by the ban. In Wisconsin, that could mean a $700 million industry evaporating overnight. Because Wisconsin has not legalized cannabis products as have its neighboring states of Illinois, Michigan and Minnesota, hemp-derived products are the only such products legally available for purchase. State Democrats are considering legislation that would allow both cannabis and hemp products to be sold in the state.
Rep. Andrew Hysell (D-Sun Prairie) is aware of the problem for hemp businesses. “I believe at the state level, it’s incumbent upon us as legislators to protect Wisconsin businesses and consumers,” he told the Examiner. Hysell pointed to an effort by Democrats last year to create a regulatory framework for hemp in Wisconsin. “And again, Republican leaders let those bills die,” he added.
Rep. Andrew Hysell (Wisconsin legislature)
In 2019, Wisconsin passed Act 68, protecting and regulating the state’s hemp industry, bringing the state into line with the 2018 farm bill. But according to state officials, that bill will not protect hemp producers from the new federal ban.
Gov. Tony Evers warned last session about the economic cost the ban would have. At the time, some Republican lawmakers introduced their own bills. Some wanted to ban THC-derived hemp products under state law, while others proposed competing visions for how hemp could be regulated. None of those bills made it through to  Evers’ desk.
While Hysell believes that the hemp bill Wisconsin passed in 2019 “still provides protection to hemp industry participants,” he also stated that “it’s narrower and it creates uncertainty. And so that’s why in our adult [recreational] bill, we’ll be addressing hemp as well.” 
“We are very concerned about the hemp industry, and the people that are currently producing products for consumers that are very popular,” Hysell said. “We’re concerned about the farmers, small businesses, and therefore we are aware of the possibility, if it comes to it, that there might be a need for an emergency, temporary lifeline or some sort of a fix to provide protection until the full bill can be passed.” Hysell added that Wisconsin’s hemp industry wouldn’t be in such dire straits had a bill been passed last year. “They knew this was coming, so now Democrats are going to be in a position to fix it,” he said. 
Sen. LaTonya Johnson (D-Milwaukee) also said that cannabis legalization should be an immediate concern. “I think it should have been a priority because we know over 70% of people feel like legalization should happen,” Johnson said. “We know that there are people who have invested their hard-earned money into opening CBD and THC stores and businesses because they were legal. … f those businesses aren’t open in a state where marijuana is legalized, they lose their business on Dec. 11.” 
Johnson added, “We don’t want anybody operating outside the law.” 
“Nobody who invested their money, who’s trying to make a legal living, should be forced to shut down just because the government changed its mind,” she said. “So, one thing that legalizing marijuana would do would allow those businesses to stay open. We also want to put parameters around it, too.” The details have yet to be worked out, she said. 
Hysell joined other Democrats in February to introduce SB-1045, a bill to fully legalize recreational and medicinal cannabis in Wisconsin. The bill legalized medical and recreational use of cannabis, created a framework for regulating and taxing products derived from the plant, and also provided a carveout for “intoxicating hemp products” which were a target of those who favored banning hemp. The bill legalized possession of up to 2.5 ounces of cannabis flower for adults in a public space, and up to five pounds within their private residence, among other regulations for cannabis-infused products and concentrates.
Sen. LaTonya Johnson (D-Milwaukee). (Photo by Baylor Spears/Wisconsin Examiner)
The bill also would have created a process of review to expunge previous cannabis-related convictions, protect people against discrimination from their employer based on their consumption or possession of cannabis, and fund cannabis research efforts. 
Adrian Holguin, founder and president of the California-based CannaShark Consulting, told the Examiner that the bill, SB-1045 was “almost pretty good.” Holguin said the bill had many positives. “If we could look at some of the pros that were proposed in there, stuff like being able to expunge past convictions, having a legal age limit on the product, allowing people to possess — humans in your society, free citizens — to possess a plant.” 
Holguin cautioned Wisconsin lawmakers from making the same mistakes as other states which legalized cannabis. “One that I think could be easily controlled without too many politics involved…How long it actually takes them actually to get the first dispensaries or retail outlet available for the consumer. And if you look at how long it took in Minnesota, it took almost 25 months.” In Michigan, it took about a year. 
Ensuring that there is speedy funding through the Department of Agriculture, Trade, and Consumer Protection for the necessary testing and licensing is also critical to prevent any delays. “Then they can quickly roll this out and bring safe, effective, clean product, tested product, to the market quickly instead of making the people of Wisconsin, citizens of Wisconsin, wait two years more when the federal government just closed the other window,” said Holguin, referring to the hemp ban. 
He also advised against high taxes on cannabis products that could stifle the potential gains for agriculture.  Wisconsin was once the nation’s top producer of hemp up until the end of WWII.
The Wisconsin Legislature didn’t hold a public hearing related to cannabis legalization until 2022. Republican Sen. Mary Felzkowski also tried unsuccessfully to introduce her own proposals for a restrictive medical cannabis program as recently as 2025. Gov.-elect David Crowley has said that he supports cannabis legalization. 
Hysell says Wisconsinites have lost out. “I guess in 2022, the Legislative Fiscal Bureau said that we generated $36 million for the Illinois state coffers,” he said. “This is really common sense legislation. And I’m really excited that now that we have a trifecta, we can make it a reality, instead of having to constantly advocate and have that advocacy fall on the deaf ears of Republicans.”
For Hysell, cannabis possession and use is an issue of personal freedom. “The idea that we should give people the right to make choices, the choices they want to make, as long as they’re not hurting other people,” said Hysell. “I don’t know why Republicans have a problem with that. And I still don’t understand. But they did. And fortunately, now that we have the trifecta, we’re going to take action, as we promised, to finally fix this.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Facing a tumultuous world and bombarded by influences, teens need advice and solid guidance
description: As I got my coffee the other day at the coffee shop I frequent, I realized that today’s youth must be struggling. The barista looked distressed, and while I wasn’t trying to read into it, I started thinking about the intense pressures and burdens that youth must feel in this world we are handing to […]
text:
Teenagers face many challenges in today's world, writes our columnists. But there are many people willing and able to help them. (SDI Productions via Getty Images)As I got my coffee the other day at the coffee shop I frequent, I realized that today’s youth must be struggling. The barista looked distressed, and while I wasn’t trying to read into it, I started thinking about the intense pressures and burdens that youth must feel in this world we are handing to them.
The team at Florence Crittenton Services realize these pressures and burdens are real and that the teens need care, respect and immense support. Florence Crittenton is a a nonprofit providing mental and behavioral health services, and they have offices in Topeka and in Lawrence on Massachusetts Street. They have administrative offices and a residential center on Arrowhead Road in Topeka, along with a center for integrative health.
The Florence Crittenton CEO is Dana Schoffelman, Jolee Eckert is the chief program officer, and Taylor Porter is the medical director. They have therapists and other team members who work to help individuals in need of mental health care.
When I was a teenager, I wrote a book for teen girls to help them along their journey. I signed a book contract with a major publisher in Nashville, Tennessee, when I was just 15 years old. I wanted to write it because I had gone numerous times to the bookstore and didn’t find any books that I could relate to. What better way to help teen girls than to write from a teen’s perspective, from me to them?
The book was a big hit. It sold all four printings, and used copies are still available on eBay, Amazon and other online sites. I am thankful.
Time have changed, but the challenges remain. Let’s face it, the world can be overwhelming for a teenager. The world is overwhelming enough for adults.
Children and teens need extra support. Cara Weeks Neuburger and her team at the Lawrence Creative Therapy Center truly care about children and teens (and also adults) in need of mental health care. They offer a variety of services from art therapy to music therapy to counseling. I know Cara, and she used to work at the former Valeo Behavioral Healthcare in Topeka. She is brilliant and her team truly gives it their all to help those in need.
Identity is such a huge issue for teens. With a world that broadcasts messages from every direction telling them what they need to do and who they need to be, it’s important for teens to receive help navigating a big, scary world.
I remember when I was younger: Life was a challenge. Thankfully, my faith helped me through, but I also received help from a doctor and a counselor. Of course, my family has always been there for me. Family support is vital.
There’s no shame in reaching out for help. Help is out there, one just needs to know where to look. I believe we need to ask teens and children how they are doing and how we can help. We need to know we are not alone. No one is alone. We are all in this together.
Rebecca Lyn Phillips is a published author, speaker and mental health advocate. Through its opinion section, the Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: Lawmakers already preparing data center moratorium as they look ahead to January
description: As Maine lawmakers prepare to return to Augusta in January for a new legislative session, they’ve got at least one unresolved issue waiting for them: data centers and how to regulate them. The Legislature began working on the hot-button challenge this past year, but ultimately got little across the finish line and into state law. […]
text:
Supporters of a proposed data center moratorium lined the halls of the Maine State House to encourage lawmakers to override Gov. Janet Mills' veto of the bill on April 29, 2026. (Photo by Kaitlyn Budion/Maine Morning Star)As Maine lawmakers prepare to return to Augusta in January for a new legislative session, they’ve got at least one unresolved issue waiting for them: data centers and how to regulate them.
The Legislature began working on the hot-button challenge this past year, but ultimately got little across the finish line and into state law. They successfully passed a law to exclude data centers from some tax incentives, but failed to overcome Gov. Janet Mills’ veto of a moratorium. 
That proposed ban has already been resubmitted — with much of the same language — by Sen. Nicole Grohoski, whose bill would halt development on data centers larger than 20 megawatts until Nov. 1, 2027. 
The Hancock County Democrat said she thinks the public concern about data centers has only grown in the months since the issue was last debated.
“And we’ve seen that some of these proposals are more speculative than real, and I think communities deserve to know how to determine what is real and what is not real before they spend a lot of time assessing if a proposal is right for their community,” she said. 
The moratorium also won’t face the same hurdles from the governor’s office, as Gov-elect Hannah Pingree repeatedly expressed her support for it on the campaign trail. 
Mainers tell advisory council they’re concerned about data centers — and the risk of missing out

“​​We have seen the damage in Virginia and Texas: higher electric bills, strained grids, pollution and communities not getting promised benefits,” Pingree said in a statement to Maine Morning Star. “I’ve said I support a moratorium on data center development until Maine has real safeguards for our energy grid, our water and our workers, and that position hasn’t changed.” 
One key addition to the new proposal is that it includes an emergency preamble, which would allow it to take effect immediately — if lawmakers can get the necessary two-thirds of support. Grohoski said she thinks that’s likely, given the widespread agreement on the need for more regulation.
Grohoski said the moratorium will give the Legislature the “breathing room” to consider other regulations for data centers. 
The Jay project
When Mills vetoed what would have been the nation’s first moratorium in April, she said it was because the bill did not have an exemption process for projects like one proposed in Jay. 
Two months later, the company involved in the former paper mill development backed out, stalling the project. But it has been revived by site owner JGT2 Redevelopment, which earlier this month filed site location and air emission license applications with the Maine Department of Environmental Protection. 
A public notice published in the Lewiston Sun-Journal said the applications are for a project to develop part of the mill into a data center, and would include using existing buildings to house computer equipment, installing diesel standby generators for emergency power and building a new wastewater system. 
Tony McDonald, with JTG2 Redevelopment, said in a statement the developers never walked away from the data center project.
“This isn’t a new project or a new application,” he said. “It’s the same project, the same owner, the same site, moving forward through the state’s public review with DEP.”
McDonald said the project will reuse existing building and electrical infrastructure from the mill, so that no upgrades to the electric grid will be necessary. And the plans for the water system have changed, with the proposed data center using a closed-loop system with no discharge into the river. 
He said he expects the project to create anywhere from 800-1,000 construction jobs, and 125-150 permanent jobs operating across three shifts. 
“This project will put the mill back on the tax rolls following its 2023 closure, which will be welcome revenue for the town,” McDonald said. 
He said there will be an open house for the project Dec. 10, and details can be found on the project website. 
David Madore, deputy commissioner at the DEP, said in an email that the department is reviewing the applications, and has not received any requests for a public hearing. 
With the project still in the early stages, it’s difficult to say how it might be affected by new state legislation. 
But Pingree said Jay should not be the “testing ground” for data centers before Maine has strong protections in place. 
“Jay deserves good jobs and investment at the mill site, but not at the cost of ratepayers, neighbors or the environment,” Pingree said.
McDonald said he is aware of the new legislative proposal, but maintains that the project in Jay is an “outlier.”
“We look forward to discussing with elected officials some of the advancements we have made since the original plan and why this project is important to the people of Jay,” he said. 
Other regulations
Several Maine towns approve data center moratoriums on local ballots

The moratorium isn’t the only step lawmakers are planning to take in the new session. 
Sen.-elect Sophie Warren (D-Cumberland), who is currently serving in the Maine House of Representatives, has submitted a bill to incorporate key elements of the Maine Data Center Advisory Council recommendations. 
Warren said she thinks it’s fair to expect data center companies to contribute a lot to the local area because “these are developments tied to some of the largest corporate interests, not just in our country but in our world.” 
The council was first proposed in the moratorium bill language, but after Mills vetoed it, she created the council with an executive order. 
The council has met several times this year, and is finalizing recommendations for new regulations, due to the Legislature by Jan. 29. 
Warren said she is particularly interested in the recommendations around energy affordability and clean energy for data centers, and doing more than requiring projects to bring their own energy supply.
“It’s important to appreciate that bringing your own power is a requirement, but it’s really a floor, not a ceiling, for what is required from those that want to come here and build here,” she said. 
She said she’d also like to see public reporting requirements for data center projects, noting that in her town she only learned of a potential project through word of mouth.
“So some of this is also about equipping the public and to empower local control to some extent,” Warren said. 
She said it’s important for the regulation to start at the state level because, with such complex projects, it’s difficult for small towns to tackle. Several towns passed ordinances banning or restricting data center development during the election.
“There’s a lot that we are hearing from local communities saying, ‘We don’t have the money, time or resources to appreciate the full picture here, and we deserve more support and to understand what the implications are here,’” Warren said.

title: Commentary: The reality TV approach to governing comes crashing down
description: Reality TV star, U.S. Transportation Secretary and former Wisconsin Congressman Sean Duffy didn’t have many words of comfort to offer the 1.5 million air travelers stranded in airports across the country Friday — or to anyone in the U.S. planning to fly on an airplane any time soon.  The system failure that led to the […]
text:
Sean Duffy, a member of Congress at the time, and President Donald Trump in a photo taken and posted on Instagram during Trump's first term. (Photo from Sean Duffy's Congressional Instagram account)Reality TV star, U.S. Transportation Secretary and former Wisconsin Congressman Sean Duffy didn’t have many words of comfort to offer the 1.5 million air travelers stranded in airports across the country Friday — or to anyone in the U.S. planning to fly on an airplane any time soon. 
The system failure that led to the grounding of every flight nationwide for only the third time in modern history was entirely the fault of previous administrations, Duffy declared, speaking at a hastily organized Friday night press conference watched by beleaguered passengers sitting on the carpet at closed airport gates from coast to coast.  
“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” he explained. He made no apologies and would not promise that another massive grounding won’t happen again. Instead, he demanded that Americans everywhere pick up their phones and call their members of Congress to demand he be given another $50 billion on top of the $12.5 billion the FAA already received in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — most of which, according to members of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, remains unspent. 
Duffy was vague about the details of how he will spend the additional money. But he was full of praise for President Donald Trump (the “greatest president in history”) whom he credited with leading a wildly successful effort to improve the nation’s air traffic system. The encomiums had to sound a little weird to grounded passengers at U.S. airports. “We are moving at a speed that has never been seen before,”  Duffy said of FAA upgrades. He took pains, over and over, to state that it was the old system, not the upgrades, that failed on Friday.
Then Markwayne Mullin, mixed martial arts champ and Department of Homeland Security secretary, who stood beside Duffy at the press conference wearing a hangdog expression, let the cat out of the bag:
“As Secretary Duffy of the FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology, and that new equipment and new technology — it was overwhelming the older system,” Mullin said, before an agitated Duffy practically shoved him away from the mic.
“It’s the old hardware that went down,” Duffy insisted. 
But, as Mullin clarified, that doesn’t mean the problem wasn’t caused by poorly executed upgrades to a new system.
In September, the Government Accountability Office put out a report criticizing the FAA’s rapid modernization rollout and warning about the agency’s lack of coordination, budgeting and planning: “FAA has not developed an integrated master schedule for phase 1,” of the upgrade project, the GAO found. “Instead, FAA has 11,389 individual project schedules that are not integrated. As a result, individual projects are scheduled for installations at the same sites, generally without optimizing the schedules to reduce impacts to controller operations.”
In other words, what Markwayne said.
There will be plenty of investigation that will shed more light on Duffy’s management of the FAA, and the massive system failure that occurred there on his watch. 
Michael Alfonso headshot courtesy of campaign
Of particular interest in Wisconsin is the role of Air Space Intelligence, the company responsible for a new AI rollout at FAA, and a contributor to Duffy’s son-in-law’s congressional campaign in Wisconsin’s 7th Congressional District. 
FEC filings show that Air Space Intelligence donated $2,500 to newly elected U.S. Rep. Michael Alfonso’s campaign on March 31, 2026. Alfonso, 26, the youngest member of Congress, who arrives with the lightest of resumes, won in part thanks to his father-in-law’s efforts landing a primary endorsement from “the greatest president in history.” Alfonso will hold the same 7th District seat previously occupied by Duffy himself. The AI company that contributed to his campaign in March received a lucrative award in June from the FAA — a no-bid $875 million, 12-year federal contract to design the new Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories (SMART) system that rolled out across the country on Tuesday, Nov. 10 — and became a target of increased public concern after the nationwide grounding of air traffic on Friday, Nov. 13. 
Duffy strongly denies that the AI system was related in any way to the data glitch that led to the mass grounding of flights. 
That may prove true. But a lot of air traffic controllers are disputing Duffy’s explanation for the failure. And, as is the case with so many Trump administration officials, his own conflicts make it impossible to take Duffy at his word. Following Trump’s lead, Duffy is trying to acquire an ownership interest in Air Space Intelligence for the FAA, POLITICO reports, “a striking departure for the federal government.”
The whole reality TV approach to governing is a striking departure from the public interest. Nothing brought that home quite like Duffy’s preening press conference after Friday’s flight disaster. He had nothing to offer travelers to make things better or reassure people he will keep them safe, but he did apologize for wearing jeans — after previously scolding American air travelers for not dressing up. Superficial appearances are everything in reality TV world, along with enriching yourself. Both Duffy and Alfonso — who made a star turn in his father-in-law’s recent road trip reality TV series and whose obsessively groomed look is more Mar A Lago than Northwoods — are creatures of Trump’s takeover of American politics. If the midterms are any indication, voters have had enough of all that. If there’s one thing we learned Friday it’s that sweatpants come in handy when you have to sleep on the airport floor.

title: Trump’s signature bill brings big changes to Ohio in the new year
description: In Ohio and Washington, D.C., a brand new lawmakers are game-planning a new legislative agenda under Democratic control. Meanwhile hundreds of thousands of Ohioans are bracing for impacts from the outgoing Congress’ biggest legislative achievement. President Trump signed the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act into law on July 4, 2025, but its provisions ta[...]
text:
President Donald Trump gestures to the crowd at a rally in Dalton, Georgia, on Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder)In Ohio and Washington, D.C., a brand new lawmakers are game-planning a new legislative agenda under Democratic control. Meanwhile hundreds of thousands of Ohioans are bracing for impacts from the outgoing Congress’ biggest legislative achievement.
President Trump signed the so-called One Big Beautiful Bill Act into law on July 4, 2025, but its provisions take effect on a staggered timeline stretching all the way out to 2035.
As we ring in the New Year, significant changes will kick in for Medicaid, and other provisions will restrict healthcare for immigrants who are lawfully present in the country. Americans who donate to private school scholarship programs will also get a new federal tax break worth up to $1,700.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In July of 2027, student loan deferments will expire for borrowers who claimed economic hardship or unemployment. In October, states will have to begin covering a portion of the food assistance program known as SNAP (the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program) based on their error rates. Ohio’s error rate in 2025 would shift 5% of program costs onto the state — or approximately $160 million, according to the Ohio Job and Family Services Directors’ Association.
At the end of the year, the bill would eliminate tax credits for renewable energy projects and components.
Those provisions, particularly when it comes to Medicaid, are significant enough that incoming Democratic majorities may try to force the Trump administration to accept legislative changes. Absent that, many vulnerable populations will see a diminishing safety net as they move into 2027.
Healthcare changes
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act paid for more than $900 million of its tax breaks by cutting into Medicaid. Adding work requirements to the program saves an estimated $336 million, and moving to a six-month renewal timeline saves an additional $60 million.
Tara Britton from the Center for Community Solutions explained those savings are mostly people losing coverage.
“Folks are stuck in this administrative process and end up losing coverage a lot of times inappropriately,” she said. “That’s where the savings come from.”
Medicaid work requirements affect adults between 19 and 64 who got coverage when the program expanded as part of the Affordable Care Act. There are roughly 700,000 Ohioans in the expansion population. For many, Britton said, Medicaid is their only source of coverage. Workers might have a job that doesn’t offer health insurance, or they might not qualify because they’re working several part-time jobs. Also, private health insurance is probably a nonstarter. People in the expansion population make less than 138% of the federal poverty limit — roughly $22,000 for an individual and $44,550 for a family of four.
Late last week the U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced an optional six-month delay in states’ enforcement of work requirements. Ohio Department of Medicaid spokesperson Stephanie O’Grady stressed the federal guidance “provides limited enforcement flexibility for states, but it does not eliminate the work required to determine eligibility.”
“Ohio is on track to implement the requirements on January 1,” she said.
When that happens, recipients will have to demonstrate they worked or volunteered for 80 hours in a given month to maintain their Medicaid coverage. For about 80% of workers, Britton said, the state has wage data to easily verify eligibility. The state is lacking necessary data for the other 20%, which amounts to about 155,000 Ohioans.
“They see no other data in any other system that shows that they are either meeting work requirements or meet one of those exemptions,” Britton said. “Those are the folks that we are concerned will fall through the cracks,” Britton said.
Those people might be experiencing homelessness or have a health exemption that goes back further than officials are looking. The state might just have an old address.
If a Medicaid participant loses coverage over work requirements, they’ll have a difficult time if they need to purchase coverage, because the One Big Beautiful Bill Act also bars them from accessing premium tax credits.
Starting Jan. 1, Medicaid recipients will have to start renewing their coverage every six months instead of annually. That change will take effect on a rolling basis, Britton explained. So, if you had an annual renewal in October, for instance, you’d move to the six-month timeline beginning in Oct. 2027.
For many, that’s an added hassle. But Britton worries it could be a shock for those 155,000 Ohioans who aren’t interacting much with state officials.
“When an acute issue comes up and someone ends up in the emergency room, that may be where they discover they haven’t renewed,” she said. “Could be that they’re going to get a maintenance medication, and that’s when they find out that they have lost coverage.”
Last month, immigrants who are in the U.S. legally, such as refugees, asylees, and people with temporary protected status, lost access to Medicaid. In January, they’ll lose access to premium tax credits and Medicare as well.
Ohioans receive millions in tax credits through Scholarship Granting Organizations

Scholarship tax credits
Back in 2021, Ohio lawmakers created a tax credit for donations to scholarship-granting organizations. Under state law, the attorney general must verify the groups are nonprofits using the majority of their funding for scholarships with a priority on low-income students.
In Ohio, taxpayers can get a credit of up $750 for donations to qualifying organizations. During 2024, the most recent tax year on record, filers claimed $35.5 million in tax credits. That’s already $10 million more than state officials projected for fiscal year 2027.
Starting in January, the federal government will roll out a supersized version of that credit worth up to $1,700. But to Piet van Lier, the deputy director of advocacy group Honesty for Ohio Education, the state’s program isn’t one the federal government should be emulating, saying the money is “foregone revenue.”
“That money will not be collected by the government to be used for critical services, whether it’s special needs, special education, or Title One for lower income children in public schools,” van Lier said. “This is money that the government won’t have to spend on education and other important things that we rely on the government for.”
Van Lier emphasized he has no problem with school choice, but he opposes siphoning off public funding to support it. And because students can pair a school choice voucher with a scholarship, state education funding gets a double whammy: tuition funding walks out the door with the student, while taxpayers contribute less to the state.
“It’s part of the ongoing weakening of support for public education,” Van Lier said. “We’re taking what is really a public good, a common good, and making it into sort of a consumer asset.”
Private schools that receive scholarship funding on behalf of students get to pick and choose who they enroll. Van Lier worries kids with special needs or lower academic achievement could have fewer enrollment opportunities than other groups.
And there’s also the problem of physical proximity.
“There aren’t any private options in eight counties statewide at this point,” Van Lier said. “More than half the counties, have like four or five or fewer small schools, right? So it doesn’t really provide a lot of options for the for people in big parts of the state.”
