name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT lawmakers mull priorities, practices for 2027 legislative session
description: Lawmakers will get raises, but the 2027 legislative session's committee assignments and other key details are still under discussion.
text:
The names, salaries and top leaders of the new General Assembly are settled, but most committee assignments and other details key to how business will move at the Capitol are a work in progress as the legislature prepares for the arrival of 39 new members and even more lopsided Democratic majorities.
Legislative salaries will increase in the two-year term that begins on Jan. 6 by 3.6% in 2027 and 3.2% in 2028, a consequence of a bipartisan bill passed in 2022 that pegs pay to a federal measure of wage growth, the Employment Cost Index. The first raise pegged to the index came in the 2025-2026 term.
The second calculation under the indexing provision will raise the base legislative pay in the part-time legislature to $46,608. Pay for the top two leaders, the House speaker and Senate president pro tem, will go to $60,591.
No lawmaker gets only the base pay. An additional $4,500 for unvouchered expenses is paid to House members, $5,550 to senators. Also, many lawmakers have a leadership title that come with higher pay, such as the $54,182 paid to committee co-chairs and assistant leaders.
The election two weeks ago produced Democratic majorities of 33-3 in the Senate and 116-35 in the House, the biggest ever in the Senate and the largest in the House since the post-Watergate election of 1974. Democrats currently hold advantages of 25-11 and 102-49.
House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford, and Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff, D-Norwalk, who has been endorsed by his caucus to become the Senate’s top leader, president pro tem, said in separate interviews they are working on committee assignments and legislative priorities. 
“To me, my moonshot is true property tax reform,’’ Ritter said, declining to provide details. “There’s a lot of conversations I have to have. It covers special education, it covers PILOT. Let’s go big.” 
PILOT is payments in lieu of taxes, the method for the state to at least partially reimburse municipalities for revenue lost due to hospitals, universities, state offices and other institutions exempt from local property taxes.
Duff cast his priorities more broadly, all falling under the umbrella of affordability:
“Anything we can do to help make our state more affordable for the working class, for the middle class, for seniors,” Duff said. “It’s the No. 1 issue we heard at the doors on the campaign trail. What all that looks at like the end of the session is up for debate.”
The legislature is not expected to expand the number of standing committees to accommodate the larger Democratic majorities, but the leaders are likely to increase the number of subcommittees.
“The approach for me is really to think about the legislature as an institution and the role we have right now. The states are where the action is at,” said Duff, the president-elect of the National Conference of State Legislatures. “We now have very big issues that states are working on, because Congress in Washington is not functioning. We have to think differently about how we approach policy. Adding more committees doesn’t address that issue.”
Democrats regained control of the U.S. House and Senate, but the new Senate majority will not be filibuster proof. And the blue wave, of course, leaves President Donald Trump and his veto pen in the White House.
Sen. Rob Sampson, R-Wolcott, who will be the leader of the three-person state Senate minority, said Monday that the diminished minority will require adjustments in how three senators will be able to staff the two dozen joint committees of the General Assembly.
“It’s going to be a combination of leaning on our House Republican counterparts and our Senate Republican staff,” Sampson said. “They’ve got to become an early warning system for three senators, so we can pick our shots. We have no choice.”
The current Senate minority leader, Sen. Stephen Harding of Brookfield, lost his reelection bid, but he is expected to return as a senior adviser to Sampson.
“There is nothing public yet,” Sampson said. “We have not finalized our staffing budget with the majority.”
But Sampson left no doubt he wants Harding to return on his staff.
“Sen. Harding is fabulous asset to the caucus,” Sampson said. “I am hoping he will remain in the picture.”
Sampson said he will be seeking a rule change necessary to maintain a modicum of GOP influence — the ability of a single senator to request a roll call on amendments offered on the Senate floor, as opposed to a voice vote. 
Under current rules, 20% of the body must favor a roll call on an amendment. With only three Republican senators, the GOP will control only 8% of the seats. With 35 of the 151 seats, House Republicans will continue have more than 20% of the membership.
“Whether you have 35 or 50, procedurally the rules fall the same way,” said House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora, R-North Branford. “The approach has to be that Republicans have to get in the game early and be an active participant in the process.”
Candelora said that means being involved at the committee level in the development and screening of legislation, which he says has been the approach of his caucus.
Committee assignments generally are not made public until December, and Ritter will begin to interview his 26 new members Wednesday to assess their desires for committees.
Three major committees will see no change in their House chairs.
Ritter said Monday that Rep. Toni Walker of New Haven will return to Appropriations, Rep. Maria Horn of Salisbury to Finance, Revenue and Bonding, and Rep. Steven Stafstrom of Bridgeport to Judiciary.
One potentially awkward seating assignment has yet to be made: The House chamber has four seating sections, and the one where Candelora and most other Republicans now sit has 36 desks. 
On Jan. 6, there only will be 35 Republicans — meaning one Democrat will have to sit across the aisle.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Merger of NorthWestern Energy, Black Hills lands in court
description: The same day NorthWestern Energy announced its merger with Black Hills Corp was complete, a state agency decision to approve it landed in court. In a joint press release Monday, the utilities announced they’d formed a new company, Bright Horizon Energy. “Today marks the beginning of an exciting new chapter as Bright Horizon Energy,” said […]
text:
Electricity pylons (Photo by Getty Images). The same day NorthWestern Energy announced its merger with Black Hills Corp was complete, a state agency decision to approve it landed in court.
In a joint press release Monday, the utilities announced they’d formed a new company, Bright Horizon Energy.
“Today marks the beginning of an exciting new chapter as Bright Horizon Energy,” said Brian Bird, president and CEO of Bright Horizon, former CEO of NorthWestern, in a statement.
“By bringing together our talented employees, complementary operations, and shared commitment to safety, reliability and affordability, we are creating a stronger, more resilient company positioned to meet the growing energy needs of our 2.2 million customers across eight states.”
The $15.4 billion merger proposal was announced in August 2025, and last week the Montana Public Service Commission approved it on a 3-2 vote.
Montana was the final state that needed to grant approval for the merger to close.
But Monday, two parties that participated in the Public Service Commission case filed a petition in Lewis and Clark County District Court to declare the PSC’s final order on the proposal void.
The PSC closed part of the meeting last Tuesday.
In their petition, 350 Montana and Montana Farmers Union alleged the closure violated the Montana Constitution’s requirement that government meetings be open to the public.
The groups argue the PSC’s move to shut out the public “without notice, explanation, or any legal reason to do so” was an infringement on people’s right to know and participate in the decisions of their government.
In a related public records request also filed Monday, the groups asked for information about who participated in the closed session, what took place, and “what materials were considered or changed.”
Represented by lawyer Monica Tranel, the groups also allege the PSC did not account for the risks of the merger on Montana ratepayers, and as such, is compelling them to “pay for the capital Bright Horizon has promised to AI data centers.”
The order said Bright Horizon capital is obligated in eight states to 40 entities including Microsoft and Meta, and Montana will lose oversight of investment decisions in the merger.
Additionally, the parties argue the PSC didn’t adequately evaluate the 370 megawatts that NorthWestern Energy acquired from Puget Sound Energy at the Colstrip Power Plant.
Court filings ask the judge to void the PSC order on the merger “to the extent it authorizes merger consummation” and to stop the deal because “loss of control of Montana’s largest utility is at stake.”
The court filing said once the merger closes, the Montana PSC’s regulatory leverage disappears because corporate control of the enterprise will be in South Dakota.
Monday, Tranel said the merger isn’t yet final; it remains subject to reconsideration for 30 days, and the court filing said the closure is extended to Feb. 18 to account for potential judicial review.
The petition also asks the judge to stop the utilities and unregulated affiliates from selling or transferring the Puget shares of the Colstrip Power Plant.
A spokesperson for the PSC said the commission had not been served and had no comment. A spokesperson for NorthWestern said the utility does not comment on pending litigation.
In 2026, NorthWestern Energy and Black Hills Energy reported $19.9 million in merger related costs, according to NorthWestern. A utility spokesperson said those costs are paid for by shareholders and will not be recovered through customer rates.
The combined merger costs for 2025 were not available Monday from NorthWestern.
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, Nebraska Public Service Commission, and South Dakota Public Utilities Commission earlier approved the merger.
Although the merged company has a new name, the news release Monday said local customers should not expect immediate changes to branding, payment processes, outage reporting or customer support.
The new company is expected to serve electric and natural gas customers in Montana, Arkansas, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, South Dakota, Nebraska and Wyoming.
At PSC meetings including the one last week, many members of the public expressed opposition to the merger, citing concerns Montanans would have to subsidize the costs of data centers.
But a couple of representatives of the business community urged the PSC to support the deal as a tool for economic growth.
PSC President Jeff Welborn and Commissioner Randy Pinocci voted against the merger. Commissioners Jennifer Fielder, Annie Bukacek and Kirk Bushman supported it.

name: Nevada Current
title: Ford’s transition team co-chaired by attorney whose firm represents Kalshi against Nevada
description: Parties in Nevada’s court battle against the prediction market Kalshi are declining to comment on Governor-elect Aaron Ford’s inclusion on his transition team of John Bailey, a founding partner in the law firm that is representing Kalshi against the state.  “We have no comment,” a spokesperson said Monday on behalf of the Nevada Gaming Control […]
text:
(Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Parties in Nevada’s court battle against the prediction market Kalshi are declining to comment on Governor-elect Aaron Ford’s inclusion on his transition team of John Bailey, a founding partner in the law firm that is representing Kalshi against the state. 
“We have no comment,” a spokesperson said Monday on behalf of the Nevada Gaming Control Board, which is warding off Kalshi’s bid to compete with the state’s sports books, absent the required license.  
The Nevada Resort Association, which represents major resorts and is a party to the lawsuit, also declined to comment. 
Ford, who as AG, has represented Nevada gambling regulators in their effort to rein in Kalshi, raised eyebrows last month when his campaign sent out a news release touting Kalshi’s odds of Ford unseating Gov. Joe Lombardo. 
Lombardo’s spokesperson deemed the campaign pitch a conflict of interest and called Ford’s news release “absolutely absurd.” 
Now, Ford is seeking guidance from Bailey, an expert in gaming law, whose firm enjoys Kalshi’s legal largesse.
Bailey will serve as a co-chair of Ford’s transition advisory committee, along with Lieutenant Governor-elect Sandra Juaregui and Ford’s wife, Berna Rhodes-Ford, the campaign announced Thursday. 
Bailey also served on Gov. Steve Sisolak’s transition team. 
In a separate move Monday, Ford named Asha Jones as chief of staff, a position she previously served in for Nevada’s Democratic U.S. Rep. Steven Horsford. Prior to that she was district director for former Nevada U.S. Democratic Rep. Ruben Kiehuen. Jones has also worked for Sen. Harry Reid and Shelley Berkley, the former Democratic congresswoman who is now mayor of Las Vegas. More recently, Jones served as a vice president of corporate affairs for Brightline West, and as director of development for Boyd Gaming.
Politics is replete with instances of strange bedfellows – relationships that confound common sensibilities.
“That’s not a way to endear yourself to the gaming industry. It’s curious,” former gaming executive Richard Schuetz, who also served as a member of the California Gaming Control Commission, said of Ford’s selection of Bailey. 
“It’s always good to have a diversity of opinions. You don’t want to just listen to people reading off the same song sheet,” Schuetz said. “But I think it’s important to understand that Bailey’s influence could have a dramatic impact on the gaming industry.”
Ford’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
Earlier this year, a three-judge panel of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled against Kalshi, which is fighting an order from Nevada gaming regulators to stop taking sports bets in the state. 
The prediction market is represented by Bailey’s partner, Dennis Kennedy. 
Nevada is among a number of states fighting Kalshi and other prediction markets in court. 
In November, the Ninth Circuit denied Kalshi’s request for a rehearing before the entire court. Kalshi is expected to appeal the ruling to the U.S. Supreme Court. 
Disclosure: Bailey, who previously represented hard money lender Jeff Guinn, the son of former Gov. Kenny Guinn, alleged this reporter accepted gifts and money in exchange for writing stories about Guinn, who was being sued by investors. The Nevada Supreme Court ruled in 2013 that Guinn was attempting to circumvent the Nevada Shield Law that protects reporters.

title: Trial scheduled in Van Buren County animal-neglect case
description: A Van Buren County dog breeder facing 34 counts of animal neglect is scheduled to go to trial early next year. In late July, Van Buren County officials criminally charged Wuanita Swedlund, 35, of Farmington, with 27 counts of simple misdemeanor animal neglect without death or serious injury, plus seven serious misdemeanor counts of animal […]
text:
This dog was photographed by USDA inspectors in January 2023 at a kennel operated by Wuanita Swedlund of Iowa. (USDA photo courtesy of Bailing Out Benji)A Van Buren County dog breeder facing 34 counts of animal neglect is scheduled to go to trial early next year.
In late July, Van Buren County officials criminally charged Wuanita Swedlund, 35, of Farmington, with 27 counts of simple misdemeanor animal neglect without death or serious injury, plus seven serious misdemeanor counts of animal neglect with injury.
Swedlund has pleaded not guilty to all of the charges and a trial is now scheduled for Jan. 27, 2027.
In an affidavit attached to the criminal complaints, Deputy Sheriff Spencer Rider alleged Swedlund had failed to provide adequate food and water to the confined animals on her property, causing the animals unjustified distress and suffering.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
During a June visit to Swedlund’s kennels, Rider alleges, officials observed water bowls containing no potable water for animals to drink; food bowls contaminated with feces; kennels with an excessive buildup of feces and organic matter, indicating the kennels had not been cleaned for a prolonged period of time; a flea infestation, and a Yorkshire terrier that was in need of dental care.
On June 30, 2026, deputies seized 32 dogs, plus one cat and one rabbit, from Swedlund’s property.
In June 2026, the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service sued Swedlund for allegedly barring federal officials from conducting “unannounced” inspections of her dog-breeding operations. The USDA asked the court to issue an injunction granting the agency access to the property.
On July 10, 2026, U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher issued the injunction, stating that Swedlund’s noncompliance with the federal Animal Welfare Act “goes well beyond bureaucratic handwringing. The evidence shows that Swedlund has housed hundreds of dogs since acquiring her USDA license in 2023. She has consistently failed to provide her animals with adequate facilities, access to water, or access to medical care. It is evident that the animals in Swedlund’s care suffered needlessly — precisely the type of harm that the Animal Welfare Act sought to prevent.”
Van Buren County District Court Judge Joel D. Yates has transferred ownership of the animals to the PAW Animal Shelter in Fort Madison for eventual adoption. In his ruling, Yates said the evidence showed the “animals were neglected by not having access to appropriate food, potable water, sanitary conditions, proper ventilated shelter and necessary veterinary care.”
Swedlund spoke to the Iowa Capital Dispatch in July, saying she doesn’t believe any of the animals suffered from any type of neglect. “All my animals were healthy,” she said at the time.
Court records indicate USDA first issued Swedlund a license in July 2023. Since then, the records show, she has been cited for numerous violations of the Animal Welfare Act, some of which were tied to the death of eight puppies from three different litters.
In that case, USDA alleged Swedlund told inspectors she had found three dead bulldog puppies after feeling a strong, cold draft at the front of their enclosure. Inspectors reported Swedlund had placed duct tape over the hole that caused the draft, but the tape was peeling away at the time of the inspection and the cold draft could still be felt.
Three more puppies from a litter of rottweilers were found dead, the USDA says, and one puppy was severely injured and later euthanized after a husky broke into an enclosure housing a sheepdog and her newborn litter. name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Arkansas still set to enforce Medicaid work requirements Jan. 1 despite option of 6 extra months
description: The Arkansas Department of Human Services still plans to enforce work requirements for Medicaid enrollees starting Jan. 1, despite the federal government allowing states six more months to put the mandate in place. The Arkansas Department of Human Services is “reviewing the details” of the additional six months allowed before implementation but has not chang[...]
text:
The Arkansas Department of Human Services building on Main Street in downtown Little Rock. (Photo by John Sykes/Arkansas Advocate)The Arkansas Department of Human Services still plans to enforce work requirements for Medicaid enrollees starting Jan. 1, despite the federal government allowing states six more months to put the mandate in place.
The Arkansas Department of Human Services is “reviewing the details” of the additional six months allowed before implementation but has not changed its plan to put the mandate in place Jan. 1, acting communications chief Keith Metz said in an email.
The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced the six-month grace period Friday, a day after two top Congressional Democrats raised concerns that states needed more time to put systems in place to keep eligible Americans from losing Medicaid coverage.
Many states unsure how to implement new Medicaid work requirements, KFF survey finds

Most Medicaid enrollees between the ages of 19 and 65 will be required to work, participate in community service, or attend an education program at least 80 hours a month in order to keep their health insurance, according to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a sweeping 2025 tax and spending cut bill.
Officials in multiple states said earlier this year that they were unsure how exactly to determine if someone meets the new work requirements or is exempt.
Those exempt from the work requirements include pregnant people, parents of dependent children, people who have complex medical conditions, tribal community members, those in the foster care system, people who were in foster care who are below the age of 26 and individuals released from incarceration in the last 90 days, among others.
The Department of Human Services has been preemptively working to determine Medicaid enrollees’ continued eligibility before the work requirements go into effect.
Arkansas Advocates for Children and Families said Monday that the extra time allowed was encouraging and the state’s decision not to take that time was frustrating.
“Arkansas’s Medicaid participants are already going through many changes that are confusing,” the organization said in a statement. “Arkansas should take the maximum amount of time allowed to make sure the reporting system is as accurate as possible, as other states have chosen to do, rather than rushing implementation of the work reporting requirements.”
More than 800,000 low-income and disabled Arkansans receive some form of Medicaid coverage. As of Nov. 1, nearly 209,000 are on the state’s hybrid Medicaid expansion program, known as Arkansas Health and Opportunity for Me, or ARHOME.
Official: Moving Arkansas Medicaid expansion enrollees to new program would take more than 6 months

In July, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services verbally denied a five-year extension of the expansion. Human Services Secretary Janet Mann asked for a two-year reprieve to develop a new program. The Trump administration informed Mann earlier this month that it will keep ARHOME active for six months starting Jan. 1.
Six months is not long enough to transfer all Medicaid expansion enrollees to either managed care or fee-for-service Medicaid, state Division of Medical Services Director Elizabeth Pitman told lawmakers last week.
Formulating a new expansion model will be a high priority in the legislative session that begins in January. Pitman and Mann both told lawmakers that ending the program completely is not an option.
Arkansas’ program uses Medicaid money to purchase private insurance for low-income residents. The first-in-the-nation model was approved in 2013 as an alternative to expanding Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act.
Arkansas was the first state to impose work requirements on Medicaid expansion recipients, a mandate that was approved during President Donald Trump’s first term. More than 18,000 Arkansans lost coverage before a federal judge blocked the policy in 2019.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Burleigh County ballot mistake did not affect results, election official says
description: A ballot mixup at Burleigh County polling location on Election Day would not have changed any election results, according to a county election official. County canvassing boards met Monday to certify local election results ahead of North Dakota’s State Canvassing Board meeting Wednesday.  Dozens of voters in Burleigh County were given the wrong ballot by […]
text:
Thomas Larson, election coordinator for Burleigh County, speaks to the Burleigh County Canvassing Board while holding a stack of set-aside ballots on Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)A ballot mixup at Burleigh County polling location on Election Day would not have changed any election results, according to a county election official.
County canvassing boards met Monday to certify local election results ahead of North Dakota’s State Canvassing Board meeting Wednesday. 
Dozens of voters in Burleigh County were given the wrong ballot by election judges at one Bismarck  polling location.
The ballots involved legislative candidates from District 7 on the northside of Bismarck. There were 134 District 7 voters who were given a ballot for District 8, which did not have any legislative candidates competing this year.
Election error caused some Bismarck voters to receive wrong ballot

Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, would go on to defeat her District 7 Democratic-NPL challenger Kevin Horneman 4,402 to 1,914. Republican House candidates Greg Vetter and Steve Sauter received 4,147 and 4,029, respectively, and defeated the Dem-NPL District 7 House candidates Tiffany Williams-Rice and Jason Thoms, who received 1,866 and 1,786 votes.
The margins of victory were large enough that the 134 votes would not have affected the outcomes. 
“Essentially, the judges were giving out the wrong ballots,” said Thomas Larson, election coordinator for Burleigh County. 
The polling location had four different ballots that could have gone to voters depending on where they lived, he added.
“None of our other polling locations had this issue. It was an isolated situation,” Larson said.
Thomas Larson, election coordinator for Burleigh County, speaks to the Burleigh County Canvassing Board on Nov. 16, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
The mistake was discovered Election Day morning but voters were unable to change their ballots once they were inserted into the tabulation machines.
“Once a ballot is cast, there’s nothing you can do about it,” Larson said. He added the county plans to conduct more immersive training for election judges ahead of the 2028 election to ensure they are set up and prepared for the issue “not to happen again.”
He said the error at a single polling location does not reflect the accurate work of election workers across the county in the lead up to Election Day during the early voting period.
“At the Event Center, for 10 days during early voting and on Election Day, we have 33 different ballot styles there and this wasn’t an issue,” Larson said.
North Dakota Monitor reporter Michael Achterling can be reached at machterling@northdakotamonitor.com.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT delays Medicaid losses from work requirements until July 2027
description: The “hold harmless” period means that while work requirements go into effect Jan. 1, no one will lose coverage for noncompliance before July.
text:
New federal work requirements for the Medicaid HUSKY D program are slated to go into effect in January, but Connecticut residents who fail to comply won’t lose coverage before July, according to a Monday announcement by Gov. Ned Lamont and the state Department of Social Services commissioner Andrea Barton Reeves.
Beginning Jan. 1, HUSKY D enrollees must meet work requirements, also being referred to as “community engagement requirements.” 
To keep coverage, HUSKY D enrollees will have to prove they work at least 80 hours or earn a minimum of $580 per month. The requirement can also be fulfilled by demonstrating at least 80 hours of monthly participation in school, community service or a qualified training program. Several exemptions exist.
On Friday, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced it would provide states the option of implementing a “hold harmless” period through and including June 30, 2027. During these six months, HUSKY D members who are otherwise eligible won’t lose coverage just because of failure to meet the work requirements.
The decision is meant to give states more time to implement the changes. Lamont and Barton Reeves announced on Monday that Connecticut will elect to implement the “hold harmless” period.
“This additional time will help our residents meet the changing federal requirements and ensure our systems are working the way they should,” Lamont said in a statement. Barton Reeves called the “hold harmless” period “a true benefit to our members.”
The work requirements were originally passed in 2025 as part of House Resolution 1, commonly referred to by President Donald Trump as the “One Big Beautiful Bill.”
Sen. Matt Lesser, D-Middletown, co-chair of the state legislature’s Human Services Committee, said the federal government’s decision to extend a hold harmless period could be the result of the Democrats’ sweep in the midterm elections.
“Elections have consequences,” Lesser said. “My hope is that this is the sign that the writing is on the wall for the president’s disastrous domestic policy agenda.”
The hold harmless period is only a six months reprieve from coverage losses, and as of now, the Medicaid work requirements are still going into effect. But several Democrats who won their races in the midterm elections campaigned on permanently reversing some of Trump’s healthcare policies, including the Medicaid changes.
Even with Democratic majorities in both chambers, Trump still has the power to veto any proposal to reverse the Medicaid changes. Overriding his veto would require getting Republicans on board. Or Democrats could opt to negotiate a deal with Trump, if he’s open to it.
Last week, before the announcement of the hold harmless period, State Comptroller Sean Scanlon said state officials hoped Democrats would be able to repeal the Medicaid changes, but their success likely depends on Trump’s willingness to negotiate.
“We’re really hoping that that is something that they get done in the first couple weeks of a new Congress,” Scanlon said. “Of course, the president is still the president. What his appetite is to do deals with the Democrats and resolve some of these things is really unclear and I don’t think anybody knows at this point.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Newly elected Oklahoma senators take oath of office ahead of start of Senate term
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – They came to the Senate chamber humbled, with a sense of gratitude, awe and excitement for the future. Oklahoma Chief Justice Dustin P. Rowe on Monday administered the oath of office to the newly elected and reelected senators in the Senate chamber. Some fought back tears. Others thanked voters and introduced friends […]
text:
Sen.-elect Jessica Winegeart, R-Calumet, introduces her family after taking the oath of office Monday in the Senate chamber. (Photo by Barbara Hoberock/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – They came to the Senate chamber humbled, with a sense of gratitude, awe and excitement for the future.
Oklahoma Chief Justice Dustin P. Rowe on Monday administered the oath of office to the newly elected and reelected senators in the Senate chamber.
Some fought back tears. Others thanked voters and introduced friends and family members.
They will officially become senators on Wednesday. 
House members will be sworn in on Tuesday.
“I’m not one to be a big crier, but I was welling up, you know, just to see all the hard work that I and several other people that helped me through the process come to fruition, come to the beginning and end at the same time,” said Sen.elect Aaron Forst, R-Owasso.
Forst defeated incumbent Sen. Dana Prieto, R-Tulsa, in the Republican primary.
“It’s been a year and a half of campaigning,” Forst said. “It’s been a long trail. We had a lot happening. This was not your standard race in our case by far. It’s taken a toll on my family.”
His main focus will be on childcare.
“It’s overregulated, underfunded and we’ve got to do something to fix that,” he said.
Sen.-elect Curtis Erwin, R-Elgin, is replacing Sen. Dusty Deevers, R-Elgin, who didn’t make it out of the primary.
“The race was long, but all of my opponents were very respectful,” he said. “They ran really clean races.”
Sen.-elect Jessica Winegeart, R-Calumet, decided to run for senate after serving on her local school board. She replaces Sen. Darcy Yech, R-Kingfisher, who was term limited.
“I was able to affect change in my community, to see the positive outcomes, to see the things that I could be involved in,” she said. “And I want to do that on the next level.”
She said being sworn in was “completely surreal, overwhelming.”
“You know, I really had to hold it together because it’s such a huge moment in your life,” she said. “It’s such a huge honor, but also a huge responsibility. You feel the weight of that.”
Senate President Pro Tem Lonnie Paxton, R-Tuttle, said his advice to the newcomers is to build relationships and stay in contact with constituents.
“Don’t get isolated,” he said. “Don’t get tunnel vision. Don’t think we are better than anybody else. We’re here serving the public, and they’re not serving us.”

title: Federal government fights Arkansas’ efforts to sue Kalshi
description: The federal government has asked a judge to block Arkansas’ lawsuit against the online prediction market Kalshi, saying the state doesn’t have the authority to regulate the company. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission filed a lawsuit last week in federal court in Arkansas against the state over its investigation into Kalshi. Attorney General Tim Griffin[...]
text:
(Getty Images)The federal government has asked a judge to block Arkansas’ lawsuit against the online prediction market Kalshi, saying the state doesn’t have the authority to regulate the company.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission filed a lawsuit last week in federal court in Arkansas against the state over its investigation into Kalshi. Attorney General Tim Griffin earlier this month sued Kalshi and accused the company of running an illegal gambling operation.
The CFTC complaint, however, said that federal law gives the commission exclusive jurisdiction to regulate prediction markets like Kalshi.
“To restore the commission’s exclusive jurisdiction, the state’s pending enforcement action against Kalshi, as well as any future enforcement actions or investigations against federally regulated (designated contract markets) and related entities, must be enjoined immediately,” the commission’s lawsuit said.
Arkansas is the 11th state the CFTC has sued over regulation of prediction markets, the agency said. 
“As prediction markets continue to prove their value in being useful for risk management and providing the public with valuable information about the future, Arkansas seeks to shut down event contracts ranging from sports and politics to other important world events,” Chairman Michael S. Selig said in a news release.
Griffin’s office on Monday said it disagreed with the commission’s argument and said that Arkansas regulates gambling to protect consumers. 
“Instead of obtaining the licenses, submitting to the oversight, complying with the restrictions, and paying the taxes required of lawful gambling operators in Arkansas, Kalshi opened its platforms to Arkansas consumers, including individuals as young as 18 years old, encouraged them to wager real money on sporting and entertainment events, and profited from those wagers,” spokesperson Jeff LeMaster said in a statement.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Parent leaders hold our communities together. It’s time the state built a pathway to support them.
description: Parent leaders need a pathway that connects their leadership to college and careers, and a direct line from their lived experience to the agencies and organizations that need it.
text:
HUONG VU WAS a television journalist in Vietnam. Peace Junaid was a nutritional biochemist in Nigeria. When they immigrated to Massachusetts years ago, both put their careers on hold for their families, and neither expected to find a way back to their careers. 
Today, Massachusetts families turn to parent leaders when the rules change overnight. Housing, health care, and child care now cost more than many families can bear, and federal changes have already unraveled much of the safety net beneath them. When families are left guessing where to turn, the answer is often a parent who has already figured it out, at school pickup, in a frantic WhatsApp thread, or at an after-school meeting. 
Systems across Massachusetts already understand that parent engagement matters, and many have worked hard to make room for it. Yet despite those efforts, too many parent voices are still underrepresented. Real leadership, where parents help shape the decisions that affect their families and then help carry them out, is not yet happening. That is not for a lack of caring. It is a lack of infrastructure. 
Parent leaders already carry valuable skills: outreach to families others miss to help them navigate and connect to the right resources and systems; communication that bridges languages, cultures, and the gap between families and institutions; and advocacy that pushes their needs to the forefront. What they need is a pathway that connects their leadership to college and careers, and a direct line from their lived experience to the agencies and organizations that need it. Goodwill does not scale. Infrastructure does. 
The two of us came to this from opposite directions. One of us arrived from Colombia 30 years ago with a law degree, became a mother, and eventually did family engagement work to elevate parent leaders, something she has done for the past 20 years. The other spent 30 years in corporate strategy, then 15 more in pro bono consulting and funding early childhood programs across Massachusetts. 
We reached the same conclusion: The stability of our communities rests on parent leaders, and they need a foundation to grow. 
So we co-founded Mass ParentCorps to build a statewide infrastructure for parent leadership, together with parent leaders and the organizations that support them. We raise awareness of what parent leaders contribute, expand their pathways to college and careers, bring their voices into policy, and attract investment to the field.  
We started with the Mass ParentCorps credential, which honors the expertise of parents already leading in their communities. They take a course at one of our partner community colleges and present an applied learning project, earning six to nine college credits along with the credential. Then we connect them to opportunities to continue their education or pursue new work. 
We started by listening to the Departments of Early Education and Care and Elementary and Secondary Education, to the parent leaders, and to community agencies, including Families First, Union Capital Boston, East Boston Social Centers, Family Nurturing Center of Massachusetts, and Vital Village Networks, which helped shape the model. And then we went to Urban College of Boston, where President Yves Salomon-Fernandez opened the door without hesitation. 
Together, with support from Eastern Bank and the Commonwealth Children’s Fund, we recruited 19 parent leaders, representing 10 community agencies, into our first credentialing cohort. This fall, we partnered with Middlesex Community College to launch a second cohort of 21 parents. Joanna Geller, director of policy, research, and evaluation at the NYU Metropolitan Center for Research on Equity and the Transformation of Schools, is researching and evaluating the model. 
From one parent leader a whole ecosystem rises. As a parent gains a path forward, their children see a leader at home, communities are engaged, and responsive systems add up to a healthier economy.  
Huong’s path shows what infrastructure can do. After she arrived here, her career stopped, until a home visitor brought her a basket of resources and led her to a parent-child playgroup run by the Dorchester Family Engagement Network at the Boys & Girls Clubs of Dorchester.  
That playgroup became her workplace. She began as a volunteer with a Vietnamese book club, was promoted to parent leader, and was among the first parents there trained to use a developmental screening tool to help families understand how their children are growing. Today she is a full-time family engagement specialist on the club’s staff, working with hundreds of families every year. What she wants next is for policymakers to see her work for what it is: a profession. 
At that same Boys & Girls Club, Huong saw a leader in Peace Junaid before Peace saw it in herself, and offered her a role as a parent partner. “It takes others to see something in us to help lift us up,” Peace says. Both women were part of our first cohort. Today, Peace plans to combine her training as a biochemist with her leadership to help women care for their own health, and to become, in her words, “the CEO of my own dreams.” 
Their stories echo those of hundreds of parents across Massachusetts who run family nights at community centers, sit on school councils, and connect a newly arrived family to a pediatrician, a food pantry, and an English class in the same afternoon. They work as parent partners, parent leaders, and family engagement specialists at family engagement networks, community centers, family resource centers, early education programs, and youth organizations. 
Some organizations already understand what parent leaders are worth. These have long trained and paid them, often stretching limited budgets to do it. That deserves real credit. Elsewhere, many parent leaders are still treated as volunteers, doing essential work on the side until they burn out. 
Massachusetts already knows how to invest in families. It is the only state to make pandemic-era child care grants permanent, with $475 million for Commonwealth Cares for Children this year, and free community college has reversed a decade of enrollment decline. But these policies work only when families know about them, trust them, and can navigate the paperwork.  
Parent leaders make that happen. The bridges are being built. Now we must invest in the people who walk families across them. 
It is time to make parent leadership a Commonwealth priority: 

Recognize parent leadership as a skill set. State agencies should recognize a parent leadership credential in hiring and contracting, so Huong’s work counts as the profession it is. 


Build on what’s working. Fund at scale the paid roles many agencies already offer parent leaders. 


Connect leadership to college and careers. Parent leadership training should carry credit toward certificates and degrees, so a biochemist like Peace builds on her science background instead of starting over. 


Put parents at the table. Parent leaders should help write the policies that shape families’ lives. 

On Tuesday, November 17, our first cohort will share their experiences at a forum at Urban College of Boston. Joined by college leaders, researchers, and community partners, they will discuss how parent leadership can open doors to higher education, strengthen communities, and inform statewide policy. We invite policymakers, funders, and employers to listen and help turn these lessons into action. 
Huong and Peace each carry the skills of a leader. Massachusetts has depended on parent leaders like them to hold our communities together. Now it is time to do more than celebrate their contributions. It is time to recognize their value, invest in their potential, and build the pathways that allow their leadership to flourish. 
Magda Rodriguez-Villafane is president and co-founder of Mass ParentCorps. Don Hawley is CEO and co-founder of Mass ParentCorps.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Demographic cliff poses concern for neighbor-state enrollment, Iowa Board of Regents reports
description: Jason Pontius’s first comment to the Iowa Board of Regents about enrollment trends was his prediction for headlines — enrollment at Iowa’s three public universities remained more-or-less flat from last year to this year. However, the underlying story stretches into the future of high school graduates, both their number and who decides to pursue higher […]
text:
The Iowa Board of Regents met on Nov. 12, 2026. States bordering Iowa are set to see worse declines in high school graduates than Iowa itself, potentially harming university enrollment. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Jason Pontius’s first comment to the Iowa Board of Regents about enrollment trends was his prediction for headlines — enrollment at Iowa’s three public universities remained more-or-less flat from last year to this year.
However, the underlying story stretches into the future of high school graduates, both their number and who decides to pursue higher education.
Colleges and universities across the U.S. have been preparing for the demographic cliff of fewer students graduating high school for years, including those in Iowa despite the state projecting to see less of a dip than other states.
Pontius, associate chief academic officer for the board of regents, said in past meetings he hesitated to call the decline a “cliff,” but told board members at its November meeting that the number of Iowa high school graduates right now is likely the highest the state will see for the next 20 years. States surrounding Iowa will also see their graduating classes sink, impacting out-of-state student enrollment.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“These are the traditional students we’re talking about,” Pontias said. “That pool has gotten smaller, and so it provides additional challenges for us going forward. Our undergraduate population is about 95% traditional students right now.”
Total student enrollment at the University of Iowa, Iowa State University and University of Northern Iowa decreased by one half of a percentage point — 352 students — between fall 2025 and fall 2026, according to the enrollment report discussed by the board at its November meeting last week. Undergraduate student enrollment across the universities grew by .2%, or by 98 students.
Overall, total student enrollment at the three universities in fall 2026 was 71,520, the highest seen since 2022 but nearly 10,000 students below the higher education system’s peak in 2016.
While Iowa lags one year behind the rest of the U.S. in the enrollment cliff, Pontius said new data projects further declines in high school graduates from 2036-2041, which will represent itself in Iowa as a second decline after a brief level period.
“This is the highest number of high school graduates in the state of Iowa we are likely to have in the next two decades,” Pontius said.
Declines in high school graduates are expected across the U.S., Pontius said, varied between states but averaging out to a 12% drop over the next 15 years.
From 2026 to 2041, Pontius said Iowa is expecting a 9% decline in high school graduates. In the top five states Iowa universities bring students from, Nebraska will also drop by 9%, followed by Minnesota with 13%, Missouri at 14%, Wisconsin at 16% and Illinois at 29%.
Despite other states already dealing with the enrollment cliff, Pontius said out-of-state enrollment increased for this year by 1.3%, to a total of 26,142 students. UNI, which offers in-state tuition to students from neighboring states, saw a 28% increase in Illinois students and a 55% jump among Minnesota students, alongside growing numbers from other states.
“We get about 11,400 students right now from the state of Illinois,” Pontius said. “So a major decline there is problematic and adds an additional challenge to our attempt to kind of maintain enrollment in our three public universities.”
Shifts in student’s choices for their education are also impacting enrollment, Pontius said, with midwestern public flagship institutions seeing growth between 2009-2024 and regional public institutions seeing declines. Many things could contribute to this trend, he said, and while the University of Northern Iowa hasn’t been entirely exempt, it has been “bucking this for the last few years.”
UNI was the only state university to see enrollment growth from fall 2025 to fall 2026, increasing by 1.8% while the UI saw a .6% decrease and ISU saw a 1.1% decrease.
Data from surveying Iowa high school students for their post-graduation plans and enrollment numbers show that for community colleges, both intent to enroll and actual enrollment have been dropping, while going straight into employment has been rising and intent and actually going to a state university has been “holding roughly flat.”
One question Pontius said he often gets when enrollment declines at Iowa public universities is whether students are leaving the state to attend college, which has not been happening. In the 15 years that metric has been tracked for, Pontius said it “has been very flat the entire time.”
“We retain a very large number of our students who go to college in the state of Iowa, and that has always been the case,” Pontius said.

text:
Circuit Judge Richard A. Smith has ordered all court filings unsealed in a Greenville homicide case in which over 100 pieces of DNA evidence went missing. They will be made available to the public on the Mississippi Electronic Court system on Dec. 7.
Smith sealed the court filings after he canceled a hearing in May, when public officials were set to testify on the chain of custody of the missing evidence. The evidence ranged from a rape kit to fingernail scrapings to a strip of tape, and was tied to a rape and manslaughter appeal by King Brown Jr. Brown was convicted in 2005 after a third trial of the rape and killing of a 6-year-old Greenville girl. 
King Brown Jr. listens to the judge during his sentencing hearing at the Washington County Circuit Court on Nov. 2, 2026. Credit: Leonardo Bevilacqua/Mississippi Today
Smith said he did not want to subject the public officials set to testify to undue embarrasment. 
Several circuit clerk employee affidavits suggested district attorney’s office employees visited the evidence room prior to the specimens’ disappearance. An unsigned district attorney’s office statement denied the allegations.
Additional testimony by Washington County Circuit Clerk Barbara Esters-Parker, Deputy Clerk Cynthia Lakes and Deputy Clerk Willinna Hawkins were provided under seal in May.
In June, Andrew Coffman, an attorney for the Reporters Committee for the Freedom of the Press, made a motion on behalf of Mississippi Today to restore public access to information on whether district attorney’s office employees or circuit clerk’s office employees bear blame for the evidence’s disappearance.
Coffman also argued that Smith’s previous order violated the right to review court records, which are public records by default. 
His motion was granted over five months later on Monday.
That ruling came two weeks after Smith suspended the remainder of Brown’s sentences, which had totaled 50 years. Now, Brown will serve five years of supervised release. Without the evidence that might have exonerated him, he remains a rapist and killer under Mississippi state law.

name: VTDigger
title: Dismissed Bennington County murder case heads back to court
description:
The suspect is currently in custody serving a 12½-year prison sentence on federal drug and firearm charges.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Dismissed Bennington County murder case heads back to court.
text:
The Vermont Supreme Court in Montpelier on Tuesday, June 30, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The prosecution and defense are taking different views of a recent Vermont Supreme Court decision in a Bennington County murder case.
The state’s highest court, in a decision issued Friday, called on Judge Kerry McDonald-Cady to consider specific factors laid out in case law before deciding whether to dismiss a murder charge against Deven Moffitt, 36, formerly of Bennington, with prejudice, meaning it could not be refiled by the prosecution.
The judge had sided with Moffitt’s attorney more than a year ago in dismissing the charge with prejudice, prompting the appeal. 
Moffitt was charged in 2022 with second-degree murder in the 2019 death of his former girlfriend, Jessica Hildenbrandt, 43, of Ballston Spa, New York. Her remains, according to police, were found near an abandoned gravel pit in Searsburg. 
“We conclude that the court had authority to impose a sanction up to and including dismissal with prejudice, but that it should have considered the Sauve factors before permanently ending the prosecution,” Justice Nancy Waples wrote in the Vermont Supreme Court’s unanimous ruling.
Those factors, from the 1995 case State v. Sauve, include the seriousness of the charged offense, the evidence of guilt and the existence of any misconduct in the investigation and prosecution.
“We appreciate the opportunity to continue the pursuit of justice for Jessica and her family,” Bennington County State’s Attorney Erica Marthage said in a statement Friday. 
Vermont Defender General Matthew Valerio, whose office represented Moffitt in the appeal, said in an interview Monday that he didn’t expect the outcome of the case to change.
“It seems like a good one for the defense,” Valerio said of the high court’s ruling. “The court could write a more detailed opinion that includes the Sauve factors and come to the exact same result. So, it wasn’t the result that was wrong.”   
The Vermont Supreme Court decision is the latest legal twist in the case that had been working its way through the court system for several years and included prosecutorial missteps along the way.
In the case, there was an initial DNA match using a database linking the remains found in Searsburg to Hildenbrandt, according to court records. 
However, when additional testing to confirm the identity of the remains was not completed by the start of a scheduled trial in early 2025, the prosecution asked for delay to allow for expedited testing.
McDonald-Cady, the judge, ruled that the delay was not reasonable as the state already had enough time leading up to the trial to do that testing, with the original case filed against Moffitt in 2022.
The prosecution then moved to dismiss the case without prejudice, allowing it to be refiled at a later time. Moffitt’s lawyer in turn filed a motion to dismiss the case with prejudice, meaning it could not be filed again.
The judge agreed to dismiss the case with prejudice, concluding that the prosecution was improperly attempting to grant itself the continuance that the court had denied. 
The prosecution appealed that ruling to the Vermont Supreme Court leading to Friday’s decision.
Moffitt is currently in federal custody. He had been sentenced in June 2025 to 12½ years in prison following his convictions on federal drug and firearms charges.

text:
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, speaks to news reporters at the state Capitol in Oklahoma City on May 8, 2025. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — The leader of the Oklahoma House on Monday was nominated by the chamber’s Republicans to continue in his role next session. 
Rep. Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, was selected by his Republican peers during a closed-door caucus meeting and is likely to serve as the next Speaker of the House, according to a news release.
“I am honored to continue serving the people of Oklahoma in this role,” Hilbert said in a statement. “I recognize the weight of this responsibility and the work that lies ahead. There are significant challenges in our state and our responsibility is to take on those issues with a long-term vision, making meaningful progress today while laying the groundwork for a stronger Oklahoma for generations to come.”
He still needs to be elected during a public vote by the full chamber during its organizational day Jan. 5 when all 101 members are present. 
House members are set to be sworn in Tuesday for the upcoming session. 
As speaker, Hilbert oversees the House’s operations, appoints lawmakers to committees and leadership positions, and directs the flow of legislation. 
He is also third in line to replace the governor, behind the lieutenant governor and leader of the Oklahoma Senate. 
Hilbert’s party will maintain control over the House in the upcoming session, but it will shrink slightly as Democrats were able to flip six seats previously held by the GOP. 
He was first elected by his caucus in 2024 as the youngest House speaker in the state’s history. 
Hilbert was reelected by his constituents this year for another two years, marking his fifth of six potential terms. 
House Democrats also selected Rep. Melissa Provenzano, D-Tulsa, to lead their caucus for the upcoming session. She said she was “honored to serve with such a diverse, smart, and compassionate team.” 
“We will not waste time taking advantage of this incredible opportunity,” Provenzano said in a statement. “The work has already begun, and we look forward to doing the job Oklahomans entrusted us to do.”

name: WyoFile
title: Gordon stalls $13M grant to trona company that’s cutting 350 jobs in southwest Wyoming
description:
The grant is on hold until the state examines “the economic impacts to Sweetwater County … from the shifting global dynamics affecting Wyoming trona production,” Gov. Mark Gordon said.
The post Gordon stalls $13M grant to trona company that’s cutting 350 jobs in southwest Wyoming appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Gov. Mark Gordon will take “no action” for now on a $13 million state taxpayer-funded grant request by WE Soda, the London-based trona miner and soda ash producer that plans to cut 274 workers in southwest Wyoming beginning in January and a total 350 over the next two years.
“The conversation has changed, as a whole, from when this [Wyoming Energy Dominance Fund] application was first submitted,” Gordon said in a prepared statement Monday. “Before committing state severance tax resources, we need to have a better understanding of what the overall conditions this critical industry is facing, and what the future may look like.”
WE Soda announced Nov. 4 it would reduce its Wyoming workforce from about 850 to 500 over the next two years, primarily due to its new plan to shift its Westvaco trona mine from underground mining to drill-and-pump solution mining. 
WE Soda workers wait at a bus stop in Rock Springs for a ride to work their shifts at the company’s trona mine and soda ash operations. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
Prior to the announced layoffs, the company applied for — and the Wyoming Energy Authority recommended — a $13 million grant from the state’s new Energy Dominance Fund. WE Soda said it would use the money to build a “high-pressure natural gas supply connection from the Williams’ MountainWest Overthrust Pipeline system” to its Westvaco operations, an investment that’s not immediately tied to its plan shift to solution mining.
The union representing workers at WE Soda’s trona and soda ash operations — United Steelworkers Local 13214 — rallied workers and the community to implore Wyoming officials for help and for Gordon to pump the brakes on the grant and to instead “find a way to support the workers who made that corporation successful.”
Many southwest Wyoming leaders and residents echoed the sentiment.

The Brewery in Green River. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)

“The whole thing sucks,” a Green River bar manager told WyoFile on Thursday. She didn’t want to share her name for fear of retribution toward workers and local businesses. “I don’t think the state should subsidize an industry that is depleting our job market. We struggle with that anyway. This is going to make it worse.
“WE Soda,” she added, “can take a flying fuck into a rolling donut.”
The Energy Authority, which administers the state’s Energy Dominance Fund, told WyoFile last week that it had recommended the $13 million grant be approved before it learned of the company’s plans for major job cuts.
Gordon on Monday directed the agency “to conduct an expedited thorough examination of the economic impacts to Sweetwater County and the state from the shifting global dynamics affecting Wyoming trona production.”
The Energy Authority “stands ready to deliver on Gov. Gordon’s request to examine how this global market is changing and what those changes could mean for Wyoming,” Energy Authority Executive Director Rob Creager said in a prepared statement. “This work will give the state a stronger foundation for evaluating investments and identifying where support can make a lasting difference.”
A handful of companies mine trona in southwest Wyoming and process it — on site — into soda ash, the primary material used to make glass, myriad household products and industrial products such as large batteries. Wyoming once held about 14% of the global soda ash market worth some $1.3 billion in exports, and its operations directly employed some 2,500 workers in 2025.
Shifting Westvaco operations from underground mining to drill-and-pump “solution” recovery is necessary, WE Soda has said, due to market pressures from China and Mongolia flooding the global market with cheaper-to-produce soda ash.
WE Soda workers, joined by their families, attend a union meeting Nov. 12 in Rock Springs. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
The proposition of a state grant to help Wyoming operators compete in the tightening global market, local elected officials have said, is enticing but confounding due to the fact WE Soda’s job cuts are going to devastate the economy in southwest Wyoming.
“People won’t be able to pay their taxes, houses will go up for sale because people are going to lose their jobs,” Mayor-elect Stan Blake told WyoFile. “We have to help the miners who live in Green River.”
Gordon commended WE Soda for “working to get out in front of these major shifts.” But, he said, “the state needs to better understand how to efficiently and effectively support the industry, workers, families, and ancillary businesses that Sweetwater County depends on. State support through the WEA’s ongoing work in this area is vital.”

title: 4 companies to split $12M in federal funds to connect final eligible Nebraska locations to broadband
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska’s Broadband Office announced roughly $12 million in new federal funding would be distributed across four companies looking to connect the final 12% of locations across the state eligible for broadband internet connections under the Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment program. The NBO reopened its BEAD applications for a second round ea[...]
text:
An ultra fast broadband tower is seen on a rural farm. (Sandra Mu/Getty Images)LINCOLN — Nebraska’s Broadband Office announced roughly $12 million in new federal funding would be distributed across four companies looking to connect the final 12% of locations across the state eligible for broadband internet connections under the Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment program.
The NBO reopened its BEAD applications for a second round earlier this year after at least three companies backed out of signing their subgrants following changes to the program under a new presidential administration.
A BEAD on Nebraska broadband: State reopens provider applications with over $300M still in limbo

In late 2025, state lawmakers learned of changes coming to BEAD through President Donald Trump’s “Benefit of the Bargain” initiative. The update came a day after Gov. Jim Pillen announced that Nebraska had planned to use just $44.5 million of the $405 million the state was initially awarded through BEAD to connect unserved Nebraska locations to broadband.
In May, NBO announced the seven companies that did sign subgrants, following three weeks of repeated questions from the Examiner about the contracts. The companies were tasked with connecting 88% of the roughly 14,000 BEAD-eligible locations in the state.
The remaining 12% represented about 1,705 eligible locations, according to Monday’s press release, that will now be served by four companies that provide both fiber and licensed fixed wireless. An additional $11.9 million of BEAD funding has been approved with these awards along with about $4.1 million in matching funds.
Among the awardees are:

AMG Technology Investment Group LLC/Nextlink – serving 1,461 licensed fixed wireless locations
Midstates Data Transport LLC/Stealth – serving 155 fiber locations
Northeast Nebraska Telephone Co. – serving 224 fiber locations
Quick Current – serving four licensed fixed wireless locations

SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
While federal officials and Pillen had argued the original BEAD program was ineffective due to burdensome regulations imposed under the Biden administration, not all of Nebraska’s broadband advocates were convinced.
Gage County farmer Emily Haxby expressed concerns about the restructured program’s de-emphasis on fiber internet, which she said was unmatched in its scalability and reliability compared to other methods. However, it’s also one of the most expensive methods.
Nearly 80% of the second round BEAD awards went to providers looking to provide licensed fixed wireless broadband over fiber. Nebraska’s BEAD technology composition now stands at 10% fiber, 67% fixed wireless and 23% satellite, according to the press release.
U.S. Sen. Deb Fischer and others were concerned about what would happen to the more than $300 million in leftover BEAD funds for Nebraska. The NBO said the office is preparing for a new round of BEAD funding and has received a list of supplemental BEAD locations in Nebraska from the National Telecommunications and Information Administration.
Jay Omar, spokesman for Nebraska’s Department of Transportation, clarified that the upcoming round of BEAD funding, along with the additional $11.9 million in federal funds, all will come out of Nebraska’s initial $405 million allocation.
“These are more positive steps forward in connecting Nebraskans and communities around the state to reliable, high-speed broadband,” Pillen said in the press release. “But there is still work to be done. We have just received guidance on the next step of the program to capture additional unserved locations. My office is already working hard to bring the next phase of this federal investment home to Nebraska.”
