To understand today’s conflict requires turning back in time, toward events that date back centuries, then tracing grievances from recent years through to the present. 
It revolves around what is happening on the 14-acre parcel where the current housing is located, which is owned by the stateʻs Department of Land and Natural Resources and borders Hawaiian homelands. The refuge McMillan built is to be relocated and expanded to the Makapuʻu side of the same property. 
There, the expansion — Hui Mahiʻai Village — is planned with water, sewer and electrical hookups that its forerunner doesn’t have. McMillan is to lead it and the current residents are to be joined by the dozens of additional homeless people she plans to welcome.

Waimānalo resident Mialisa Otis inspects a map of the proposed Hui Mahi’ai Village project in Waimānalo. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)

The project has set neighbors who have known each other since childhood against one another. Tensions have spread to streets nearby, including a human blockade of trucks headed to the work site. An October community meeting became so heated that police officers hovered to keep an eye on things.
Funded by public and philanthropic dollars, the expansion is a joint project of the state Office of Homelessness and Housing Solutions and the nonprofit aoi Foundation. In 2018, the foundation built a homeless village near Sand Island, Kahauiki, where about 700 people now live. The nonprofit’s development arm, Mahiʻai Development, was given a 65-year lease in February for the Waimānalo ​property.
Nearly everything about the new project is subject to debate, even basic facts, with no apparent common ground.
“If the emergency proclamation was not in place here, the community would not have let this happen.” Hiwahiwa Kaheaku-Rodenhurst, Waimānalo resident
Yet, to the dismay of opponents, it has been fast-tracked under Gov. Josh Green’s 2023 emergency proclamation on homelessness. That means the project legally leapfrogged certain initial zoning and permitting processes and environmental reviews so that work could proceed faster — although it must still meet health and other safety codes. 
“If the emergency proclamation was not in place here, the community would not have let this happen,” said Hiwahiwa Kaheaku-Rodenhurst, a  Waimānalo resident who is a leader of the opposition. 
For McMillan and her supporters, the kauhale expansion is a clear win-win. It will house more of the nearly 200 people who have been identified as homeless from Kāneʻohe to Kailua to Waimānalo, they say, and continue the work she has won plaudits for by creating a close-knit community of people whose lives are on the upswing as they recover from hard times.
“The goal really is to serve our community and get people off of the streets into a sustainable, healthy, stable home where they can jump off from into a new path,” said Jun Yang, director of the state’s homelessness office.
“The root cause of the opposition is they just don’t like homeless people.”Kalaninui Akau, Waimānalo resident
The project’s supporters maintain that at its core, the opposition is mostly a reluctance to have a kauhale nearby.
“The root cause of the opposition is they just don’t like homeless people,” said Kalaninui Akau, who grew up in Waimānalo, where more than half of residents are Native Hawaiian. Akau still lives there, and has produced promotional videos for McMillan — most for free — about Hui Mahiʻai ʻĀina. 
Others say it threatens a way of life.
“We grew up here, it was country,” said Cindy Parker, who was raised in the same house on ‘Oluʻolu Street where she raised her own family, on Hawaiian homestead land bordering the new kauhale property. 
Parker looked beyond her backyard to where she used to see monkeypod trees and koa haole, neighbors’ cows and sheep, owls at night. 
That all has been replaced by a bed of earth that raised the land about 13 feet to prepare for construction of the new housing project. 
Parker’s property flooded during the March Kona low storms, she said, because a retaining wall erected around parts of the site prevented water from draining toward the mountains as it used to. Portions of the wall have since been removed following discussions with the developer, but now Parker has other concerns, too: She has trouble breathing these days, which she blames on dust kicked up by backfill dirt being brought in.
“This is not,” she said, “what we want.”
The Land


Blanche McMillan sits under a tree at Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina, the village she created in 2020 to house people living along Kalanianaʻole Highway in Waimānalo. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Waimānalo resident Tracey Parker backyard looks out on the plot of land where the Hui Mahi’ai Village is proposed. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Waimānalo resident Mialisa Otis, center, talks through the chain link fence with Carly Parker, left, and Cindy Parker. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


On her phone, Mialisa Otis shows a photo of construction on the land where Hui Mahi’ai Village is being planned. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Heavy equipment has begun to grade the proposed Hui Mahi’ai Village plot, although neighbors have complained that some earth movement led to flooding. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Security cameras have been added to  the proposed Hui Mahi’ai Village plot. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


The complicated history of land in Hawaiʻi looms large in the current clash.
After the Great Mahele of 1848, King Kamehameha III designated roughly 4,000 acres of the Waimānalo area’s Crown Lands, including where Hui Mahʻai Village is to be built behind what is now ‘Olu‘olu Street. Seized in the illegal 1893 overthrow of the Hawaiian Kingdom, all those lands were eventually transferred to the U.S. government. 
In 1959, when Hawaiʻi became a state, the land was transferred again, to the state Department of Land and Natural Resources, which still owns and manages it. Under the laws that governed Hawaiʻi’s admission as a state, public trust lands are to be used for “the betterment of the conditions of Native Hawaiians,” among other conditions.
That has shaped how many opponents view the kauhale project. When the facilitator of a contentious Oct. 6 community meeting suggested Hawai‘i’s fractured history through conquest and imperialism makes Native Hawaiians susceptible to division, one opponent called out: “It’s not about Hawaiians having a difference. It’s about how it all began.”
In more recent years, in 2015, the state land and resources department approved a community garden project on the property to be run by McMillan and a local nonprofit. 
That project sputtered, McMillan said. And in 2020, she switched tracks. 
With Covid advancing, and more than 350 people living alongside Kalanianaʻole Highway, she invited anyone who wanted to follow her to move onto the departmentʻs land, located behind her childhood home. She asked them to help her clear it of junk and brush and build homes for themselves. 
“The government, they said, ‘You have to stop.’ I said, ʻI ain’t stopping for you. I’m going to continue doing my work for the people.” Blanche McMillan, who founded Hui Mahiʻai ʻĀina
The land was zoned for agricultural uses and in a flood zone, so no building was allowed, but that proved no obstacle for McMillan. Within a few months, more than 30 people took up her invitation. 
“The government, they said, ‘You have to stop,’” she says today. “I said, ʻI ain’t stopping for you. I’m going to continue doing my work for the people. I don’t care what you say or what you do. I’m going to do it.’”
McMillan, 72, came from a family of 17 children, all raised in a small house next to the property where Hui Mahiʻai ʻĀina is now located. These days, when she’s not making the rounds of the village, she can often be found sitting in front of her childhood home with village residents. She watched her parents take care of hungry people in town and others who were lost, lonely and in need, she said, and became determined to follow their lead.
“I said, ‘One day I’m going to become what they were,’” said McMillan, who is universally referred to as Aunty Blanche. “Today that’s what I am. And when the pandemic happened, “I knew there was time for me to walk the talk and do the work.”
McMillan has a voice that needs no microphone, laughs quickly and rarely expresses doubt. She frequently cites God and love as her guides. In conversation, she often starts sentences with: “You know what, let me tell you something.”
There may be nobody in Waimānalo who doesn’t know her — including those who now find themselves questioning the wisdom of her plans.
“Aunty Blanche is a respected elder and has been for many years,” said Kimeona Kane, chair of the Waimānalo Neighborhood Board.
Kane believes the expansion project has strayed too far from McMillan’s original intent of helping people from Waimānalo. It has been forced onto the community, he said, causing “significant chaos.”
“There’s been a lot of generational and intergenerational infighting,” Kane said. “It’s been very harmful for the community because now we have polarizing positions where people are starting to attack personal beliefs and lots of other things are taking place.”
As McMiIlan’s village grew and became a fixture, though, government officials came around to her side. 
During his first state of the state speech in January 2023, Green signed his emergency proclamation on homelessness, officially launching the kauhale initiative. That month, an annual count found 6,223 people homeless in Hawaiʻi, the great majority on Oʻahu. 
In announcing the proclamation, Green singled out McMillan as a homeless advocate who was “showing that it takes the embrace of a village to help people find their way to a permanent home.”
“Business as usual won’t work anymore,” he said, “there is simply too much on the line to accept the status quo.”
‘No One Can Stop Her’


Resident Hi’i Spencer, right, shows a photo of her with her boyfriend Darien to Blanche McMillan outside her hale at the Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Resident Joey Santiago outside her hale at Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina, built during the pandemic by and for homeless people. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Residents of the current Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina share a common outdoor eating area. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Resident Kainoa Choy sits outside at Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina, where some live in cottages and others in tents. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Cancer survivor Richard Muraoka reflects on his time living at Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina, where he came after living in a Kapolei park. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina resident Christine Felix talks to Blanche from inside her family home on the property. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


By late 2024, the governor’s initiative had a full head of steam, with nearly 20 kauhale opened. The state’s homelessness office — then headed by Yang’s predecessor, John Mizuno — proposed building a bigger kauhale on the Waimānalo property in collaboration with aio Foundation.
The new kauhale would absorb Hui Mahʻai ʻĀina and house 188 people altogether, in 116 single, double and family units, and include a communal kitchen, health clinic, classrooms and a garden to also serve the larger community.
“I was very impressed with the model, but with this wahine as well. No one can stop her.” Dawn Chang, then executive director of DLNR
In a sign of how much favor McMillan had gained by then, she and the village she had skirted the law to create were held up as examples to follow.
“I was very impressed with the model, but with this wahine as well. No one can stop her,” Dawn Chang, then executive director of the Department of Land and Natural Resources, said at the October 2024 board meeting where the application for the expansion was unanimously approved.
It was made clear the project had blessings from the very top.
“The governor is in full support of this project, full support of Aunty Blanche,” Brandon Mitsuda, special assistant at the homelessness office, told the board members. “She is the model we follow, and anything Aunty Blanche needs, we help her.”
But the meeting also offered some of the first glimpses of the dissension to follow when Kane, of the Neighborhood Board, said the community hadn’t been properly involved in the process before that point.
“As much as we love and really appreciate what Aunty Blanche is doing, there has been very little to no community involvement with this new expansion,” he said.
Kane said he had told Mizuno that Waimānalo residents had not been adequately consulted and Mizuno had promised to pull it from the agenda. That didn’t happen, Kane said.
After first agreeing to discuss the matter, Mizuno declined to talk with Civil Beat.
At the 2024 meeting, board member Wesley “Kaiwi” Yoon asked Kane whether the project might face complications in the future: “Do you anticipate any hihia with this initiative going forward?”
Kane answered carefully. Some community concerns about the original village hadn’t been addressed, he said, and so the expansion was likely to face pushback of some sort despite a local desire for “supporting the need and effort to address the issue of homelessness in our community.” 
He said: “I anticipate that there will be some concerns shared in and around the area. However … there is still a beautiful love that Aunty Blanche has brought to this particular topic and issue within our community. So it’s hard to tell at this point what it’s going to look like.”
What It Looks Like
Waimānalo resident Hiwahiwa Kaheaku-Rodenhurst pauses at the entrance to a cave believed sacred to the Native Hawaiians. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Two years later, the opposition has crystallized. Foes have formed a nonprofit, Pono ʻOluʻolu, to fight the project. They have collected nearly 1,000 online signatures, and are seeking legal help to stop construction.
Tense encounters have played out on the streets around the site. Village residents who serve on McMillan’s security team have trailed opponents on ATVs as they walked nearby. Members of the team showed up to keep watch, stony-faced, as opponents gathered by the roadside this summer planning to block trucks from entering the property. 
Differences have spilled over at community meetings, too, where it’s clear opponents are tallying grievances and objections — among them an insistence that rules underlying the governor’s proclamation have not been followed.
A February 2024 archaeological inspection by a firm hired by Mahiʻai Development had uncovered some recent grading and clearing of the site, well before the Department of Land and Natural Resources approved the project. 
Likewise, they point out that in November 2025, months before the lease was approved this February, work started in earnest to clear and backfill the property with trucked-in dirt to elevate it above flood levels.
And they have called attention to a letter the state office of homelessness sent to Mahiʻai Development in August confirming the project was certified under the emergency proclamation. That proves, they claim, that the project had been proceeding illegally for months. 
Yang, however, said the letter was just a paperwork step since the project was already certified.
Opponents are also worried about the length of the 65-year lease. The proclamation’s terms include a condition that the property be used for homeless housing for at least 20 years  — which they say opens the door to more unwelcome types of development after year 20.
They say their concerns about flooding are not being fully addressed — the developer says they have been — and that the site’s cultural importance is being brushed aside.
“So all these kūpuna here — this is going to be an Otake Camp, you watch.”Gary Silva, Waimānalo resident
Pointing toward the kauhale site, Gary Silva compared what would happen there in a flood to a North Shore community extensively damaged in the March Kona low storms.
“We’re very low here, everybody is low compared to up there,” he said. “So all these kūpuna here — this is going to be an Otake Camp, you watch.”
Silva, who grew up in Waimānalo, owns a horse ranch that his uncles started about 65 years ago a quarter mile or so from where the kauhale is planned, just beyond ʻOluʻolu Street. It too flooded during the March storms. 
He helped build many of the villageʻs tiny homes when McMillan was getting started. Now he is dead set against its expansion.
As officialdom has come to favor McMillan, Silva said she has come to enjoy her new stature among government officials too much.
“She’s trying to get all this land from the governor so she can build herself up,” he said. “It doesn’t make me feel well.”
Besides flooding concerns, Silva said the expansion would disturb nearby cultural sites.
Chief among those, he said, is a cave called Ke Ana Luawai, just mauka of the project site. Surrounded by lāʻau lapaʻau — medicinal plants — the cave holds a freshwater spring that Silva said centuries ago sustained wounded Hawaiian warriors seeking respite from battle. 
“It’s super sacred ground,” Kaheaku-Rodenhurst agreed. “You do not desecrate it. You do not disrespect it.”


Waimānalo residents Onepookela Craig-Rodenhurst, Tracey Parker, Bernard Sampaga and Hiwahiwa Kaheaku-Rodenhurst marvel at a cave believed to be sacred to the Native Hawaiian people. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Waimānalo resident Mialisa Otis explores the Ke Ana Luawai cave, just mauka of the project site.  (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Mialisa Otis holds seashells found inside the cave, which holds a fresh water spring thought to have sustained wounded Hawaiian warriors. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Waimānalo residents Bernard Sampaga, left, and Gary Silva examine an ancient Hawaiian petroglyph on a rock wall. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


“It’s super sacred ground. You do not desecrate it. You do not disrespect it.”Hiwahiwa Kaheaku-Rodenhurst
Kaheaku-Rodenhurst and her husband, Onepookela Craig-Rodenhurst, both Hawaiian sovereignty activists, were asked by Pono ʻOluʻolu to help fight the project and are forming another nonprofit, Kupa’a o Waimānalo, to fund and spearhead legal action against the project.
“A lot of people are being woken up,” she said. 
Yang said he first learned about the cave at the Oct. 6 community meeting. “I am interested if these are something of significance, we’d love to be able to see if we can find a way to preserve them,” he said.
A report from ASM Affiliates, a California-based cultural resource management firm, said it had reviewed literature about the site and inspected three acres of its surface in February 2024. The report described the historic nature of the Waimānalo area as a landing site and occasional battleground for Hawaiians from neighbor islands, but said the firm had “identified no historic properties within the project area.” 
Opponents say that report is inadequate.
“It’s just the surface. They’re just kind of kicking rocks around,” said Mialisa Otis, who lives on Waimānaloʻs backroads and has led efforts to block trucks carrying backfill from entering the property.
The letter Yang’s office sent to Mahiʻai Development in August confirming certification of the project under the proclamation noted that the state’s historic preservation department requested ongoing archaeological monitoring at the site because it does not have enough information to determine what might be below the ground’s surface. 
An archaeologist monitor has been on site, Yang said, and has submitted a report that the state is now reviewing.
How It Was ʻFramed’
Waimānalo resident Bernard Sampaga goes over a property map of ʻOluʻolu Street, which borders the planned Hui Mahiʻai Village parcel, with resident Tracey Parker in the driveway of her Waimānalo home. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
As the fight over the kauhale continues, Kane’s 2024 comments to the Department of Land and Natural Resources board about a lack of consultation have grown into wider complaints that the community has been largely ignored.
Opponents acknowledge that just two of them turned up at a Nov. 13, 2024 meeting at Hui Mahiʻai ʻĀina, a month after the application to develop a kauhale on the land was approved. But they say a second meeting, held on the property right before the Nov. 15, 2025 groundbreaking, came too late in the process for any real input to be gathered.
“It was in the news. Nothing. No comment. Nobody was upset. No one was saying, ‘Oh, why is this project here?’”Rep. Lisa Marten, whose district includes Waimānalo
Supporters of the project cite the lack of major opposition at those meetings as evidence that opposition has been drummed up only more recently.
“It was a large event,” said Rep. Lisa Marten, whose district includes Waimānalo, referring to the 2025 meeting. “It was in the news. Nothing. No comment. Nobody was upset. No one was saying, ‘Oh, why is this project here?’”
Marten emphasized that she did not initiate the project, although she does support it and attended the groundbreaking. She said she has spent hours batting down incorrect information from both sides in the dispute, including McMillan’s statement to HNN that she wants to house up to 1,000 people and opponents’ social media posts showing condominium towers on the site. 
Opponents name Marten among the officials who have stymied their input. At a March meeting this year on the property to discuss neighbors’ concerns about flooding, drainage and security, Otis said Marten told people like her who don’t live on ‘Olu‘olu Street that they couldn’t participate. 
Marten remembered things differently. 
Otis invited her to the March meeting about the flooding at the Parker residence, along with other issues, Marten said. She then initiated another meeting the following month to address those concerns and invited immediate neighbors and the project’s engineer and developer to it. She said Otis and others arrived uninvited at that meeting, but stayed and participated.
“I wanted to immediately figure out solutions to those solvable problems,” Marten said. “I didn’t want it to be about other people’s issues with the project that were not directly impacted by those drainage and security issues.” 
The meeting led to the installation of security fences between the kauhale site and neighboring properties in response to worries that future kauhale residents would enter neighbors’ yards uninvited, and the engineer agreed to new drainage measures, Marten said.
During another meeting later that month, at Waimānalo Beach Park, Otis said McMillan tried to overwhelm opponents by bringing along a crowd of more than 60 Hui Mahiʻai ʻĀina residents. 
Marten, who is chair of the House Committee on Human Services and Homelessness, said that it was only when the opposition broadened the scope of its complaints — from flooding and security to issues about encroaching on Hawaiian homelands and cultural and environmental concerns — that the pushback really grew.
“It became a social media thing with just a lot of propaganda and misinformation,” she said. “That’s when a lot of people across the community who don’t even live nearby, even in other communities who don’t even live in Waimānalo, became very concerned about it because it was framed as taking away Hawaiian rights.”
She added that she believes community members have unrealistic expectations about how much they can shape such projects.
“The community wishes they could choose what happens with every plot of land,” Marten said. “But they don’t get to.”
An Apology

The Koʻolau Mountains tower over some of the hale built by and for homeless people during the pandemic at Hui Mahi’ai ʻĀina. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)

On Oct. 6, the showdown reached the Waimānalo Hawaiian Homestead Association hālau, a pitch-roofed pavilion open to the air on all sides where gatherings are more often for large celebrations — of events such as weddings, birthdays or graduations — that mark people coming together rather than being driven apart.
With the meeting about to get underway, McMillan stood before a crowd spilling outside, and said she was sorry.
“If I have done anything wrong, I apologize,” she said. Many in the audience applauded. 
McMillan didn’t explain why at the time, but later made it clear that her apology was not because she had done anything wrong.
“The Lord had told me forgive the people, what they’re doing to us, to all of us in Waimānalo,” she said. “So I needed to let the whole Waimānalo community know who I was. And I made sure that I forgive each and every one of them.” 
Sponsored by Green’s office, the meeting had been promoted as a town hall to answer questions about the project. Officials were there to describe Hui Mahiʻai Village, including Yang, representing the state office of homelessness, and Duane Kurisu, a prominent businessman who is president of aio Foundation and leader of Mahiʻai Development.
Opponents were there in force, too, including Parker, Otis and Kaheaku-Rodenhurst.
Kumu Hinaleimoana Wong, a longtime community leader asked by the governor’s office to facilitate the meeting, opened it with a pule. But the effort to start off on a peaceful note failed.
A group in the audience erupted as Wong finished, holding signs that read, “Betrayers,” “Shame” and “Judas,” and “Pilau,” “Kapulu,” and “Haumia Nui,” or corrupt, desecrating and filthy. 
Craig-Rodenhurst began chanting in a staccato kepakepa style to convey, he later said, his ancestors’ argument against violating sacred land — and to call for it to be preserved.
“If more development happens, the more of our history gets lost and then everything is just in the books,” he said later.
After the outburst subsided, Wong — an artist, educator and political and cultural activist — tried to explain her role as a neutral facilitator. There was more loud applause. But as Wong, at the time a candidate for Oʻahu resident trustee for the Office of Hawaiian Affairs, continued, someone else shouted, “Are you Hawaiian with us, or are you Hawaiian with them?” 
“Let’s be clear,” Wong responded. “No matter how any kanaka feels. Support. No support. That’s not who I’m being tonight. I came because even when you talk any kine to me, I’m still gonna tell you I love you.”
At one point, a clearly frustrated Kurisu told the naysayers: “You know what? I’m not kanaka. But we’re building it for you.” Shouts of both derision and support greeted his statement.
Nearly three hours later, as officials tried to bring the meeting to a close, the vice chair of the Waimānalo Neighborhood Board raised the specter of historic land rights. 
“The land … is, in fact, Crown lands and it’s deemed Crown lands because of our kingdom,” Kūʻikeokalani Kamakea-Ohelo said.
Would it, he asked, be transferred back to the Department of Hawaiian Homelands in the future so “we can ensure that kānaka are taken care of in compliance with 1959 Admissions Act?”
His question was met with scattered applause, but nobody answered it.
“The divide can be made smaller by reminding ourselves we come from the same set of genealogies. We’re the survivors.”Kumu Hinaleimoana Wong, longtime community leader
As people started to stand, gather in new groups and disperse, Wong tried to close the night on a hopeful chord, circling back to the experiences Native Hawaiians have faced and share.
“The divide can be made smaller by reminding ourselves we come from the same set of genealogies. We’re the survivors. We’re all the survivors after the collision with foreigners,” she said. “We’re the ones that never succumb to the diseases. And we’re still hanging on despite all of the injustices to the community. 
“So I ask all of you, no matter where you stood tonight: Please aloha one another.”

Tracey Parker, right, embraces Mialisa Otis at Parker’s residence just outside the proposed Hui Mahi’ai Village plot in Waimānalo. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)

Later she said she understood the oppositionʻs anger.
“Anything encroaching upon what little is left, anytime you have anything that’s going to serve beyond Hawaiian interests in a community that has endured and survived historical and generational trauma,” she said, “this is the reaction that you’re going to get.” 
McMillan is tired of the controversy.
“What the governor says, it goes. It doesn’t matter,” she said. “He’s doing the right thing. He’s taking care of the people.”
Those opposed to Hui Mahiʻai Village have judged without knowledge what she does and what it will be, she said.
“It makes me sick because we’re Hawaiian. And it’s unreal what they do. But you know what? I don’t pay attention. I just do what I have to do,” she said. “You should put your two hands together and your mouth and your brains into this property and help me out.”
Work on the project has stopped in recent weeks while Honolulu’s permitting department and the state’s office of historical preservation review plans submitted by the kauhale’s developers, including the report of the archaeologist required to monitor the site. 
It’s a normal part of the timeline, Yang said, unlikely to lead to a lengthy delay. “We’re just waiting on these next steps as we work through the process,” he said.
“When my friends talk to me, what they tell me is, ‘You guys going lose. You’re going up against millionaires and the state.’” Cindy Parker, who lives near the proposed kauhale property. 
Kane, the Neighborhood Board president, said he believes only legal action could slow or halt the project. 
“Not even being able to take a pause right on this and just help figure it out, that has been crazy to me,” he said.
The opposition is nonetheless digging in, flooding social media with posts making their case, researching the land’s history, preparing to take to the streets again if necessary. 
They remain undaunted by the odds.
“When my friends talk to me, what they tell me is, ‘You guys going lose. You’re going up against millionaires and the state,’” Parker said, referring to Kurisu, who heads the development company. “What I always tell everybody that tells me that is, ‘Well, we’re going to give it our best shot and we’re going to do our damnedest to stop it.’”
The post Clash Over Kauhale Pits Neighbor Against Neighbor In Waimānalo appeared first on Honolulu Civil Beat.

title: Firefighter Accused Of Rape Pockets $150K Not To Work As Inquiry Lags
description:
A Honolulu fire battalion chief accused of rape in Feburary 2025 has been collecting his $150,000 annual salary at home as a workplace investigation drags on. 
The post Firefighter Accused Of Rape Pockets $150K Not To Work As Inquiry Lags appeared first on Honolulu Civil Beat.
text:
A Honolulu fire battalion chief accused of raping a colleague at fire headquarters has been getting paid to stay home for nearly two years as the department conducts an internal investigation.
Blake Takahashi was accused of locking a female subordinate in his office on Valentine’s Day 2025 before raping her. He turned himself in to police six days later and has been on paid leave ever since, the department confirmed to Civil Beat. 
The administrative investigation has dragged on even as a criminal investigation apparently concluded. 
The Honolulu Prosecuting Attorney declined to file charges, according to a lawsuit filed by the alleged victim last month. The lawsuit does not say exactly when prosecutors declined to file charges. The prosecutor’s office would not comment.
While administrative investigations can take longer than two years, the vast majority are wrapped up in less than six months, according to a 2024 Civil Beat review of paid leave periods for 350 employees across more than 24 state and county agencies. 

Civil Beat: 
Government Workers In Hawaii Get Paid Not To Work As Misconduct Investigations Drag On For Months Or Years

Because the allegations in this case are so serious, the department should be pressing to complete its review thoroughly and quickly, said Ted Hong, a Hilo-based employment attorney. Hong said he has represented clients who’ve been accused of similar crimes in the workplace, and in his experience, the internal investigations are usually done within three to six months. 
Honolulu Fire Battalion Chief Blake Takahashi (center) was named manager of the year in 2024. He is pictured with Chief Sheldon Hao and Deputy Chief Jason Samala. HFD/2024
“Something this serious, it has to be resolved quickly,” he said. “When these types of investigations linger for a year or more, it affects morale within the department.” 
For the last 21 months, Takahashi has continued to collect his salary, which is about $150,000 a year. The department must also pay more to cover his shifts, either by paying another battalion chief overtime or temporarily promoting someone of a lower rank to fill in. 
Takahashi’s attorney, Thomas Otake, did not respond to calls and text messages seeking comment for this story. But Otake previously told Civil Beat that Takahashi denies the allegations. Takahashi did not return a voicemail seeking comment. 
If Takahashi were to be charged and convicted of a felony, he could be at risk of losing part of his pension under the state’s pension forfeiture law. 
‘Unacceptable’ Investigation Length 
The investigation is being conducted jointly by the Honolulu Fire Department and the city Equal Employment Opportunity Office, fire department spokesman Jacob Pekelo said in an email. 
When asked why the department’s investigation was taking longer than the criminal investigation, he said the department was “not familiar” with the prosecutor’s process nor what the prosecutor reviewed. He added that the investigation is ongoing and the department does not have a projected completion date. 
The alleged victim, who has been identified only as Jane Doe, accused Takahashi of inviting her into his office to discuss work matters on the evening of Feb. 14, 2025. He then encouraged her to drink alcohol with him, and made sexual advances toward her, as she pulled away and told him “no,” the lawsuit says. 
The Honolulu Fire Department generally fills high-ranking vacancies by temporarily promoting someone from the rank immediately below.  Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2024
He locked the door, physically restrained her and raped her while she cried “tears of pain and fear,” the lawsuit says. 
The department has yet to release any determination from its internal investigation, which has caused Doe distress, according to the lawsuit. 
A recent Civil Beat public records request for surveillance footage from fire headquarters the night of the alleged rape was denied by the fire department, which cited its ongoing investigation. 
Fire officials will likely have to release some evidence from their investigation during the discovery process now that a civil lawsuit has been filed, Hong said. But much of it could remain sealed from public view because of the pending investigation. 
Nicole Kalakau, an attorney representing Doe, said the slow pace of the investigation is a major reason why Doe wanted to sue the department. In the suit, Doe accuses the Honolulu Prosecuting Attorney of declining to file charges against Takahashi to protect him and shield the county from liability. 
Kalakau called the length of the internal investigation “unacceptable.” 

Blake Takahashi has been on paid leave since February 2025. Fire Department/ Candace Akiona

“It leaves you to wonder whether (the department) was simply hoping to wait Jane Doe out, betting that if they stayed silent long enough, she’d give up and go away,” she said. “Meanwhile, Battalion Chief Takahashi keeps collecting a paycheck, and Jane Doe is stuck with no answers and no way to move forward.”
Kerrie Urosevich, CEO of the Domestic Violence Action Center — an organization providing support and legal services for victims of domestic violence — said the message the protracted investigation sends to women in the workplace is: “The system is going to fail you.” 
While she said she recognizes the need for due process and the importance of a thorough investigation, the lack of answers from the department raises more questions. 
“Why does it take two years to investigate an incident like this? And why are taxpayers paying that kind of money to pay somebody on paid leave?” she said. “For me, it tells me they didn’t value the situation enough to investigate in a timely way, and to me, that’s a culture problem.” 
Bobby Lee, president of the Hawaiʻi Fire Fighters Association, the union representing firefighters statewide, said because battalion chief is a managerial position, Takahashi is not represented by the union. Lee declined to comment on Takahashi’s case, but said generally, when there is a vacancy in a high-ranking position in the department, someone immediately below will step up to fill it. 
In this case, a captain would normally move up to fill in for the battalion chief position, a third-tier firefighter would move into the captain role, and so on. 
“It basically pushes one person up to cover the next person,” he said. 
How Long Should Investigations Take? 
Lee said when investigations involve union members, the union tries to push for them to get resolved as quickly as possible, but they can sometimes drag on for years. He recalled one case involving a Big Island firefighter charged with negligent homicide that lasted seven years. 
But that is not the norm. 
According to Civil Beat’s 2024 review, the average paid leave period for employees under investigation was six months while the median was three months. 
Investigations into allegations of workplace misconduct usually take 3-6 months. Honolulu fire’s investigation into Takahashi has dragged on nearly two years. Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2024
Debra Allen, a Honolulu-based private investigator who does workplace investigations, said she has conducted investigations that lasted a little over a year, but it’s rare. 
Internal investigations are supposed to run concurrently, but entirely separately, from criminal investigations, she said. While police investigate whether any crimes were committed, workplace investigations focus on any policies that may have been violated.
When a third-party investigator, like Allen, who owns 808 Investigations, completes its review, it will usually present a final report to the agency, which in turn will determine whether any discipline will be doled out to the employee. 
Butch Galdeira, chair of the Honolulu Fire Commission, which is responsible for oversight of the fire department, also declined to comment for this story, citing the pending lawsuit. 
Hong said the burden of proof in an internal investigation is much different than that of a criminal investigation. For prosecutors to file charges, they must believe that they can prove their case beyond a reasonable doubt. 
An employer only needs to have “clear and convincing evidence” that a worker violated policy in order to take disciplinary action, he said. That would mean they considered the allegation substantially more likely to be true than untrue, though they could still have some doubt. 
Even though Takahashi was never charged criminally, an internal review could still deem him eligible for termination or some other disciplinary measure. 
“It makes no difference what happens on the criminal side,” Hong said. “The department and the city and county have their own standards of conduct for employees.” 
He also said he sees little reason for the investigation to take so long. 
“Barring one of the key witnesses being in a coma for two years,” he said, “I can’t see how this should be taking this long.”

title: Why Are We Trying To Get Rid Of Maui’s Police Chief?
description:
John Pelletier has listened, earned trust, made changes and proved himself. That's good leadership.
The post Why Are We Trying To Get Rid Of Maui’s Police Chief? appeared first on Honolulu Civil Beat.
text:
No, really. Why?
We needed a change in the Maui Police Department. We needed someone with the qualifications, experience, and willingness to make that change.
And we got John Pelletier.
He earned the position through an open, measurable process. He was selected for his qualifications alone. No relationships. Just skills.
His plan was to change the authoritarian system of policing we knew to community-led policing. That is what he meant when he talked about 21st-century policing. He had a plan, implemented it, used metrics to evaluate its progress, and adjusted based on what those metrics showed.
That’s the bare minimum we should expect from accountable leadership.
But we made him work for us without a hint of care.



Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

We did not care if we were dismissive, purposefully ignorant, hypercritical, or unkind because we believed he deserved it. Because he wasn’t one of us. He wasn’t from here. And he was police.
For the first few years, I refused to like him. I stayed very critical of him.
And I understand why others would, too.
Maui Police Chief John Pelletier says he believes he was put on leave because of what he says are investigations into corruption in the mayor’s office.  (Cammy Clark/Civil Beat/2024)
Our fundamental cultural flaw here is: If I don’t know your auntie or the high school you went to, you don’t belong here.
You don’t belong here. That’s heavy.
Nā Kānaka are still reeling from the grief and loss of what once was and are picking up the broken pieces of that identity. I feel that so deeply.
I’m not kanaka. My cultural pottery may be different, but the motions of searching for the scattered pieces of who we once were and trying to put them back into something even close to what once was, under the conditions we’ve been left in, are painfully familiar.
That pain doesn’t go away just because it started generations ago. That wound heals slowly because of what we face every day.
As if I can blame anyone for not accepting change?
I understand the desire to protect yourself. To refuse to engage with a system that has given you so many reasons not to trust it.
It took me years to do anything different. To see a person behind a uniform.
The world of policing is weird.
So many rules and so much structure. Sameness. It feels unnatural. They’re not robots.
They’re people.
People who flow between the rigidity of the law and the complexity of humanity, trying not to break either one. That’s a weird world to exist in.
The thing is, we have really good people at MPD who decided to become police officers.
They could have been veterinarians or professors or pitmasters or kumu hula or chicken farmers, but for whatever reason, life led them to policing in Maui County.
Being led by some … outsider.
It is hard to lead humans. Even harder when they don’t inherently trust you.
No one in Maui County who had suffered an injustice was going to inherently trust John Pelletier. He was going to have to do the work to prove himself.
And he did.
One of the first things Chief Pelletier did was create the MPD Multicultural Advisory Counsel. I am a founding member.
Instead of closing the door on the toughest critics of MPD, John invited us in.So, we yelled at him in his own office.
I refused to give him compliments or praise. I often reminded him in our MMAC meetings that it was not my job to praise him. It was my job to hold him accountable (fairly).
I tested him. I forced him into uncomfortable spaces to see if he could handle them.
But he was patient. He listened. He learned. He made changes.
That’s good leadership.
It took me five years to let my guard down. And these are not my stolen lands. I’ve never been incarcerated. I’ve never had a mental health crisis that required first responders. I’ve never been unhoused. I am economically stable. I am free.
It still took me five years.
We need every bit of knowledge and skill we can get.
The resistance is not lost on me.
But should we keep doing this?
We are in an environmental crisis.
We need every bit of knowledge and skill we can get.
We need to manage the resources we have. All of them. Including the people.
Chief John Pelletier is a resource. His experience, his ability to manage complex organizations during a crisis, his willingness to learn — for us.
Have we been squandering a resource?
From every book I’ve read and every story I’ve been told about Hawaiian leadership, one thing has been clear to me.
Nā Aliʻi were smart.
They knew how to manage resources. They knew how to incorporate new technologies.
They understood consequences. They knew how to be open to change and how to cleverly utilize it to benefit everyone.
Which brings me back to: Why are we doing this?
Maybe the why is that we are being taught something right now.
Maybe we are being taught that good resource management isn’t just knowing how to use a resource.
Maybe it’s having the wisdom to recognize one in the first place.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Kaua‘i’s Mayor-Elect: ‘I Don’t Want To See Coco Palms Rebuilt’
description:
Mel Rapozo, who will be sworn in as mayor next month, plans to open an investigation into the development’s rebuilding permits. 
The post Kaua‘i’s Mayor-Elect: ‘I Don’t Want To See Coco Palms Rebuilt’ appeared first on Honolulu Civil Beat.
text:
Kaua‘i Mayor-elect Mel Rapozo plans to open an investigation into the validity of county permits to rebuild the iconic Coco Palms hotel 34 years after it was ravaged by Hurricane ‘Iniki.
Community groups have already sued the county over the issue, which stems from permits the Planning Commission granted the developer in 2015 and 2018. The case is pending before the Hawai‘i Supreme Court. 
“I believe there are some serious problems with that development,” Rapozo said during Civil Beat’s mayoral forum in September.
He added that he didn’t understand how the permits could still be valid more than a decade after being granted. He said he wants to understand how the project got to where it is today and why the county’s current administration has allowed the development plans to proceed.
Earlier this year, the resort’s developers secured a $431 million loan to rebuild the Eastside resort. Construction is expected to begin in 2027 with an opening in 2028.
Originally opened in 1953, Coco Palms sits on the former home of Kaua‘i’s last reigning queen and was made famous for being where Elvis Presley’s “Blue Hawaii” was filmed.
The grounds of the former Coco Palms Resort, photographed in March before additional structures were demolished. Craig Fuji/Civil Beat/2026
The resort has been closed since the 1992 hurricane. Several developers have attempted to resurrect it while facing community opposition, lawsuits, concerns over Native Hawaiian burial grounds and state land use violations.
This latest rebuild attempt comes at a time when the county has considered several policies to strengthen structures against the increasing threat from wildfires, sea level rise and flooding, and as the island chain experiences more tropical storms. 
Jonathan Day, chief financial officer of Reef Capital Partners, Coco Palms’ current owner, wrote in an emailed statement that the Utah-based real estate investment company respects Rapozo and looks forward to working with him and his administration.
“The project’s permits were approved unanimously by the Kauaʻi County Planning Commission, and their validity has since been carefully examined and affirmed by the County of Kauaʻi, the Planning Commission and the Hawaiʻi courts,” he wrote. “We are confident any further review will reach the same conclusion.”
‘A Huge Problem For The County’
The Planning Commission granted Coco Palms its zoning, special management area, variance and other permits under a 1997 law that allowed structures destroyed by Hurricane ‘Iniki to be rebuilt to their former condition and footprint in compliance with county rules and permitting requirements at the time of the storm.

Mayor-elect Mel Rapozo the night of the Nov. 3 general election. Akasha Rabut/Civil Beat/2026

The resort, which sits across the highway from Wailua Beach in a low-lying flood plain, largely doesn’t need to comply with newer county rules, such as for shoreline setbacks that were increased to account for sea level rise. But buildings do need to be elevated to meet floodplain management requirements. 
Rapozo, who served on the County Council on and off for 18 years and is currently chair, has said over the years that he doesn’t understand how development permits can last beyond 10 years.
He wants an investigation into how those permits were approved, how they’re still valid and why the county’s attorneys haven’t acted against the development.
“I question the process that occurred for Coco Palms,” he told Civil Beat. “I question it a lot.”
He did not respond to requests for further comment this week.
The mayor’s office declined to comment due to pending litigation over the resort’s permits.
Many of the buildings at Coco Palms were demolished, but the chapel still stands. Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026
The Planning Commission imposed 29 conditions on Coco Palm’s developers. Among them are requirements to create burial, archaeological monitoring and debris management plans, only use certain types of lighting to protect seabirds, provide a set amount of parking, contribute affordable housing, and meet certain deadlines.
The developers were also required to provide the county an in-lieu fee of $93,750 instead of building a dedicated right turn lane on Hale‘īlio Road; that fee was paid in 2017. Developers paid another $93,750 in lieu of widening Apana Road for two-way traffic.
That means the responsibility of building the dedicated right turn lane and widening the road are on the shoulders of the county, Rapozo said.
“I cannot tell you why that condition was granted, but it was and that creates a huge problem for the county,” he told Civil Beat.
Changing Views
Rapozo said 15 years ago, he was supportive of Coco Palms being rebuilt. He’s now against it because many in the community oppose it.
He dislikes that the developers still haven’t contributed affordable housing to the community. He also thinks the rebuilt hotel, which is slated to have 350 rooms, will cause a safety hazard if residents in Wailua and Kapa‘a need to be evacuated.
In past years, Rapozo considered exploring the use of eminent domain to preserve the property for public use.
A view of the construction area at Coco Palms, which originally opened in 1953 and closed after sustaining major damage from Hurricane ‘Iniki in 1992.  Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026
In June, he requested that the county’s Open Space Commission explore acquiring part of the resort’s land. The resort sits on several parcels, a couple of which are owned by the resort’s current owner, Reef Capital Partners, and the state owns others.
The commission discussed that request at its Aug. 13 meeting, saying that an acquisition would align with its goals of preserving historic, cultural, scenic and open-space areas but that its cost would exceed the roughly $3 million currently available in the Open Space Fund. Some members suggested exploring whether a local nonprofit could be a partner in a potential acquisition.
The commission decided to further research the property and a potential acquisition, which would also require seeking funding from the County Council.
Rebuild Progress
In its latest annual status report to the Planning Commission in March, Reef Capital Partners said 13 of its permit conditions were completed, 11 were underway and seven were forthcoming.
Among those underway were requirements to use local contractors and sustainable building techniques, fulfill its affordable housing requirements, and work with the county on sewer and water needs. The resort is also required to provide 20 public parking spaces, a bike share program, a guest shuttle program and other traffic mitigation efforts. 
Coco Palms developer Reef Capital Partners is refining its demolition plans for additional structures, including the Seashell Restaurant across the street from the main resort. Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026
Day of Reef Capital Partners said in his statement that the company was pleased to make multiple contributions to the county as part of the project approval process. It’s also not aware of any plans by the county to expend funds in excess of what it has paid. The company voluntarily made significant contributions to local infrastructure, including donating land to widen Kūhiō Highway.
Reef Capital Partners is required to either deliver 30 workforce housing units or make a multi-million dollar contribution to the county’s housing fund before the resort can open, based on its agreement with the county.
Day added that the company is honored to be restoring one of Kaua‘i’s most storied places in a culturally sensitive and environmentally sustainable way. It anticipates the project will create hundreds of construction and hospitality jobs and generate millions of dollars in annual tax revenue for the island.
Local community group Friends of Maha‘ulepu two years ago tried to get the resort’s permits revoked, arguing to the Planning Commission that the developers didn’t meet all the conditions attached to those permits. The group has also taken issue with the project’s location in a tsunami and sea level rise zone and its impacts on the environment, cultural resources and traffic congestion.  
The commission denied the group’s petition, and the group appealed the decision in civil and appellate courts. The case has reached the Hawai‘i Supreme Court, which has yet to schedule oral arguments.
The Coco Palms Resort has been closed since Hurricane ‘Iniki destroyed it in 1992.  Noelle Fujii-Oride/Civil Beat/2026
Bridget Hammerquist, president of Friends of Maha‘ulepu, said she is glad the mayor-elect will be opening the investigation and looks forward to having a new mayor that starts holding developers accountable.
“I hope somebody will finally wake up and realize that it is an environmentally devastating area for a 351-room new luxury resort,” she said.
Day said in his statement that Reef Capital Partners believes the Friends of Maha‘ulepu lawsuit largely raises issues the Hawaiʻi courts have already decided in the company’s favor.
“We remain committed to restoring Coco Palms in a way that respects the ʻāina, culture and people of Kauaʻi,” he said.
Friends of Maha‘ulepu also filed a lawsuit at the end of October against the Hawai‘i Green Infrastructure Authority, a state agency, and Coco Palm’s developer and lender. The group argues that the infrastructure authorty gave Coco Palms $245 million in state funding without conducting necessary environmental reviews and for redacting more information than allowed under state law about Coco Palm’s use of state lands and funds. Hearings have yet to be scheduled.
