name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT officials push back on Trump’s proposed rule changes for 2030 US Census
description: Connecticut elected officials are pushing back on a Trump administration proposal to overhaul how the U.S. counts residents.
text:
Connecticut elected officials are pushing back on a Trump administration proposal to overhaul how the U.S. counts residents for the 2030 census.
The proposed U.S. Census Bureau rule changes would exclude certain undocumented immigrants—and even some legal immigrants. And they’d stop collecting demographic statistics on race, ethnicity and sexual orientation.
The changes won’t benefit Connecticut, said Governor Ned Lamont said Friday.
Lamont said the Trump administration seems to be trying to reduce federal allocations to states like Connecticut.
“It’s just a game where they are trying to move people and resources artificially from blue states to red states. That’s why we have to stand up, and say no to that,” Lamont said.
She’s prepared to use her position to keep the proposal from being implemented, said U.S. Representative Rosa DeLauro, who is set to chair the House Appropriations Committee in the next Congress.
“I am going to continue to work to make sure that every person is counted. Every community is counted and that every person is represented. And every state receives the resources that it needs,” DeLauro said.
The proposed changes could undercount up to 250,000 people in Connecticut, according to Lt. Gov. Susan Byziewicz, who heads the state’s census committee.
“That is a potentially significant loss of federal funding and it severely undercounts the number of people in our state,” Byziewicz said.
Connecticut joined a coalition of 24 states that submitted comments to the Census Bureau opposing the changes before the comment period ended earlier this month.
The bureau could finalize the new rules by the first quarter of next year.
This story was first published Nov. 16, 2026 by WSHU.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: Michigan’s new lawmakers must deliver on affordability
description: Last week, at least 4.8 million Michiganders cast their ballots, and preliminary reports certainly indicate a record-breaking turnout. In January, a new governor will take office and a new Legislature will be sworn in, including many lawmakers who will step into their roles for the first time. But whatever your opinion of the results, things […]
text:
Michigan Capitol building. (Photo by Susan J. DemasLast week, at least 4.8 million Michiganders cast their ballots, and preliminary reports certainly indicate a record-breaking turnout. In January, a new governor will take office and a new Legislature will be sworn in, including many lawmakers who will step into their roles for the first time. But whatever your opinion of the results, things did not magically change on election day.
It’s no secret that “affordability” was a key theme during campaign season, but for Michiganders, the affordability crisis has been brewing for some time. All around the state, from Detroit to Ironwood, people continue to face stagnant wages and higher costs for basics like food, housing, and childcare.
Our new administration and lawmakers must take note that affordability is more than a line on campaign mailers. Michiganders need them to make economic security a top priority.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The median wage in Michigan has increased by just 3.87% since 1978 when adjusted for inflation. According to the 2026 United for ALICE report, 1.63 million Michigan households — 40% of the state — are either in poverty or struggling to make ends meet. Most of them are working, but not able to get ahead. A recent report from the Michigan League for Public Policy explored the affordability crisis and identified important solutions. We hope our new leaders will take note.
Let’s address work. A full-time job should cover rent, food, and utilities, but for many workers in Michigan, it doesn’t. A living wage is vital if we want to keep families and communities strong. Beyond wages, Michiganders need to know that their job is safe if they need time to recover from a serious illness, to welcome a new child, or to take care of a loved one. A statewide paid family and medical leave program will strengthen economic security, support the workforce, and improve health for parents, children and caregivers.
Costs are clearly a significant barrier for many, and not just due to recent spikes caused by tariffs and inflation. Childcare, for example, has been out of reach for many families for decades. Right now, for a full-time worker earning minimum wage, infant care in a center eats up over 49% of their household budget. That’s $14,000 per year to care for just one child. And at the same time, childcare workers are woefully underpaid and receive few benefits. The state can dedicate revenue for childcare and invest directly in the early childhood workforce.
Crowd gathered in Lansing for the Michigan United Coalition’s annual Capitol Day and Mothering Justice Action Fund’s annual Mamas March. April 29, 2026 | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance
Childcare isn’t the only cost creating roadblocks for families. Housing costs are skyrocketing, with the median Michigan rent increasing 31.5% since 2019. It’s time to slow the pace of housing costs, improve the supply of housing and make sure tenants have the protections they need to stay in their homes. But housing expenses don’t end at the monthly payment. Utility bills also continue to rise, driven by aging infrastructure and increased equipment prices. The state can make sure providers are able to maintain services without passing the burden on to households.
Along with enacting new solutions, lawmakers also have a responsibility to protect the programs that already work. Medicaid and SNAP keep millions of Michiganders healthy and fed, but our new leaders need to push back on the federal cuts and red tape that are putting both programs at risk and work to mitigate the harm from these changes.
Rx Kids, which gives cash to new moms and babies, has shown excellent results in health and economic security and should be expanded statewide. And we know that the federal Child Tax Credit (CTC)  has a history of reversing poverty — it’s time to create a state-level CTC to help families make ends meet.
We know this work is hard, and we know Michigan will have to pay for it. That starts with looking at our tax system, which needs to be modernized to generate more revenue. In the short term, that can mean raising taxes on unhealthy habits and industries like tobacco and vape products, as well as gambling. Longer term, it could mean a true overhaul of the current flat tax, which benefits wealthy corporations and individuals while leaving workers with low incomes to pay an unfair share.
The election on November 3 answered the question of who will have a seat in the Capitol, but we hope that January will allow us to see true leadership. Lawmakers will not agree on every detail, nor should they. But they must agree that solving Michigan’s affordability crisis should be their number one job.

name: Nevada Current
title: Nevada Charter School Authority flags underperforming schools
description: Two Las Vegas charter schools may be at risk of closure following years of poor academic performance. Explore Academy’s middle school and DPAC Nevada’s elementary school both received three consecutive 1-star ratings in the Nevada School Performance Framework. Nevada state law sets that as a trigger for the mandatory termination of a charter contract, though[...]
text:
(Getty Images)Two Las Vegas charter schools may be at risk of closure following years of poor academic performance.
Explore Academy’s middle school and DPAC Nevada’s elementary school both received three consecutive 1-star ratings in the Nevada School Performance Framework. Nevada state law sets that as a trigger for the mandatory termination of a charter contract, though the law allows for schools to potentially restart under a new contract.
The Nevada State Public Charter School Authority Board, which met Friday, did not take action on the underperforming schools, but staff noted that “further action on these schools will be determined” at a future meeting.
Explore Academy opened in 2020 and has never received higher than a 1-star rating. It did not meet the three consecutive year threshold earlier because the state suspended star ratings during the covid pandemic. 
DPAC Nevada, previously known as Democracy Prep at the Agassi Campus, opened in 2017 and has never been rated higher than a 2-star school. For the past three years, it has been rated a 1-star school. The most recent ratings, which reflect the 2025-26 academic year, were released in September.
DPAC Nevada was originally part of the Democracy Prep Public Schools, a national network of charter schools, but it broke away last year and changed its name. The current academic year is its first as an independent charter school.
In a letter of support for the school, one parent argued the recent change in management is a reason to keep the school going.
“Please give that leadership a defined period, with clear targets and public progress reports, to show what it can do with the right support,” wrote parent Marlon Nicholas, who said his autistic son is “known, supported, and challenged” at DPAC.
Democracy Prep and Explore Academy were part of a slate of charter schools that became delinquent on contributions to the Public Employees’ Retirement System of Nevada (PERS). According to the SPCSA, both schools are now caught up.
The Charter School Authority Board approved notices of concern for 13 schools that received 1- or 2-star state ratings and a ‘below’ or ‘does not meet the standard’ rating on the SPCSA’s Academic Framework.
Those schools:

Delta Academy (middle & high schools)
Do & Be Arts Academy of Excellence (elementary & middle schools)
Equipo Academy (middle school)
Explore Academy (high school)
Honors Academy of Literature (middle school)
Imagine Schools at Mountain View (elementary school)
Leadership Academy of Nevada (elementary school)
Legacy Traditional School, Cadence (elementary school)
Legacy Traditional School, North Valley (elementary school)
Vegas Vista Academy (elementary school)
WYLEES (middle school)

Additionally, Honors Academy’s elementary school’s existing notice of concern was elevated to a notice of breach. It was issued the notice of concern last year as a 2-star school and dropped to a 1-star school this year. Its rating in the SPCSA’s internal rating system also dropped significantly.
Representatives from the schools that received notices of concern appeared before the Charter School Authority Board on Friday to discuss their plans for improving their performance.
Honors Academy of Literature Executive Director Andi Morency emphasized that her school is committed to improving but also expressed concern the performance rankings used by the state may not be fair to smaller schools.
“Small schools make up only a small proportion of the SPCSA’s portfolio,” she said. “However, 6 of the 11 schools receiving notices of concern today — 55% — enroll fewer than 350 students.”
She continued: “We’re not aware of any research that shows that small schools tend to underperform. We believe that this pattern likely points to a systematic measurement error” for schools with lower enrollment “and not necessarily weaker instruction.”
Five charter schools had their notices of concern or breach removed following rating improvements: Learning Bridge Charter School’s elementary school, Discovery Preparatory Academy Hillpointe’s middle school, Founders Classical Academy’s elementary school, Freedom Classical Academy’s elementary school, and SLAM Nevada’s elementary school. This means the charter schools are now considered in good standing.
The bulk of Friday’s Charter School Authority Board meeting focused on issuing notices of concern to underperforming charter schools. However, SPCSA schools as a whole received higher ratings, according to presentation materials.
Among SPCSA schools, 38% received 5 stars, compared to 15% of schools statewide; 22% received 4 stars, compared to 15% statewide; 22% received 3 stars, compared to 21% statewide; 9% received 2 stars, compared to 28% statewide; and 10% received 1 star, compared to 21% statewide.

name: California
title: Californians are paying for the oil industry’s risky Plan B: burying carbon dioxide
description: Carbon capture storage, which buries CO2 emissions underground, benefits from federal tax credits, state incentives and oil industry lobbying.
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Liza Tucker
Liza Tucker is a consumer advocate for Consumer Watchdog.


The United Nations says we’ve blown past the deadline for limiting worldwide global warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (or 2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times.
To avoid catastrophe, we’re supposed to use unproven technology at a vast scale to suck carbon dioxide out of the air while slashing emissions — in other words, throw spaghetti against a wall to see what sticks.
One tool gaining attention is carbon capture and storage technology, which draws CO2 from industrial smokestacks and buries it.
The trouble is carbon capture storage, touted by the oil industry, is a bust. And it keeps us handcuffed to climate-destroying fossil fuels.
The better choice is to vastly expand what is proven: Ramp up renewable energy, energy efficiency and electrification, while cutting greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel production and transportation. What’s missing is the political will and the investment to do that.
Today carbon capture storage technology permanently buries less CO2 than a single large power plant can emit in a year, a ProPublica investigation revealed in June. And not one carbon capture storage project has come close to industry claims of up to 95% capture rates.
Yet, under relentless oil industry lobbying, California has gone whole hog on this multibillion-dollar boondoggle — turbocharged by federal tax credits and state incentives — before carbon storage rules are even set.
Last year California lifted a partial moratorium on building compressed CO2 pipelines, which would carry this lethal asphyxiant to burial. The law did not require that an odorant be added to warn residents of a gas leak, nor did it prescribe a stringent buffer zone between communities and the pipelines.
If a cloud of CO2 is released, it can displace oxygen near the ground, suffocating people and stopping vehicles.
That already has happened. In 2020 a CO2 pipeline ruptured in Satartia, Miss., sending 45 people to hospitals and causing 200 evacuations. News accounts reported victims shaking, struggling to breathe, falling unconscious and foaming at the mouth.
Now Montezuma Carbon, a company in the San Francisco Bay Area, envisions transporting CO2 from plants and utilities in the region via a 40-mile pipeline, and injecting it into saline aquifers two miles beneath the Montezuma Wetlands and its thriving wildlife. Nearby communities already are galvanized against it.
About 20 miles west of Bakersfield, California Resources Corp., the state’s biggest oil producer, is already injecting compressed carbon dioxide from its cryogenic gas plant into a depleted reservoir. The carbon capture storage project began operating in May. There’s no guarantee that won’t leak upward through the Swiss cheese-like structure of old oil wells.
If the government didn’t prop up the proposed carbon capture projects, they would collapse, as California Resources has admitted. Such projects “depend on financial and tax incentives established under federal and state laws, regulations and governmental programs to be economically viable,” the company’s 2025 fiscal report stated.
Most of California Resources’s nearly 40,000 wells produce little or no oil, according to an analysis by FracTracker Alliance. California has 1.2 billion barrels of proved oil reserves remaining — roughly 14 years’ worth at the state’s 2025 production rate — the Energy Information Administration reports.
Exploiting new oil reserves is expensive and requires jumping through legal hoops. No wonder California Resources is pushing carbon capture storage as its Plan B — at public expense.
But every dollar spent on carbon capture storage — instead of wind, water and solar — increases CO2, air pollution, energy costs, pipelines and total societal costs, a 2025 Stanford-led study concluded.
The state should instead pull the plug on carbon capture storage and ensure California Resources and other drillers put up the money to plug their wells and clean up their messes.
That way billions of dollars can be redirected to what we know works.

name: Nevada Current
title: Conversation ‘starting point’ on youth homelessness has changed, policy has yet to catch up
description: Nevada’s approach to helping youth experiencing homelessness has come a long way from where its social services infrastructure was even a decade ago.  Homeless providers, youth-serving nonprofits, and many youth with lived experience gathered last week at the 10th annual Nevada Youth Homelessness Summit to reflect on those changes while calling for stronger [...]
text:
Arash Ghafoori, executive director of Nevada Partnership for Homeless Youth.
(Photo: Micheal Lyle/Nevada Current)Nevada’s approach to helping youth experiencing homelessness has come a long way from where its social services infrastructure was even a decade ago. 
Homeless providers, youth-serving nonprofits, and many youth with lived experience gathered last week at the 10th annual Nevada Youth Homelessness Summit to reflect on those changes while calling for stronger investments and support.
Though some things have improved for the better in Nevada, “I honestly thought we would have figured it out by now,” said Arash Ghafoori, executive director of Nevada Partnership for Homeless Youth.
“As many as 33,000 unaccompanied young people could experience homelessness in Nevada in a single year,” he said. “That’s an estimate and it tells us that we cannot be satisfied with the status quo.” 
The figure came from the 2025 Youth Experiencing Homelessness Statewide Report which estimated that 33,443 youth under the age of 24 in the state could experience homelessness or lack adequate stable housing in any given year. 
The report not only found that during 2024 roughly 2,800 youth ages 12 to 24 were identified in the Homeless Management Information System, which tracks service interventions among unhoused people, but that the state lacked funding and infrastructure to address their specific needs. 
Speakers at the summit said they are working on a follow-up cost analysis to determine how much inaction costs the state versus investing in  removing barriers standing between  youth and stable housing.  
One of the biggest improvements over the last few years, Ghafoori said, has  been making progress toward tailoring the state’s social safety net the specific needs of the younger homeless population. 
“Ten years ago, we spent a great deal of time explaining why young people needed their own response rather than a smaller version of the adult system,” Ghafoori said. “Today, more institutions, policymakers, community members, and funders understand that. We still have a long way to go but we changed the starting point of that conversation.”
One area he pointed to was trying to eliminate the financial burdens youth experiencing homelessness face when pursuing higher education. 
In 2025, service providers backed Assembly Bill 397, which included provisions requiring the Board of Regents to waive registration and laboratory fees for students who have experienced homelessness.
The bill passed with bipartisan support but Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo vetoed the bill, citing separate provisions in the legislation dealing with tuition fee waivers used by Nevada’s National Guard would result in unintended consequences.
“Young people spent years advocating for better access to higher education,” Ghafoori said. “Think about the young people who gave their time, shared their experiences, and believed the door would finally open. Sadly, higher education is still closed for too many young people experiencing homelessness.” 
Though there remains challenges at the state level to address funding and policy barriers, advocates at the summit also noted problems created at the federal level.
The prospect of addressing youth homelessness is coming against federal changes and the “grim reality for federal funding,” said Katie Meyer Scott, the youth homelessness director for the National Homelessness Law Center. 
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed into law in July 2025 makes significant cuts to food assistance programs and health care access, including Medicaid. 
New work eligibility requirements to qualify for Medicaid are scheduled to go into effect in 2027. 
While foster youth will be exempt from the changes to Medicaid, some estimates show “up to 2.3 million young adults ages 19 to 24 could still lose Medicaid with the implementation of these changes,” Scott said. 
Those curtailments to health care coverage are an additional barrier to youth as they try to exit homelessness, she added. 
Over the last two years, the Trump administration, through revised grant requirements and guidelines, has been prioritizing treatment over housing, and pushed local governments  to treat homelessness as a crime.
”They are trying to chill advocates’ efforts to fight against those kind of criminalizing laws by essentially saying, ‘hey if you apply for this funding you’re basically agreeing you will not only not try to fight against these laws, but you’re going to show your support of these laws and work with law enforcement to do so,’” Scott said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Here’s what to know about Medicaid changes coming in 2027
description: The much-talked about changes to Medicaid will go into effect Jan. 1. In CT, they will affect those on Husky D. Here’s what you need to know.
text:
President Donald Trump’s “One Big Beautiful Bill Act” — also known as House Resolution 1, or H.R. 1 — includes major changes to the federal Medicaid program that are set to take effect on Jan. 1.
Medicaid is the government health insurance program for people whose incomes fall below certain limits. The program is known as “HUSKY” in Connecticut.
The changes apply to residents enrolled in HUSKY D, the Medicaid program for adults without children. 
On Friday, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services announced it would provide states the option of implementing a ‘hold harmless’ period through June 20, 2027. The decision is meant to give states more time to implement the changes.
Here’s what you need to know.
What are the changes?
Beginning Jan. 1, HUSKY D enrollees will be required to meet work requirements, also being referred to as “community engagement requirements.” They will also have to prove their Medicaid eligibility every six months, up from every 12 months today. 
To keep coverage, HUSKY D enrollees will have to prove they work at least 80 hours or earn a minimum of $580 per month. The requirement can also be fulfilled by demonstrating at least 80 hours of monthly participation in school, community service or a qualified training program.
Several exemptions exist, including, but not limited to, people who are:

Already meeting work requirements for SNAP
Parents, guardians and caregivers of a dependent child under 14 or an individual with a disability
Enrolled in drug or alcohol treatment or a rehabilitation program
Pregnant or postpartum
Veterans with a total disability

Enrollees have to comply with the changes as of their first renewal in 2027. For example, a HUSKY D member due for their first renewal in February 2027 would have to begin demonstrating compliance that month and then would be due for their next renewal six months later, in August 2027. 
Those states that implement the hold harmless period will still have to “assess whether individuals meet the work requirement or are excluded from it, but they will not deny applications or disenroll otherwise eligible individuals solely for failure to meet the requirement,” according to the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services’s press release.
One change to Medicaid already took effect Oct. 1. The program no longer covers several groups of lawfully present immigrants, including refugees, asylees and victims of human trafficking. An estimated 3,200 residents lost HUSKY as a result.
Will the changes affect me?
The new requirements only apply to people with HUSKY D, not those with HUSKY A, B or C. The state has created medicaidmattersct.org, a resource to help people navigate the changes. The site includes a questionnaire so people can figure out if the HUSKY changes apply to them.
[RELATED: Hartford coalition will help residents navigate Medicaid changes]
People looking for one-on-one support can reach out to their local Community Action Agency, where you can meet with a trained staff member or Community Health Worker Navigator. They will review your individual case and advise you on whether the changes apply to you and how to navigate them. You can find your local Community Action Agency here. 
Could the midterm election results reverse these new policies?
Democrats won majorities in both the House and the Senate during the most recent midterm elections. Many of the candidates who won their races campaigned on reversing some of Trump’s healthcare policies, including the Medicaid changes.
But even with Democratic majorities in both chambers, Trump still has the power to veto any proposal to reverse the Medicaid changes. Overriding his veto would require getting Republicans on board. Or Democrats could opt to negotiate a deal with Trump, if he’s open to it.
State Comptroller Sean Scanlon said state officials hope Democrats will be able to get something done, but their success likely depends on Trump’s willingness to negotiate.
“We’re really hoping that that is something that they get done in the first couple weeks of a new Congress,” Scanlon said. “Of course, the president is still the president. What his appetite is to do deals with the Democrats and resolve some of these things is really unclear and I don’t think anybody knows at this point.”
After Friday’s announcement about the hold harmless period, Sen. Matt Lesser, D-Middletown, said he hoped the change “provides an indication that Donald Trump is hearing the American people and will join Congressional Democrats in completely repealing his Big Awful Bill. If not, they should compel him to do so.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: The companies Utah consumers complain about the most
authors: Sydnee Chapman, The Utah Investigative Journalism Project, Kayli Jacob, Utah Investigative Journalism Project
description: The following story was reported by The Utah Investigative Journalism Project in partnership with Utah News Dispatch. A 78-year-old living on Social Security while battling leukemia who was left in a panic after a plumbing company turned his water off and left before finishing replacing pipes on his mobile home.  A bedridden, elderly woman dependent […]
text:
A 2024 Utah law allows public access to consumer complaints against businesses that had at least 10 complaints filed against them within a 12-month period. (Illustration by Rachel Pixton for The Utah Investigative Journalism Project)The following story was reported by The Utah Investigative Journalism Project in partnership with Utah News Dispatch.
A 78-year-old living on Social Security while battling leukemia who was left in a panic after a plumbing company turned his water off and left before finishing replacing pipes on his mobile home. 
A bedridden, elderly woman dependent on oxygen who was charged thousands of dollars for a toilet and sink unclogging. 
A homeowner who made payments on their newly installed solar panels for the better part of a year before discovering that the installation company never turned the panels on. 
These are a handful of the Utahns mentioned in complaints to the Utah Division of Consumer Protection after dealings with allegedly problematic companies in a state with a long-held reputation as the fraud capital of the United States. While the state Legislature passed a bill in 2024 making certain consumer complaints public, the change hasn’t had much impact on the average Utahn. 
“It’s probably not in consumers’ minds generally at this point because we haven’t really made anything public using this law yet,” said Blake Young, the division’s former deputy commissioner who recently left the agency. 
Prior to the 2024 law, complaints to the Utah Division of Consumer Protection were not public. The bill, however, pulled back the curtain. It allows public access to consumer complaints against businesses that had at least 10 complaints filed against them within a 12-month period. The division can also release them if it takes public action against a company or at the discretion of the division director. 
The Utah Investigative Journalism Project obtained 307 of those public complaints through an open records request. The complaints included at least nine different companies in the tech, construction and travel industries and represent over $5 million in disputed funds. Emerald Pools & Spas made up the largest chunk at over $1.6 million, followed by Private Label Accelerator at nearly $1.3 million and Action Heating, Cooling and Plumbing at over $850,000. 
Action Plumbing also garnered the lion’s share of complaints, at 45%, followed by Meta at 16% and Private Label Accelerator at 12%. 
A lawyer representing Action Plumbing said those figures don’t provide a “reliable or fair measure of a company’s service record” and that the state had “an aggressive campaign to solicit additional complaints.” 
The Division of Consumer Protection won a judgment against Parker Wilde, Private Label Accelerator’s owner, after filing a lawsuit alleging he scammed over 200 people out of several million dollars by offering help to set up automated Amazon storefronts that he claimed would generate passive income. 
Wilde, however maintains that the business wasn’t a scam and said the business settled “partially because it could not afford a defense and they sought tens of millions of dollars and we simply didn’t have those funds.” Instead, he said a number of factors, like rising manufacturing and shipping costs, contributed to the downfall of the business. 
“If I could have seen the future on how things in the e-commerce ecosystem would have changed so quickly — I would have never pushed the business,” Wilde wrote in a statement to the UIJP. “Again we are all saddened that it did not work out.” 
Meta did not respond to a request for comment for this story. Neither did Emerald Pools, which still owes customers millions of dollars and is pursuing bankruptcy.
Young said the 2024 change came about because of conflicting provisions in state law about which division records were public. He added that while the law hasn’t had much of an impact yet, it’s something the division wanted to have on the books due to previous cases where officials’ hands were tied. 
“We had some cases years ago where we would have loved to have been able to do this and it just was not a door that was open for us to do,” Young said. “So now that’s a thing that we have as a tool in our pocket that we can pull out if it’s the right way to approach a problem.” 
Available remedies  
What the division can do once someone has filed a complaint is dependent on each individual case.
“Every complaint that comes in has its own special adventure,” Young said. 
When the division receives a complaint it checks to see if a law was broken and if the division can do something about it. If so, an investigator reaches out to the consumer and the business to find out what happened. There are a handful of likely outcomes from there:

A business didn’t realize its actions had broken a law and will try to make things right with the customer.
The division can work out a resolution, similar to a settlement, where the business makes things right with consumers and sometimes pays a fine. Those fees do not go to the consumers themselves. 
If a resolution can’t be reached, the division can issue a citation, which is filed like a court case and gives the business the chance to attend a hearing with an administrative law judge. 
The division can file a civil lawsuit, typically in cases involving multiple victims, large amounts of money and some additional need for restitution for consumers. 
The division can file a criminal referral with a prosecutor. 

Young said civil lawsuits are expensive for the state and less common due to the limited number of state attorneys assigned to work with the Division of Consumer Protection. Even less common are criminal referrals. 
“In our administrative cases … where we have a citation and a hearing, we can only recover fines from the company in those, we can’t get money back to consumers,” Young said. “So the lawsuit process is usually what we look to more when there’s a lot of people who need money back.”
The division filed such a lawsuit against Private Label Accelerator that resulted in a $7.9 million judgment in fines. 
Consumer Protection has also partnered with the Division of Professional Licensing to revoke Action Plumbing’s professional licenses and demand fines and file legal proceedings against the business. Those actions are ongoing. An attorney for Action Plumbing said the company disputes the state’s allegations and looks forward to presenting its side during the case. 
Mathew Thue, assistant professor of business ethics at Weber State University, said protections for consumers often fall short, especially since there is a lot of gray area between what is allowed under law and what is a deceptive practice. 
“The framework is very far from a perfect protection,” he said. “When the rubber hits the road for an average person, I don’t think the regulators are there really anywhere in most cases to help very much.”
For example, a common complaint regarding Meta was individuals being locked out of accessing their account.
One consumer said they lost years’ worth of materials from their religious proselytizing account, as well as photos of their late wife, when their personal account was disabled without warning or the chance to appeal. In another complaint a consumer said their account was suspended for alleged child safety violations but they were unable to challenge these claims as an appeal would require them to log in to their suspended account. The complaint states this had happened once before and Meta restored the account previously after finding it was an error.  
Young said there are policies in place for when complaints are submitted by the government. He said that when the public submits these requests the question becomes more nuanced, delving into whether or not a practice is deceptive or not.
Several of the complaints also described paying for a multiyear cruise that after multiple delays appeared unlikely to ever set sail, leaving would-be passengers across the world out thousands. 
One Utah consumer reported waiting more than nine months to hear back from the cruise line about refunding the $25,000 they deposited toward the cruise. 
“I’m convinced that we unfortunately have also been scammed by depositing $10,000 for a deposit for a cabin as part of our dream of seeing the world on a residential cruise,” a separate complaint reads. “My partner even sold his house to make this a reality as he didn’t want to be an absentee landlord.”
Avoiding scams and fraud 
While there are remedies available to consumers who fall victim to scams or deceptive practices, the best protection is often avoiding them in the first place. 
The division tallied the top 10 areas of complaints from 2025. In order from most to least common, they are:

Auto sales 
Auto repairs
Apartment/housing rentals
Home remodeling/construction
Solar
Home furnishings
Home alarm systems
Healthcare billing
Travel/vacations
Gyms

Young said consumers can check the division’s website and social media accounts for updates about deceptive businesses, and that they should also verify who they are dealing with, especially as artificial intelligence evolves. 
“AI is making it very, very easy for scammers to operate,” he said. “There is almost no friction to create very convincing text messages, emails and phone calls, and even websites.”
For example, one of the complaints reviewed by the UIJP details a scam where two individuals pretending to be actors from the TV show “Chicago Fire” convinced a Utahn to send them $1,200 in gift cards as well as personal information like his bank account and Social Security number. 
The scammer “promised (the victim) he would come and get him and take him to Chicago to live with him,” reads the complaint. “Every single day the scammers reach out to (the victim) saying ‘I love you babe’ etc. … Please help show him he’s being scammed. He won’t stop sending everything he has to these people.” 
Other consumers complained of companies attempting to bully them into paying for more services.
One complaint describes an Action Plumbing employee coming to a client’s home after they fired the company over a botched job clearing a clogged sewer line that left a partially-collapsed, 14-foot hole in the client’s yard. 
“He started yelling at her and she retreated into her home to lock the door. He continued yelling and pounding on her door. She was home alone and very frightened, crying, and shaking (she is usually very brave), and had to call police to have them leave her home,” the complaint reads.
When asked about this case, Action said in an email from its lawyers that using a camera on the pipe can not always show the whole issue, and that the excavation company was licensed separately from Action. They attributed the issue to being asked to leave before the work was completed. 
Action said that when a representative returned to her home to speak to the owner “she became irate and apparently called an acquaintance of hers who was a police officer from another jurisdiction.” The officer threatened them with a restraining order and would not let the representatives remove their equipment, Action said. They said they have submitted a complaint against the officer, and have also provided supporting documents regarding this case to the Department of Consumer Protection in 2024.
Both Young and Thue said that if something sounds too good to be true, it likely is.
“If something ever just feels off, trust that feeling,” Young said. “It’s very important that whenever anyone is in a heightened situation, stop and think and try and get some time and space to think about whether that seems real or not.”
Several consumers in the complaints also reported feeling pressured or wary about interactions with the companies but pushing forward anyway. 
One reported that the estimate they received for a new AC was “sky high” but that they felt pressured to sign off the same day because a sales rep said there was only one unit left and it would sell before they called back. 
Another said an “extremely pushy” Action technician told them their electrical panel was in a severe state and posed a high fire risk.
“At the time, I felt their reasoning was not sound but felt pressured to decide,” the complaint reads. “I had to take out a loan from a third party as well as rely on financial assistance from my parents.” 
Action said their technicians allow clients to make their own decisions on purchases and services. “Action does not allow its technicians to ignore problems they see in a customer’s home. Action technicians are trained to inform customers of any issues they observe during their visit and provide the customer with options for how to address those problems,” Action said in an email, adding that the company had not received any complaints about the work done for the client who had to take a loan. 
“Action is committed to transparent and ethical business practices,” the lawyer wrote in an email. “Employees are trained to present options clearly so that customers can make informed decisions. When a situation genuinely requires prompt attention — such as an active leak or a safety concern — it would be irresponsible not to communicate that to the customer.”
The consumer reported to the state, however, that they were stuck in a broiling heat wave without air conditioning and felt like they had no options.
“I cried when I had to make this payment due to the extreme financial burden this would place on me,” the consumer wrote to state regulators. “The technician did not offer any smaller units, though they did use their iPad to explain why I needed a unit this large and expensive.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: A pool company took Utahns for millions. The response destroyed their faith in the legal system.
authors: Sydnee Chapman, The Utah Investigative Journalism Project
description: The following story was reported by The Utah Investigative Journalism Project in partnership with Utah News Dispatch. The deal Ashley Crum received was a bad bargain by most standards: $100,000 in exchange for a gaping cement hole in her yard and multiple liens on her home.  But that was the situation she found herself in […]
text:
An unfinished pool left by Emerald Pools & Spas is seen at the home of Ashley and Dax Crum in Nibley, Utah, before they paid another company to complete it. (Photo courtesy of Ashley Crum)The following story was reported by The Utah Investigative Journalism Project in partnership with Utah News Dispatch.
The deal Ashley Crum received was a bad bargain by most standards: $100,000 in exchange for a gaping cement hole in her yard and multiple liens on her home. 
But that was the situation she found herself in after contracting with Emerald Pools & Spas to construct a pool at her home in Nibley. What was supposed to be a run-of-the-mill installation had turned into a nightmare for Crum, an ER doctor, and her husband, a teacher. 
She’s since spent even more money suing the company and paying another company to finish the pool. The ordeal put the couple so far in debt that Crum says she’s now living “more paycheck to paycheck” instead of saving for her children. 
“To dig out of this hole will probably take me 10 years,” Crum said. “This was just so unfair for them to do.” 
Crum is one of a host of former clients and subcontractors who lost money to Emerald Pools & Spas. 
By its own account, the company could owe money to more than 400 businesses and individuals — including a Syracuse couple who paid almost a quarter of a million dollars for half a pool and a flooded basement, a trucking subcontractor who said he’s lost his life’s savings and his home because Emerald didn’t pay him, and a Kaysville man who paid Emerald $73,000 and received nothing. 
The company’s multiyear fall has involved two state investigations, the loss of its business license, several civil lawsuits and, most recently, a bankruptcy filing. Consumers, however, argue none of those actions have offered remedy, raising questions about the effectiveness of state regulators. 
“Honestly, I’ve lost my faith in the legal system and justice,” said Stormie West, who sued Emerald to recover a $53,000 deposit on a pool the company never started. “I just feel like I’m never going to see any of that money or a pool, and I just kind of am hopeless right now.” 
While Emerald was burning to the ground, another company quietly rose from the ashes: Blue Wave Pools and Spas. 
On paper, the new company looked a lot like Emerald. Business filings show Blue Wave initially listed the same registered agent and address as Emerald. A registered agent receives legal documents and notices for a business — they are sometimes, but not always, a business’ owner. 
Other records similarly link the two, raising questions about their relationship and why one escaped unscathed when the other, and so many of its clients, weren’t as lucky. 
“They’re just getting protected by their LLC, and I’m like, yeah, but it is obviously unethical to just switch your business in the middle of owing people a bunch of money,” Ashley Crum said. “It’s crazy to me that these guys can get away with doing that.” 
The UIJP was unsuccessful in reaching the owners of Emerald and Blue Wave. A Blue Wave employee declined to comment, instead directing a reporter to the company’s lawyer. Neither of the companies’ legal representatives responded to questions, but the current owner of Emerald has maintained the company had every intention of making good on its obligations. 
“At the time we felt confident and had full intention of just to keep going,” Emerald owner Andrew Siddoway said in a recording of a bankruptcy hearing, later adding, “You try to play defense where you can but it obviously didn’t wind up being successful as an entity.”
A failing company, a $100 deal and a ‘strange’ transfer
Things weren’t looking good for Emerald by at least August 2024. There was a cascading effect of the company having to do additional, unpaid work to redo or fix its pools due to poor craftsmanship and quality control. Yet the company was still taking on new pool contracts. 
“There was still with full intention to get through the hurdle and get projects done,” Siddoway said during a bankruptcy hearing. “Between August and October, we were looking at restructuring. How do we get more efficiency and combination of crews and just doing what we could to try to turn things around and meet with investors and whatnot.”
By the end of October, Siddoway said, the decision was made to close Emerald’s doors. The company had gone from generating $8.2 million in revenue to being nearly $50,000 in the red, according to bankruptcy filings. 
At the same time, Siddoway and Drew Wight made an unusual purchase. For $100, the duo obtained 50/50 ownership of the floundering company from Micah Green, a Utah entrepreneur whose ventures include Fizz Drinks and Green Construction in Kaysville.  
Both Siddoway and Wight had been involved in the company for years as president and vice president of sales, respectively. The deal, Siddoway said during bankruptcy proceedings, was just “memorializing” those roles, and founding owners and brothers Micah and Morgan Green were only in mentorship roles for about 18 to 24 months before the company shut down. 
“We’d been operating in running the business and in all the day-to-day operations,” Siddoway said during proceedings. “And so it wasn’t, I would say, a last-minute switch.” 
Siddoway also said that he was not involved with Blue Wave and was unaware of its ownership structure. Business filings, however, show both Siddoway and Micah Green were listed with the company until spring of 2025 and that the company incorporated the same day the Utah Division of Professional Licensing began investigating Emerald. Wight also worked for Blue Wave. 
One legal complaint alleges the relationship between the two companies and their various owners is more than coincidental. 
“Emerald has simply been attempting to reorganize as Blue Wave, LLC in an effort to avoid creditor claims and to avoid the performance of work to which Emerald was contractually obligated to perform,” reads a complaint filed in the bankruptcy case by two former Emerald customers. 
Clients also reported receiving texts from Emerald’s phone number stating that Emerald was “now Blue Wave Spas.” 
Bankruptcy filings show Emerald made only a few transfers after ceasing operations, including selling the hot tub retail portion of its business to Blue Wave and all its construction tools and equipment to a company owned by another former Emerald owner. 
Siddoway acknowledged during bankruptcy hearings that none of the deals involved much negotiation and that Emerald didn’t have its business or assets appraised, nor did they market the assets or approach other potential buyers. 
In another deal, Emerald gave $290,000 to another company that previously had 86% ownership of Emerald and that is currently owned by Micah Green in exchange for that company taking over a $345,000 debt to a supply company. It was a “strange agreement,” according to the bankruptcy case’s court-appointed administrator.  
“I can’t speak to the benefit for them. The benefit was for Emerald,” Siddoway responded in the hearing. “My understanding is that, being in construction, the Greens had relationships there to help with that.” 
Siddoway, the Green brothers and their companies also claim they are owed millions by Emerald, according to bankruptcy filings. A company filed under Micah Green’s name that Siddoway said all Green brothers are involved in has the largest claim listed in the case at $2.4 million. 
Filing for bankruptcy and ‘a big injustice’
Despite ceasing operations in 2024, the company didn’t file bankruptcy until a year and a half later. Siddoway said the delay was based on initial hopes that the company could pay or negotiate with creditors. The case is ongoing. 
“(We) hadn’t foreseen the extent and the number of claims that would come in, and then it just got to a point that we didn’t have, Emerald didn’t have, the funds to continue fighting,” he said during a bankruptcy hearing. 
John Rao, an attorney with the National Consumer Law Center, said consumers can take steps within a bankruptcy case to get higher priority among other creditors but that they may never recover all they’re owed. 
“It’s not necessarily a pretty outcome or a good outcome for consumers once a business has filed bankruptcy,” Rao said. “There are also examples of people, really the bad actors, who file bankruptcy hoping that they can stop everything and basically get out of their responsibility.”
In those cases, the court can dismiss the bankruptcy case to prevent the benefits a business receives from filing. Perhaps the largest benefit for a bad actor, Rao added, is the fact that a bankruptcy will put an automatic pause on lawsuits. 
“That could be huge if they’re being sued in a lot of individual cases where there are judgments against them,” Rao said. “All of that really stops as soon as the case gets filed.”
By the time Emerald filed for bankruptcy, over two dozen lawsuits had been filed against the company, including a consolidated case involving several consumers. Other cases awarded tens of thousands in judgments to consumers, but plaintiffs Taylor Spendlove and Michael Veater, say they haven’t seen a dime of their respective awards of $74,000 and $27,000. 
“I tried to collect money from them, but they said they didn’t have any,” Veater said. “While I don’t think I’ll ever see that money again, I am curious to see how the legal system will hopefully prevail and provide justice to the people that are impacted.” 
Court documents show Emerald filed for bankruptcy less than a month after the Green brothers, Siddoway, and Wight were notified of depositions in that case. West, one of the case’s plaintiffs, doesn’t believe the timing is a coincidence. 
“We were pretty crushed when the bankruptcy was filed,” West said. “It just didn’t seem like the timing was innocent; it seemed like it was planned.” 
Blake Young, who was the Utah Division of Consumer Protection deputy commissioner until recently, said the reality is that it can be difficult for consumers to get justice if a company goes out of business.  
“It’s not illegal to go out of business and our country has bankruptcy laws for many good economic reasons,” he said.
Dax Crum, Ashley Crum’s husband, worries allowing the bankruptcy case to move forward would be a mistake. 
“For someone at the state to just grant them bankruptcy or grant them more protection while we don’t know where any of our money went … I think is a big injustice on the part of our current judicial system,” he said.
‘A real whack-a-mole situation’ 
Emerald Pools certainly didn’t fly under state officials’ radar. In fact, the state Division of Professional Licensing and Division of Consumer Protection both investigated the company.
The Division of Professional Licensing investigation resulted in the company surrendering its contractor license. Meanwhile, Consumer Protection received 15 consumer complaints about Emerald and found it failed to complete 28 pools. The division’s legal action against the company ended in a $70,000 fine — the maximum amount allowed by state law.  
Consumers say neither division’s enforcement action made a difference for the individuals harmed by the business. 
West, who filed a consumer complaint along with her husband, was shocked by the number of consumers revealed by the Consumer Protection investigation. While she was relieved something had been done, she also expressed frustration that none of those 28 families will see any of the $70,000. 
Veater said he’s disgruntled by the state investigations and that the $70,000 fine simply adds more debt to a company that already can’t pay consumers. The Crums, likewise, wish there would have been more aggressive action from the state, including criminal charges. 
“I think these guys should be in jail, right?” Ashley Crum said.
The state did not respond to questions about its enforcement actions. 
Rao said consumer protection can be tricky for states, who are generally operating with limited resources and trying to balance which cases to go after. 
“Sometimes this can seem like a real whack-a-mole situation,” he said. “The reality is they’re often trying to deal with other criminal activities … sometimes things that are in the civil, and particularly the consumer side, there’s just not enough resources to address all the bad actors out there.” 
For the consumers impacted by the Emerald debacle, though, that reality is devastating. 
“We saved for years and were finally going to be able to get a pool, and then just to have that basically stolen from us was just so heartbreaking,” West said. “It’s just been a lot of stress on our family. This thing that was supposed to add joy to our lives has instead brought so much heartache and pain.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Lax oversight of reporting masks misuse of opioid settlement funds in NJ, critics say
description: Opioid settlement funds are meant to directly help those harmed by addiction. Without state action, towns will continue to squander the money, critics say.
text:
Opioid settlement funds are meant to directly help those harmed by addiction. Without state action, towns will continue to squander the money, critics say. (Photo by Daniella Heminghaus/New Jersey Monitor)When New Jersey agreed to a $1.1 billion settlement to end lawsuits over the deadly opioid epidemic, state officials ordered the counties and towns receiving funds to annually report how they spent it, how they made spending decisions, whether they involved the public in the process, and more.
Lakewood approached its reporting with all the care of a college student muddling through a midterm the morning after an all-night rager.
“That is a very interesting question worthy of further review,” an unnamed employee wrote in response to how they decided spending.
Asked how they involved the public in decision-making, the employee wrote: “I don’t know. I am just a book keeper that works in an office all day and is not exposed to the public.”
That was last year’s report. Township officials didn’t bother to submit a report on time this year, even though they have received nearly $1.2 million in opioid settlement funds since 2022. They did not respond to a request for comment.
To Joe Junfola, Lakewood is a glaring example of the state’s lax oversight of spending from its settlement with prescription drug makers, distributors, and retailers who fueled the epidemic. But it’s also not the worst example.
Junfola is a good government geek from Gloucester County who found what he considers fraud in towns and counties around New Jersey, with many officials offering unclear explanations of spending, fudging numbers, and even outright lying on mandated spending reports.
He started probing the spending in March when he learned police in Washington Township, where he lives, used opioid settlement funds to buy Flock surveillance cameras and two Chevy Tahoes. After filing public records requests for receipts and other underlying documents, he discovered the township spent nearly $268,000 of settlement funds on the cameras and SUVs — not approved uses under the settlement agreement — and reported the expenditures to the state as “drug education” for 500 children. Township officials did not respond to a request for comment.
He expanded his research to the 21 counties and 241 municipalities around the state that receive settlement funds and found about 20 towns that spent almost $2 million on “phantom programs,” or expenses they certified to the state that they couldn’t back up with receipts or contracts. He also discovered deceptive bookkeeping and misspending on staff salaries and police surveillance technology, vehicles, and gear. Junfola, who works as chief technology officer at an AI-first legal startup, recently published his findings online.
“Obviously, nobody in the state is looking at these reports,” Junfola said. “Washington Township was the base case for my interest due to the combination of misuse and false reporting. I expected to see the same elsewhere, and I was right. It’s more rampant than anyone knows.”



Quotation







We are at a point now where there has been so much money that has been spent on things that I never would have thought that they would spend money on.


– Assemblyman Cody Miller


Junfola joins a growing army of advocates who have increasingly sounded the alarm on misspending since Kevin Walsh, who headed the state comptroller’s office until January, rebuked Irvington last year for spending $632,000 on two “opioid awareness” concerts, steering most of the money to a township employee who moonlighted as a DJ.
In Atlantic County, Amanda Devecka-Rinear and her team at the New Jersey Organizing Project filed public-record requests for details on how Atlantic City spent almost $1.9 million last year.
In its report to the state, the city only explained half of its spending. Its explanation for that half was confusing and even contradictory, with officials simultaneously reporting in various places in a single entry that they spent about $934,000 to connect 40 or 75 people to treatment, serve 200 people, provide 500 services, and distribute 900 Narcan kits. In comparison, Atlantic County officials reported that they spent a similar amount of money on various programs to help more than 400 people and distribute 300 harm reduction vending machines, the report shows.
Besides bewildering people reading the report, such figures suggest the city isn’t getting much bang for its buck, said Devecka-Rinear, the project’s executive director.
“This is batsh*t crazy,” Devecka-Rinear said. “I’m not saying we don’t deserve to spend a considerable amount of money to assist people who use drugs. I’m just wondering if that’s what’s really happening here.”
Advocates want state officials to act to protect the money, which is meant to directly help those harmed by addiction, require more robust reporting, and hold accountable those who squander the funds.
So far, the state has not done so.
The state Department of Human Services oversees reporting, but officials there merely request, collect, and post the reports, said Eva Loayza-McBride, a department spokeswoman. They cannot advise counties and towns how to spend money, nor approve or deny spending plans, she added.
Oversight is the comptroller’s job, she said.
A spokeswoman for the comptroller’s office, though, said state law designates the department as the lead state agency in monitoring opioid spending.
Merely collecting spending reports, as the department now does, is “insufficient to ensure compliance because the data relies on self-reporting by local governments,” spokeswoman Laura Fredrick said. In his Irvington report, Walsh recommended that the department provide clearer guidance to local governments and take a more active role in ensuring compliance, Fredrick added.
With that impasse and without action from lawmakers, advocates fear opioid settlement funds could get frittered away the way tobacco settlement funds did after lawsuits over the public health toll of smoking ended in a 1998 deal that required cigarette companies to pay more than $200 billion to 46 states, including New Jersey.
“Only about 7% of those payments ever went towards public health interventions related to tobacco. The rest of it just went directly into general government spending — infrastructure, education, so not necessarily terrible things to be spent on, but it just really wasn’t the intention of those settlements for it to be used that way,” said Benjamin Scher, a researcher in the Global Health Program at Princeton University’s School of Public and International Affairs.
Under the tobacco settlement, the money was paid to states, but under the opioid settlements, funds go directly to impacted jurisdictions. That’s good, because officials best know their communities’ specific needs, Scher said.
But such fractured disbursement makes it difficult to monitor spending, assess compliance, and compare the effectiveness of spending across jurisdictions, he said.
Compounding things is the settlements’ requirement that at least 85% of the money going to states and local governments be spent on “abatement.” That’s defined loosely enough that some public officials have stretched their interpretation of abatement to cover things that have fueled misspending accusations, such as bounce houses, DJs, popcorn machines, and more at concerts and community festivals billed as “awareness” events.
“There’s going to be over a billion dollars disbursed in New Jersey over the next 20 years, and we’re right at the beginning of that,” Scher said. “The state government should be putting things in place to support proper reporting and good spending.”
 Spitballing solutions
Two bills now in the Statehouse pipeline would tighten oversight of opioid settlement spending.
Assemblywoman Maureen Rowan (D-Atlantic) introduced a bill Monday that prohibits local governments from using opioid funds to cover items and activities normally paid out of their general budgets. It also bars certain police spending, including on surveillance and training that’s not specifically tied to opioid remediation, as well as spending on campaign contributions, wastewater testing, foster and kinship care, insurance or liability costs, addiction treatments not approved by the FDA, services that could be billed under Medicaid, and more.
Assemblyman Cody Miller (D-Gloucester) talks during an Assembly oversight committee hearing on Oct. 22, 2026. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)
Assemblyman Cody Miller (D-Gloucester) introduced another bill last month that would require recipients to spend funds within 18 months, or forfeit money to the state unless they get state approval to hold onto it longer. Cape May and Essex counties and 50 towns reported that they spent no funds in the fiscal year that ended June 30, despite having millions on hand and ongoing overdoses (Essex County leads the state in both fatal overdoses and administrations of the overdose-reversing drug naloxone), according to spending reports released last month.
Miller’s bill also would establish training to educate recipients on approved uses; require recipients to repay misspent funds; and create an online link where the public can report suspected misuse, waste, or fraud.
Advocates applauded the spirit of that bill at a public hearing last month in Trenton but urged legislators to give it more teeth.
Fredrick, of the comptroller’s office, echoed that, saying the bill would require reimbursement of misspent funds but doesn’t address how improper spending would be routinely identified. Walsh had recommended that legislators clarify the Department of Human Services’ responsibilities, direct officials there to use their existing rule-making authority to issue further guidance to local governments, and consider funding independent oversight to ensure compliance, Fredrick added.
Miller said he and the bill’s other sponsors continue to amend the bill in response to public feedback. He hopes to see it voted on by the end of the year.
“In an ideal world, I would have this on the agenda for tomorrow,” Miller said. “We are at a point now where there has been so much money that has been spent on things that I never would have thought that they would spend money on. And now we have to fix it.”
Leonard Goldberg is founder of Settlement Insight, which tracks trends in lawsuit settlements. He said an 18-month deadline for spending could prevent money from sitting idle — but is just as likely to push towns into the kinds of hasty purchases that have outraged advocates.
“New Jersey’s gap isn’t the list of approved uses, it’s that no one has both the job and the tools to enforce it,” Goldberg said.
He pointed to the Model Opioid Litigation Proceeds Act, which the Legislative Analysis and Public Policy Association first released in 2021. The model law requires fund recipients to annually certify that they used the money as required and publicly report how spending fit approved uses, and a state’s auditor or attorney general to audit spending every year and report on misuse complaints and investigations. All of that would be posted online for the public to see.
Pennsylvania and North Carolina both have strong laws with some of those components in place, Goldberg added.
North Carolina requires every fund recipient to file an annual independent audit of spending and financial reports both to the public and the attorney general. Recipients have 60 days to fix disallowed expenses or face losing that amount from future payments, and the attorney general can take persistent offenders to court to recover misspent funds.
Pennsylvania created a trust that rules on spending, can withhold money if it finds inappropriate uses, and can cut funds to recipients that don’t correct misspending.
New Jersey should embrace a similar approach — name one enforcer and give it teeth by requiring it to review spending annually and withhold funds from jurisdictions that misspend, Goldberg said. Towns that fail to file required reports, as 16 towns in New Jersey did according to reports the state released last month, should have their next payment docked until they do, he added.
Staff from the Department of Human Services partner with the comptroller’s office to track down stragglers every year; of the 16 towns that missed this year’s filing deadline, only Irvington and Weehawken still have yet to file reports, Loayza-McBride said last week.
Lawmakers also should not trust towns to self-report but instead should require them to file independent audits, signed certifications, and line-item reporting showing the vendor, amount, and approved-use category for every expense, Goldberg said.
“A false certification then becomes a matter for the comptroller or the attorney general, not just a bad headline,” he said.
Junfola seconded those suggestions, adding that municipalities and counties should enlist their attorneys to review planned spending to guard against abuse.
Private companies that misuse public money would lose it and risk civil and criminal sanctions, so municipalities and counties should face that same standard, he said.
“The reports themselves are premised on the assumption of truth and honesty. As a taxpayer, it’s reasonable to expect truthful disclosure in the report,” Junfola said. “Unfortunately more often than not, that was not the case.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: After big wins, WA House Democrats face an internal duel for speaker
description: Fresh off a monster midterm that catapulted them to a supermajority, Democratic state lawmakers in Washington face a huge vote Monday on who will lead their powerful House caucus. Rep. April Berg, D-Mill Creek, is challenging House Speaker Laurie Jinkins, D-Tacoma, in a contest defined by differences in style rather than policy, and members’ desire […]
text:
Rep. April Berg, left, is making a bid for Washington state House House speaker against Rep. Laurie Jinkins, right. (Photos by Washington State Standard)Fresh off a monster midterm that catapulted them to a supermajority, Democratic state lawmakers in Washington face a huge vote Monday on who will lead their powerful House caucus.
Rep. April Berg, D-Mill Creek, is challenging House Speaker Laurie Jinkins, D-Tacoma, in a contest defined by differences in style rather than policy, and members’ desire for change over continuity.
House Democrats, whose numbers will swell to 69 with the addition of 10 seats, will meet  today at the state Capitol to fill several leadership posts. All Democrats who won or are leading their races in the Nov. 3 election are eligible to vote.
The battle for speakership is the most high-profile. Veteran lawmakers reached by the Standard wouldn’t speculate about how it will turn out. Several noted that some of the 20 caucus newcomers campaigned as disrupters of the political status quo and it is unknown how that could factor into their decision related to caucus leadership.
Jinkins, first elected to the House in 2010, has been speaker since January 2020 and is the first woman and the first lesbian to ever hold the position. She succeeded Frank Chopp, Washington’s longest serving and arguably most powerful speaker in the history of the House of Representatives.
During her tenure, the caucus has grown from 57 members to 69. This year’s incoming class of Democrats has 20 people: the 10 who won Republican-held seats and 10 others who won Democrat-controlled seats, some held by incumbents.
Berg won her House seat in 2020. As chair of the House Finance Committee, she shepherded this year’s controversial income tax law through the chamber. She began her bid to unseat Jinkins in the spring.
“The caucus will have a choice between two distinctly different leadership styles,” she said in an interview last week. 
In her pitch to members, she said she talks about the ways they can organize and manage themselves.
That’s indirect acknowledgement of frustration with how some controversial legislation is handled and how floor sessions play out. Many days are marked by extended caucus meetings, followed by lengthy periods of waiting to vote, resulting in sessions that last until midnight and beyond.
Such marathons have long been a feature of the House operation under Democrat control. They predate Jinkins, but lawmakers have grown tired of it, concerned that late nights negatively impact the health of staff and their own ability to process complex legislation, especially when extensive revisions are proposed. Behind closed doors, they have pressed for greater efficiency and earlier, shorter floor sessions, citing the Senate’s ability to adjourn closer to the dinner hour.
Jinkins could not be reached for comment for this story. 
Asked in May about the challenge, she said, “I am not perfect, that’s for darn sure. I think we’ve accomplished a lot to advance Washington state. There’s always more work to be done.”
Whoever is chosen will be deemed as Speaker-designate. The entire House will formally choose the speaker on the first day of the 2027 session.
Also Monday, the Democratic caucus will fill the jobs of majority leader, floor leader and caucus leader.
House Majority Leader Joe Fitzgibbon, D-West Seattle, was unopposed as of Friday. 
Reps. Mary Fosse, D-Everett, and Liz Berry, D-Seattle, are vying for floor leader and will succeed Rep. Monica Stonier, D-Vancouver, who is forgoing re-election to that post. Fosse is currently the deputy majority floor leader.
Rep. Brianna Thomas, D-Seattle, is seeking to be the next caucus leader. Rep. Lillian Ortiz-Self, D-Mukilteo, chose not to seek re-election.
Senate Dems keep their leader
State Sen. Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, talks on the Senate floor in January 2024. (Legislative Support Services)
The Senate Democratic Caucus set their leadership structure on Nov. 5. Democrats outnumber Republicans in the chamber by a margin of 30-19.
Sen. Jamie Pedersen, D-Seattle, was re-elected Senate majority leader with Sen. Manka Dhingra, D-Redmond, chosen to return as deputy majority leader. Sen. Liz Lovelett, D-Anacortes, will be caucus chair with Sen. Marcus Riccelli, D-Spokane, continuing as floor leader.
Sen. Bob Hasegawa, D-Tukwila, who had been caucus chair since 2021, was elected President Pro Tempore, a role that will become official following a vote by the full Senate on the first day of the 2027 session.
Senate Republicans are scheduled to hold their reorganization votes on Dec. 6 with the House Republican Caucus choosing their leaders on Dec. 11. 
The 2027 legislative session is scheduled to begin Jan. 11 and last 105 days.SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
