name: Connecticut Mirror
title: States, cities move to ban cryptocurrency kiosks as scams mount
description: States and cities across the country are cracking down on cryptocurrency kiosks as financial scams involving the ATM-like machines mount.
text:
States and cities across the country are cracking down on cryptocurrency kiosks as financial scams involving the ATM-like machines continue to mount, costing Americans nearly $389 million last year alone.
Four states — Indiana, Minnesota, Tennessee and Vermont — enacted statewide bans this year, while dozens of communities have moved to prohibit the machines or impose new restrictions on their use. A new law in Hawaii, which went into effect in October, bans consumers from depositing cash into kiosks to buy cryptocurrency.
The crackdown comes as scammers increasingly direct victims to cryptocurrency kiosks, often located in gas stations, convenience stores and grocery stores, to deposit cash that is converted into digital currency and transferred to accounts controlled by criminals.
The FBI received 13,460 complaints involving cryptocurrency kiosks in 2025, with reported losses totaling nearly $389 million. Complaints increased 23% from the previous year, while financial losses jumped 58%, according to the agency’s cybercrime report, which was released in April. 
Older Americans have been particularly hard hit. More than half of the complaints involved people older than 50, who reported more than $302 million in losses last year.
The mounting losses have prompted policymakers across the country to pursue tighter restrictions and outright bans on cryptocurrency kiosks — efforts that consumer advocates say are urgently needed to prevent further financial harm.
“Every day that these laws aren’t passed are days where victims are having money stolen from them, and that money, because it’s through cryptocurrency and the nature of the kiosk, it’s just almost impossible to get any of that money back,” said Françoise Cleveland, AARP’s government affairs director, in an interview with Stateline. 
Indiana became the first state to ban cryptocurrency kiosks in March, followed by Tennessee and Vermont in July and Minnesota in August. The measures mark a shift from earlier efforts to regulate the machines through transaction limits, fraud warnings and licensing requirements.
At least 35 states have enacted legislation addressing cryptocurrency kiosks since 2023, including 18 that passed laws this year, according to AARP, which has advocated for stronger consumer protections. 
Local governments are stepping up, too. In Massachusetts, at least 20 communities have banned cryptocurrency kiosks as of August. In late October, a crypto kiosk ban took effect in Jackson, Michigan — the first of its kind in the state. Operators must remove machines by the end of January. The fast-growing city of Star, Idaho, passed a ban in September requiring kiosks to be removed by this month.
Other municipalities have opted to allow the machines but add stricter restrictions, including requiring fraud warnings, identification checks or transaction limits.
Attorneys general in several places, including the District of Columbia, Iowa and Massachusetts, have sued cryptocurrency kiosk operators, alleging they exploited residents and failed to implement adequate safeguards against fraud. 
A three-year investigation by the Iowa attorney general’s office found that 98% of transactions at Bitcoin Depot kiosks in the state were linked to scams, compared with 94% at CoinFlip kiosks. The findings, released in February, prompted the state to sue both companies. 
Bitcoin Depot has since filed for bankruptcy, citing increasingly restrictive state regulations and bans. The company took its kiosks offline in May.
In recent years, some kiosk operators have pushed back against outright bans and some proposed restrictions, arguing that the machines serve legitimate customers and that stronger fraud safeguards, rather than prohibitions, would better protect consumers.
Earlier this year, Larry Lipka, the general counsel for CoinFlip, which operates more than 5,000 kiosks in the U.S. and other countries, testified against the statewide ban in Minnesota, arguing that regulators should strengthen enforcement instead. 
“It is inappropriate to ban a legal product because fraud is happening. Not our fault,” Lipka said. 
Some operators, including CoinFlip, have also implemented holding periods during which transactions can be reversed, offer refunds to scam victims and provide 24/7 customer support.
How the scams work
Unlike traditional ATMs, which allow customers to withdraw or deposit money from bank accounts, cryptocurrency kiosks allow users to purchase digital currencies such as Bitcoin with cash. Some machines also allow customers to sell cryptocurrency in exchange for cash.
Scammers exploit the machines by calling victims and persuading them to withdraw money from their bank accounts and deposit it into a kiosk, often providing a QR code linked to a digital wallet controlled by the criminal.
Once the cash is deposited, the machine converts it into cryptocurrency and transfers the funds to the designated digital account, called a “wallet.” Those transactions generally cannot be reversed, making it difficult for victims to recover their money. Kiosk operators also charge transaction fees, regardless of whether the transaction was fraudulent, typically ranging from 20% to 30%, depending on the company.
The scams take several forms. Criminals may impersonate law enforcement officers, government officials, bank employees or technical support representatives, falsely claiming that victims owe money, face arrest or need to move their savings to protect them from fraud.
Other scammers establish romantic relationships online or promote fraudulent investment opportunities before directing victims to deposit money into the machines.
In many cases, scammers remain on the phone with victims throughout the transaction, providing step-by-step instructions on where to find a kiosk and how to send the money.
Beyond financial scams
Although older Americans account for a disproportionate share of reported losses involving cryptocurrency kiosks, some investigators say the machines can also play a role in crimes affecting younger people.
Matt Hogan, a detective with the Connecticut State Police who investigates financial crimes, said kiosks have been used in connection with financially motivated sextortion, in which perpetrators threaten to distribute intimate images or videos unless victims pay them money.
The schemes can target teenagers and young adults, who may be coerced into sending money to prevent explicit images from being shared with family members, friends or classmates.
The FBI has warned that financially motivated sextortion increasingly targets teenage boys, particularly those between 14 and 17. Criminals may demand payment through mobile payment applications, gift cards or cryptocurrency.
“That’s definitely an up and coming problem,” Hogan said.
Hogan also pointed to the use of cryptocurrency kiosks in other criminal activity, including money laundering, narcotics-related offenses and payments involving child sexual abuse material.
Federal authorities have raised similar concerns. In an August 2025 notice, the federal Treasury Department’s Financial Crimes Enforcement Network warned that cryptocurrency kiosks were being used to facilitate scams and launder suspected drug proceeds.
A 2022 report from the U.S. Government Accountability Office also found that drug and human traffickers have used cryptocurrency kiosks to convert cash into digital currency and obscure the source of illicit payments.
“Everybody is a potential target for fraud,” said Cleveland, of AARP.
Regulation or outright bans?
Despite those concerns, Hogan expressed reservations about banning cryptocurrency kiosks altogether.
He said he supports many of the consumer protections being adopted across the country, but worries that outright bans could push criminals toward alternative methods of transferring money that may be more difficult for investigators to trace.
Transactions involving Bitcoin and many other cryptocurrencies are recorded on public digital ledgers known as blockchains, allowing investigators to follow the movement of funds between digital wallets. Advances in investigative techniques have also given law enforcement more tools to trace cryptocurrency transactions, although identifying the people behind those transactions and recovering stolen funds is still sometimes difficult.
“If these machines do get shut off, bad guys are ingenuitive,” Hogan said of potential kiosk bans. “They are able to pivot. They have no care for authority or morals, so they will pivot to a place that we likely will have less visibility.” 
Industry representatives have also pushed back against the growing wave of bans, warning of the economic consequences for businesses and the customers who rely on their services.
That debate played out in Indiana earlier this year, where lawmakers initially considered legislation requiring kiosk operators to obtain licenses, verify customers’ identities and comply with transaction and fee limits.
But after hearing testimony from law enforcement, scam victims and industry representatives, lawmakers abandoned the proposed regulations in favor of an outright ban.
“I can think of no legitimate reasons, no substantial legitimate reasons,” to warrant the kiosks, Republican state Sen. Scott Baldwin said during a February committee hearing.
CoinFlip, which had operated in Indiana for eight years, criticized the decision, saying it had worked with lawmakers in 17 other states to adopt consumer protections without prohibiting the machines.
“We are shocked to learn that the state of Indiana would eliminate an entire industry based on a lack of understanding of digital assets and the services we already provide to 17,000 Hoosiers around the state,” a company spokesperson told the Indiana Capital Chronicle.
This story was first published Nov. 16, 2026 by Stateline.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Democrats rode an election wave. Could it carry them to power in 2028?
description: Scott Miller appears to have won another term in the Missouri House. Barely. The St. Charles County Republican beat Democrat Chris Chapman by 67 votes on Nov. 3, according to unofficial results. It was a rematch. Two years ago, Miller beat Chapman by 3,288 votes. This time, the margin is close enough to qualify for […]
text:
After sweeping gains in 2026, Missouri Democrats see a path to a House majority in 2028. But winning statewide or taking the Senate remains difficult (Jim Neuger/Maine Morning Star).Scott Miller appears to have won another term in the Missouri House. Barely.
The St. Charles County Republican beat Democrat Chris Chapman by 67 votes on Nov. 3, according to unofficial results. It was a rematch. Two years ago, Miller beat Chapman by 3,288 votes. This time, the margin is close enough to qualify for a recount under state law.
Democrats flipped 16 House seats and broke the GOP’s supermajorities. Districts like Miller’s, where Republicans held on, may matter more for 2028.
In all 96 House districts where both parties fielded candidates in both 2024 and 2026, Democrats improved their share of the two-party vote. The average gain was nearly nine percentage points. And the shift extended deep into rural, Republican Missouri.
The auditor’s race provides another way to measure the shift because Republican Scott Fitzpatrick was on the ballot in both 2022 and 2026. The Democratic share of the two-party vote rose from 38.8% to 47.7%. The largest shifts came in Pemiscot County in the Bootheel, Jasper County around Joplin, and Clay and Cass counties in the Kansas City area.
Rural Missouri didn’t turn blue. Pemiscot moved more than any county in the state, and Fitzpatrick still carried it by 34 points. But the Republican advantage shrank almost everywhere, and higher turnout around Kansas City, St. Louis and Springfield magnified the shift.
Missouri Republicans suffer biggest electoral setback in a generation

A lot of ink has been spilled pouring over the results of an historic election in Missouri. Now comes the hard part for Democrats: turning a wave into power.
Republicans will hold 95 of 163 House seats in January. Democrats will hold 68. To take the chamber in 2028, Democrats need a net gain of 14.
There is a potential path. Fourteen Republican-held districts were decided by fewer than eight percentage points this year. Six are in St. Charles County, including Miller’s and two others Republicans held by 125 and 276 votes. The other eight are in St. Louis County and in Jackson, Jefferson, Boone and Jasper counties.
If Democrats gained another four percentage points of the two-party vote in every district, they would win 82 seats. That is a majority with nothing to spare.
It also assumes they lose nothing they won this year, and some of those wins are fragile. Suzanne Luther took her Jefferson City seat by 189 votes. And 2028 is a presidential year, with a bigger electorate. Republicans won every statewide race in the last two presidential elections by double digits.
The Senate offers Democrats fewer options. Republicans will hold a 22-12 majority. Three GOP seats on the 2028 ballot stand out: Joe Nicola’s in Jackson County, David Gregory’s in St. Louis County and Adam Schnelting’s in St. Charles County.
Nicola and Gregory each won in 2024 by fewer than five points, in a year Republicans carried the down-ballot statewide races by about 20. Schnelting won by about 10.
The 2026 House returns sharpen the picture. In the House districts entirely within those three Senate districts, the Democratic share of the two-party vote rose 8.4 percentage points in Nicola’s district, 8.7 in Gregory’s and 9.9 in Schnelting’s. Democrats flipped all three House seats entirely within Schnelting’s district.
Those aren’t estimates for the entire Senate districts because some House boundaries cross Senate lines. Still, the gains suggest all three could be competitive in 2028.
Even a Democratic sweep would leave the party three seats short of a Senate majority.
What two surprise Democratic victories reveal about Missouri’s blue wave

Statewide is harder still. Democrats haven’t won a statewide race since 2018, when Nicole Galloway was elected auditor. Her opponent, Saundra McDowell, was dogged by controversy and lacked anything resembling normal party financial support. McDowell ran nearly seven points behind Josh Hawley on the same ballot.
Against a conventional Republican that year, Claire McCaskill lost to Hawley by 5.8 points. This year, Quentin Wilson lost to Fitzpatrick by 4.5 points, or about 94,500 votes.
Wilson’s loss was narrower than McCaskill’s eight years earlier. But what happened in the next two presidential elections offers a warning.
In 2020, Galloway ran for governor and drew more votes than she had in winning the auditor’s office. She lost by 16 points. In 2024, Lucas Kunce drew more than 1.24 million votes against Hawley and lost by nearly 14.
There is also a gap between how Missouri votes on issues and how it votes on Democrats. On the same ballot that gave Wilson 46.4%, 55.4% of voters rejected the repeal of abortion rights and 61.8% rejected the Republican-drawn congressional map. Opposing those measures is not the same as voting Democratic.
Democrats now have a map to a House majority. Whether the gains that put it within reach can survive a presidential election is another question.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Commentary: Ayoub: Respecting the right to vote still a thing
description: Kudos to Nebraska’s county election commissioners who pulled off yet another hitchless election. They not only know what they are doing, they do it without fanfare or fuss. Props, too, for the Secretary of State’s Office for its role in the midterms.  Such precision staves off the yammering about “stolen” elections and other conspiratorial hoohaw, […]
text:
Voters fill out ballots and check in with election workers at a polling place in Lincoln, Nebraska, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Tables and voting booths fill the room as neighbors exercise their right to vote. (Photo by Michelle Montenegro/Nebraska News Service)Kudos to Nebraska’s county election commissioners who pulled off yet another hitchless election. They not only know what they are doing, they do it without fanfare or fuss. Props, too, for the Secretary of State’s Office for its role in the midterms. 
Such precision staves off the yammering about “stolen” elections and other conspiratorial hoohaw, although we were not completely spared that nonsense this time around. More on that below.
Nebraskans had previously avoided the folderol of mid-decade gerrymandering, the practice of political parties and their candidates — apparently bereft of good ideas — choosing their voters rather than voters choosing them. According to Protect Democracy, over 34 million American voters in nine states found themselves in a new congressional district on Election Day. If you’re keeping score at home, that’s about one in 10 of us.
We may have dodged an embarrassing bullet, however. It seems those voters who were rerouted by redrawing the lines showed up and showed out, turning the restricting dreams of the president, his GOP water carriers — even the Democratic California governor who played a Golden State version of tit-for-tat gerrymandering — into a nightmare when the counts came in. The math is revelatory: Democrats won in 11 of 15 congressional districts ostensibly altered to give an advantage to Republican candidates. Oops. Apparently large swaths of voters take poorly when somebody messes with their civic duty. 
Gerrymandering is not exactly voter suppression, but you can see it from there. Since the Big Lie of 2020, one hallmark of our election cycles has been state legislatures — often with dubious or nonexistent data to bolster their arguments — hell bent on adding hoops through which voters must jump to mark their X and get it counted. 
Trying to restrict voting, however, started well before that, according to the Brennan Center for Justice. Since 2010, 25 states, including Nebraska, have enacted voter restriction measures, some of which were bolstered by a 2013 Supreme Court decision discussed a few paragraphs down.
Barriers have included reducing the number of polling places, purging voter rolls without accurate data and eliminating drop boxes. The White House has attacked — without evidence — the efficacy of mail-in ballots and even asked the Supreme Court to allow the Postal Service to screen them. The high court said no. Some states, as Nebraska did in 2023, added photo ID requirements, which seem to work here. Nevertheless, they carry an original sin. They are premised on the fairy tale that the 2020 election was rife with fraud, which is also the foundation for the lie that hordes of noncitizens were poised to vote in the 2026 midterms. It’s exhausting. 
As is the president’s wont to do, and after saying he would accept the midterm results, he posted on social media his doubts about the efficacy of the midterms. “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest,” he wrote. Apparently most everyone. Response to his suggestion of impropriety has been tepid at best. The muted reaction reminded me of former Texas Gov. Ann Richards, who when questioning exorbitant government spending on failed military and economic programs said, “That old dog won’t hunt.” 
Although voters overcame considerable efforts to deny, dilute and discourage their power at the ballot box, the new Congress — in addition to addressing tariffs, war, high prices, minimum wage, ethics, healthcare, accountability and the reaffirmation of our democracy itself — could eliminate some of the voter suppression bunk above by passing the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act, which would restore a key section of the 1965 Voting Rights Act gutted in 2013 by the Supreme Court. 
Here’s how: Section 5 of the original VRA required any state or jurisdiction with a history of discriminatory practices in elections to prove they no longer stood between Americans and their votes with distempers such as poll taxes and literacy tests. The term for this proof is “preclearance.” 
For nearly five decades that was the law, until the Supremes, in a 5-4 vote, decided that preclearance was outdated, that apparently discriminatory practices were no longer in effect. Section 5 remains but no one has to abide by it. Ironically, states and jurisdictions who previously had to prove they were not discriminatory almost immediately began to institute voter suppression tactics like those mentioned above, especially in Black majority districts, proving, in a sense, that the high court had misread the tea leaves. 
When Nebraska’s quintet of representatives arrive in January to a new, bluer Congress, they would do well to put the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act near the top of their to-do list. That would underscore and in a sense further respect the work of county elections commissioners back home.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: How SC investigators found a rural wastewater manager hid 3 years of E. coli contamination
description: A wastewater plant was on the radar of South Carolina environmental regulators long before its manager was charged for violating federal law.
text:
A passing boat creates waves in Lake Murray off Dreher Island State Park in Newberry County on Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026. The Little Saluda River flows into Lake Murray. (Photo by Seanna Adcox/SC Daily Gazette)A nearly 45-year-old wastewater treatment plant owned by the town of Saluda was on the radar of South Carolina environmental regulators long before prosecutors charged its manager with violating federal law.
The Saluda Wastewater Treatment Plant racked up 100 violations over the past three years, most of them minor to medium-level, federal reports show.
“I don’t think it was at a code red level: oh my gosh you wouldn’t believe what’s going on, this is the Chernobyl of sewage plants up here,” Winston Holliday, the federal prosecutor assigned to the case, told the SC Daily Gazette earlier this month. “I don’t think it was anything like that.”
But regulators at the state Department of Environmental Services had been trying to get the operators of the plant, which serves the rural South Carolina municipality’s roughly 3,000 residents, to clean up its discharge into the Little Saluda River, a tributary of Lake Murray, said Kirk Corley, a senior special investigator for the agency.
When their advice went unheeded, they tapped Corley’s three-man investigative team to pursue criminal charges.
Then, in July 2025, more than 1,500 fish died a mile downstream of the plant after an E coli. contamination choked the oxygen from the water of the slow-moving, shallow river that Corley said is little more than a creek.
The probe heated up, and what state and federal investigators found was not only permit violations but attempts to hide the problem.
John Lorick, senior manager for the Saluda Commission of Public Works, diluted water samples to conceal E. coli levels elevated due to an inoperative chlorination system. And on dozens of occasions over more than three years, he allowed raw, untreated sewage to be released directly into the river.
How much sewage is unknown because the spills happened over such a long period, according to the agency.
“When you have somebody falsifying records, you know you’re there. You’re in criminal territory immediately,” Holliday said.
A wastewater manager faces 3 years in prison for hiding 3 years of E. coli contamination from SC

State regulators had been watching the daily water reports that wastewater plant operators were required to file.
“Our regulatory staff knows what a (daily monitoring report) should look like. They know what a healthy plant, a well-run plant or a horrible plant looks like. They’re evaluating these (reports) and they’re going, these numbers just don’t look realistic,” Corley told the SC Daily Gazette.
What they saw were numbers that were impossibly clean and they started taking their own samples downstream.
“On one of the days, when our regulatory staff went out and sampled it, the outflow came back with an astronomical number in E. coli,” Corley said. “That same day, Lorick had reported a number less than one. So, we had the same day and we had two very different readings. “
From there, investigators looked at shipment records of how much chlorine came into the plant. They noticed the plant was using way less than what was expected for a working system.
A concerned resident told investigators he had heard about goings on at the plant.
“He saw kids fishing and getting fish from the creek and it just bothered him so bad,” Corley said.
And interviews with current and former employees confirmed those suspicions.
For a while, Lorick, of Ninety-Six, denied any wrongdoing, Corley said, but eventually admitted his actions.
On Oct. 29, Lorick entered a guilty plea in federal court for violations of the federal Clean Water Act. The Greenwood County resident faces a maximum penalty of three years in federal prison and fines between $5,000 and $50,000 per violation.

A judge is scheduled to sentence him in early March, court records show.
Lorick’s attorney did not respond to messages from the SC Daily Gazette. And the chairwoman of the town’s public works commission declined to comment, citing the ongoing case.
The town of Saluda is in the process of closing down its plant by the end of the year as it connects to a new Saluda County Water and Sewer Authority wastewater treatment plant, built adjacent to the town facility. Mayor Miliken Matthews did not respond to messages from the SC Daily Gazette about what kicked off plans for an updated plant.
But Corley said his investigation showed that Lorick was upset about the decision by the public works board to close the town plant.
And while the town may not have wanted to make major investments to a plant it planned to close, it had a responsibility not to pollute and cause harm in the meantime.
“It was an antiquated facility. It could have obviously been better. There were improvements that could have been made to it. But rather than jump up and down, he took steps to minimize and overshadow the problems that the facility had,” Holliday said. “What he should have been doing was reporting it and getting in front of everybody he could, saying we need to do this, and he didn’t.”
While sewage spills aren’t rare, one that leads to criminal charges are, Corley added. Generally, warnings from regulators are enough to get wastewater plants in compliance.
“Most plants don’t necessarily make it to this point,” he said.
When they do, Holliday said, the U.S. Attorney’s Office in South Carolina is “pretty aggressive with environmental cases.”
“That is sort of baked into our culture,” he said. “I’ve been in the office since December of 2003, and every U.S. attorney I’ve worked for has supported environmental prosecution.”
“If you live in Columbia, it’s two hours from the ocean and you’re two hours from the mountain. That’s how people sell Columbia,” he added. “And I think my office has felt all along that it’s part of our responsibility to help protect and preserve that aspect of the state.”

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: ‘Process over policy’: Arch reflects on qualities of a good speaker of Nebraska Legislature
description: LINCOLN — Speaker of the Nebraska Legislature John Arch has led the Cornhusker State’s one-house legislative branch through some of its most tumultuous moments in the past four years. Arch, a legislator from La Vista, is term-limited and will be leaving the 49-person Legislature come January. In his tenure, the Legislature faced days-long filibusters where [[...]
text:
State lawmakers gather around Speaker John Arch of La Vista, center, on the final day of Nebraska's 2026 legislative session. Arch holds a frame gifted to him with signatures from all 48 of his colleagues. The picture shows a man herding cats. April 17, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examine)LINCOLN — Speaker of the Nebraska Legislature John Arch has led the Cornhusker State’s one-house legislative branch through some of its most tumultuous moments in the past four years.
Arch, a legislator from La Vista, is term-limited and will be leaving the 49-person Legislature come January. In his tenure, the Legislature faced days-long filibusters where recipes and movie scripts dominated debate sometimes more than policy arguments, in addition to multiple budget deficits following significant income tax cuts approved in 2023.
Having talked to many speakers nationwide, Arch said Nebraska is different, in part because of the one-house, officially nonpartisan Legislature. In other states, by contrast, speakers might appoint committee chairs or decide what bills can come to the floor.
“They have tremendous discretionary power, and that is just not the role of the speaker in Nebraska,” Arch said.
Speaker John Arch of La Vista reacts to a majority of his colleagues voting against passage of adjustments to the Nebraska state budget in a planned April Fool’s Day prank before switching course and passing the budget 35-13. April 1, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The race to succeed Arch has already begun before the next Legislature begins Jan. 6. State Sens. Teresa Ibach of Sumner and Kathleen Kauth of Omaha have put their names forward. Nebraska has never elected a female speaker of the Legislature.
Arch declined to weigh in on Ibach or Kauth. He said a good speaker understands their role is to secure a “predictable, rule-followed process” for the Legislature. There is some discretion, but once the speaker puts out memos outlining the process each year, “you stick to that.” 
Arch, for instance, defined “full and fair debate” as eight hours during first consideration followed by four hours in the second round of debate and two hours on final reading. Once those limits were reached, lawmakers could file “cloture” and, with at least 33 votes, end a filibuster. By contrast, most bills for which debate ends before the time limit can pass with a simple majority.
In 2025, after being reelected as speaker, Arch announced a process by which “controversial and emotionally charged legislation” would face half those time limits.
“For the role of the speaker in this Legislature, it is process over policy,” Arch said.
Ibach, Kauth detail runs for 2027-28 speaker of the Nebraska Legislature

Under legislative rules, senators and committees can give a “priority” designation to increase the chances that a bill or resolution is scheduled. Speakers try to schedule as many of those bills as possible as time allows. Lawmakers begin each session working through bills as they advance from committees before priority bills are selected.
Traditionally, speakers don’t speak very often on bills and focus on scheduling, Arch said. He noted a challenge is that the speaker is also a state senator who has opinions and votes to represent their district, which remains important. He said process becomes “your No. 1 function.”
“The institution, the process, all of that takes precedence over personal desire to see a particular policy pass,” Arch said.
Arch said he has had conversations with many lawmakers about leadership roles where they might fit best. Leadership votes are conducted by secret ballot. At least 25 votes are needed.
The next Legislature begins Jan. 6.
Speaker John Arch of La Vista, right, meets with State Sens. Danielle Conrad of Lincoln and Tom Brandt of Plymouth on the floor of the Nebraska Legislature. March 30, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)

title: Commentary: Oklahoma’s new lieutenant governor, aka our biggest cheerleader, already seems focused elsewhere
description: Who wants to tell Oklahoma’s incoming lieutenant governor that his main job will be to serve as a tourism and economic cheerleader? Fine, I’ll break it to Lt. Gov.-elect T.W. Shannon gently: His new post, which officially starts in 2027, serves mostly as a figurehead, spending days crisscrossing our great state to promote unity and […]
text:
Oklahoma Lieutenant Governor-elect T.W. Shannon speaks during the GOP Election Night Watch Party, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, at Skirvin Hotel in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)Who wants to tell Oklahoma’s incoming lieutenant governor that his main job will be to serve as a tourism and economic cheerleader?
Fine, I’ll break it to Lt. Gov.-elect T.W. Shannon gently: His new post, which officially starts in 2027, serves mostly as a figurehead, spending days crisscrossing our great state to promote unity and the strengths of our 4.1 million diverse residents.
But before he even takes office, Shannon seems focused on doing the opposite of what his new role entails. The Republican is sharing bigoted and divisive tropes, picking fights with Democrats who lost and attempting to deliver zingers to out–of–state political foes like he’s the head of a dance squad in “Bring It On.” 
The days after the Nov. 3, midterm blue tsunami, Shannon let loose a stream of Islamophobic posts on X that make him look like he’s forgotten the fate of Oklahoma’s last statewide elected official (cough, Ryan Walters, cough) who thought fearmongering and pushing for Christian nationalistic practices was good strategy. (Reminder: Facing enormous public scrutiny and angst, Walters, our former state education superintendent, resigned with 15 months left in his term.)
Shannon’s social media screed claimed the Islamist Muslim Brotherhood – groups of which the Trump administration has designated as terrorists – and the Iranian regime were celebrating the GOP losses across the U.S. His post was accompanied by an AI-generated image of Osama bin Laden resting his hands on the shoulders of newly elected Michigan Democratic U.S. Senator Abdul El-Sayed. Next to the duo, the fake image features former Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini with his hands resting on the shoulders of Zohran Mamdani, New York’s democratic socialist mayor elected a year ago. Both El-Sayed and Mamdani are American Muslims – and in case you forgot, bin Laden and Khomeini have both been dead for many years.
And if that wasn’t enough, the next day Shannon also celebrated the closure of the Council on American Islamic Relations in Florida. That followed a federal judge rejecting an emergency request to stop the state from designating the Muslim American civil rights organization group as a domestic terrorist organization.
“This is what leadership looks like: designate them as a foreign terrorist organization, then enforce the law,” he posted. “I’ll never understand why we still haven’t done this in Oklahoma. What are we waiting for??”
To clarify for Shannon, the reason Oklahoma’s chapter of CAIR has not been designated as a “foreign terrorist organization” is because there is no evidence that it is one.
(For what it’s worth, Shannon’s fellow Republican, Gov. Kevin Stitt, already demanded an investigation into Oklahoma’s CAIR chapter. He has announced nothing from the probe, and at the time, experts said Stitt’s executive order was “political theater” designed to tap into a broader anti-Muslim undercurrent.)
Last week, Shannon called Oklahoma Democrats’ U.S. Senate nominee N’Kiyla Jasmine Thomas a “radicalized feminazi” who “wants to blame her loss on racism because she’s ‘black and indigenous.’”
Shannon said on X that he’s living proof that America is not the “home of systemic racism,” but rather the “land of systemic opportunity.”
Thomas, who is Chickasaw, fired back on Facebook, pointing out that Shannon’s victory doesn’t erase systemic racism.
“Your personal experiences do not invalidate mine,” she wrote. “And your new title does not exempt you from criticism.”
So why would Shannon turn to artificial intelligence slop, misinformation and the GOP’s tired playbook? 
Maybe because he is looking to rewrite the lieutenant governor’s role of placeholder. Shannon had become something of a statewide perennial candidate, with two failed U.S. Senate bids under his belt. He finally found an office he could win, albeit one that has little power and influence over policies that matter (save for the rare occurrence of having to cast a tie–breaking vote in the Republican-dominated state Senate).
The cynic in me would think Shannon could also be looking at lieutenant governor as a springboard to higher office as some previously did with the office, including former Republican Gov. Mary Fallin and the late-Democratic Gov. George Nigh. 
But does Shannon have to do it this way? The message from voters this month was clear: They want to be able to afford to live, and they’re tired of the types of polarizing distractions Republicans have been waving around.
What makes this situation even more unfortunate is that Shannon – like El-Sayed, the first Muslim American elected to the U.S. Senate – has paved the way for people who enter politics from underrepresented backgrounds. Shannon’s campaign website celebrates him as Oklahoma’s first Chickasaw and Black speaker of the House. When he won statewide office this month, ICT – which covers Native people and tribal issues – listed him among the handful of known Indigenous Americans elected lieutenant governor. And the Oklahoma City-based Black Chronicle celebrated his win as historic.  
Shannon could use his story to let people know that Oklahoma is a place where everyone has the chance to thrive. Or to inspire a new generation of politicians. What better place to do it than a state where tribes were forcefully relocated, or where Black people seeking a life away from the Deep South built their own towns?
One can only hope he’ll remember the work that Oklahomans have actually entrusted him to do.
But for now, we’re here, with Shannon as Oklahoma’s worst head cheerleader. Perhaps, like the Toros and Clovers in “Bring It On,” he’ll reflect on the fact that we have more in common than he initially thought.
And that’s really winning the competition.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming survives together, so let’s talk about suicide
description:
The Equality State has made progress on its suicide prevention efforts, but more can be done, writes Gov. Mark Gordon.
The post Wyoming survives together, so let’s talk about suicide appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Opinion

For generations, the celebrated independent spirit of the West seemed anchored by an unspoken expectation: buck up, pull yourself up by your bootstraps and get on with it. But that is the stuff of movies and dimestore novels. True Western grit has not been found in isolated silence or solitary struggle. It is found in connection, community, respect and knowing when to step-up.  
True Western hardiness relies on two complementary beliefs: our spirit of self-reliance, balanced equally by an unwavering duty to help our neighbors — two virtues that form both sides of the Western personality. Collectively, our culture comes together for spring brandings, protecting our lands, sharing kitchen table conversations and rallying to provide food for those in need. 
We look out for each other.
I truly believe this is the most exciting time to be alive. We have so many powerful tools that provide opportunity and hope, and this is especially evident in the area of mental health.
During the fall Stronger Together Suicide Prevention Symposium, I saw teachers, veterans, healthcare workers, industry partners and community leaders united in a sense of progress. Together, in addition to better equipping law enforcement, emergency responders, counselors and peers, we are harnessing telehealth and artificial intelligence to reach people in remote rural communities, using data to connect people to appropriate care, and expanding reimbursement for mental health professionals to address workforce shortages. More than 4,000 citizens from every walk of life have been trained to assist in suicide awareness prevention, in-person and online. 
By channeling these remarkable tools along with our our Western compassion and determination we are keeping the mental health and suicide prevention conversation going. Data demonstrates how vital this commitment is for protecting lives. It’s pretty straightforward to simply check in on our friends and coworkers from time to time to build on a plain understanding, it’s ok to not be ok, and to ask for help. Compassion and caring is working. It is the way of the West.
Recently, I hosted the Western Governors’ Association in Jackson for a workshop focused on reducing the stigma surrounding mental health and expanding access to care. I want to commend WGA Chair Gov. Josh Green of Hawaii for his incredible leadership and vision in carrying this vital momentum forward. Through his signature Chair Initiative, Health Beyond Healthcare, Gov. Green recognizes true wellness goes beyond traditional clinical care to address root causes in our everyday environments — where we live, learn, work and gather.
Right here in Wyoming, we are addressing these challenges head-on. Through our statewide WY We Care initiative, we know what works to save lives: fundamental human connection, breaking down systemic barriers and normalizing tough conversations. Through the WY We Care Survivors Campaign, concerted voices of lived experiences show recovery is achievable to shatter the false myth that talking openly about suicide creates risk. 
We’ve also secured dedicated funding for 24/7 in-state answering for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, ensuring that when someone reaches out in a moment of distress, they connect directly with a trained Wyoming local person who genuinely appreciates our way of life and knows the state. 
We are also bringing real-time help directly to the frontlines through innovative partnerships. Thanks to support from the Helmsley Charitable Trust, we’ve partnered with the Wyoming Association of Sheriffs and Chiefs of Police to roll out Virtual Crisis Care. By equipping law enforcement officers with dedicated tablets, first responders can instantly connect individuals experiencing mental health distress directly to behavioral health professionals. This gives officers immediate support, de-escalates critical situations and connects people in need with care instead of confusion, the criminal justice system, or someone who just doesn’t understand. 
Looking ahead, our new statewide Rural Health Transformation Program will serve as a powerful vehicle to expand innovative telehealth and other models, using its initial funding cycles to actively back transformational behavioral healthcare.
We are driving tailored action across all generations and life experiences. 
The new Senior Life Solutions program at Memorial Hospital of Carbon County provides excellent mental healthcare to dedicated outpatient care tailored specifically to our aging population. 
The Ortus Foundation is bringing vital programs directly into our schools to build resilience in youth. At the higher education level, the University of Wyoming — under the leadership of Vice President of Student Affairs Dr. Nycole Courtney, partnering with Jed Foundation Senior Clinical Director Dr. Kurt Michael — is pioneering evidence-based practices and training to protect our college students and exploring ways to partner with the WellSpring Counseling Clinic on campus. Ralph Fawaz, executive director of Telehope, partners with Wyoming’s institutions of higher education, leading a movement on human connection. And, for those who have served our country, veteran-to-veteran peer support programs are proving that the bond of shared military experience is one of our most effective tools.
We have made progress, but we are not done. The stakes are too high. Though more are reaching out for the counsel they need, far too many continue to suffer in silence. People care. We care. Every voice is life. Let’s keep talking. Let’s keep listening. Together we will make a difference. Ride for the Brand.

The deal was also contingent on the hospital emerging out of […]
text:
Jackson Hospital is seen in Montgomery, Alabama on Aug. 17, 2026. Gov. Kay Ivey on Thursday approved a $40 million loan to the troubled hospital, which was contingent on it emerging from bankruptcy. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Gov. Kay Ivey on Thursday approved a $40 million loan to a troubled Montgomery hospital.
The transfer to Jackson Hospital came three months after it reached a deal with Blue Cross Blue Shield of Alabama, the state’s largest private insurance company, to remain open. The deal was also contingent on the hospital emerging out of bankruptcy.
“The sustainability of Jackson Hospital and the viability of a strong healthcare system with Baptist Health remains critical for our capital city and the River Region,” Ivey said in a statement Thursday evening. “The new leadership at Jackson Hospital has more work ahead to ensure a strong future, but I am hopeful that can be achieved for the people who call this area home.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jackson Hospital, which filed for bankruptcy in 2025, has struggled financially for years like many hospitals in the state, some of which have closed due to financial struggles. State charity programs and federal tax programs aim to prevent closures, but experts say it may not be enough to save hospitals.
Multiple messages seeking comment from Jackson Hospital were left Friday.  
John Quinlivan, the hospital’s CEO and president, said in June that a BCBSAL increase in compensation for patient services was critical to keeping the facility open. Quinlivan wanted payments to equal that of Baptist Medical Center South, a Level I trauma center in southern Montgomery that has 492 beds. Jackson, located near downtown Montgomery, is a Level III trauma center with 344 beds. The insurer declined, citing the differing care the hospitals offer. 
A spokesperson for BCBSAL said in a statement Friday afternoon that the company was “pleased Jackson Hospital is receiving this financial support.” 
“Ensuring our members have access to healthcare in Montgomery and the surrounding areas remains a top priority,” the statement said.
U.S. Rep. Shomari Figures, D-Montgomery, brought hospital leadership, BCBSAL, and state and local officials together in a meeting over the summer to help the parties reach an agreement. Figures, who highlighted his efforts in his reelection campaign — which relied on turnout in Montgomery — said in a statement Friday afternoon that the additional $40 million will allow the hospital to make repairs to the facility and ensure stability for the future.
“Jackson Hospital is a cornerstone of healthcare for the entire region, and my constituents, both in Montgomery and surrounding rural communities, depend on its services,” Figures said in a statement. “We, along with city, county, and state officials worked hard to keep the hospital open, and I’m encouraged by the progress made to get the hospital out of bankruptcy and back on its feet.”
The hospital reached a “verbal agreement” with the insurance company in early July, which the signed agreement is based on. The deal will allow the hospital to improve current services and add new ones, which will generate more revenue. Help from the state and local governments will keep its doors open until then.
The hospital also got $10 million from Montgomery County and $15 million from Montgomery city. Jackson Healthcare, founded by Georgia Republican gubernatorial nominee Rick Jackson, has also loaned the hospital $35 million.
Messages seeking comment from Montgomery Mayor Steven Reed and the Montgomery County Commission were left Friday morning.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Wildlife advocates and conservationists call for end to killing wolf pups in Idaho
description: Conservationists and wildlife advocates will present a petition to state officials Tuesday asking them to ban killing wolf pups and their mothers, officials drafting the petition said.  International Wildlife Coexistence Network Executive Director Suzanne Asha Stone said a coalition of advocates is bringing the petition to the Idaho Fish and Game Commission [...]
text:
A gray wolf in snow. (File photo courtesy of Eric Cole/U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service)Conservationists and wildlife advocates will present a petition to state officials Tuesday asking them to ban killing wolf pups and their mothers, officials drafting the petition said. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
International Wildlife Coexistence Network Executive Director Suzanne Asha Stone said a coalition of advocates is bringing the petition to the Idaho Fish and Game Commission on Tuesday, following a Nov. 6 article published by the Guardian and Public Domain that reported state officials in Idaho paid thousands of dollars in reimbursements payments to hunters or trappers who legally killed 12 wolf pups in Idaho earlier this year. 
Stone, who first started as an intern with the government and Nez Perce Tribe’s teams that reintroduced wolves to Idaho more than 30 years ago, said she has never seen as much public outrage and disgust as she has since the news of the dead wolf pups broke earlier this month.
Suzanne Asha Stone was member of the 1995 wolf reintroduction team. (Photo courtesy of Suzanne Asha Stone
“That’s not hunting,” Stone said in an interview Thursday. “It’s not trapping. It’s not even professional control. That is simply persecution of a species that’s hated by someone, and I just think that’s the most disturbing thing that someone could approach animals so young, and have so little empathy, no empathy for them.”
Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials could not be reached for comment.
As news of the dead wolf pups spread, some hunters said killing wolf pups reflects poorly on the state and could give hunting a bad name. 
Kevin Brown, a 70-year-old from St. Maries who breeds and trains hunting hounds, said he believes killing wolf pups is unethical, violates the hunting principles of fair chase and he found it personally sickening. According to the Boone and Crockett Club, fair chase is an ethical hunting principle of pursuing and taking wild game in such a way that does not give the hunter an improper or unfair advantage over the animals. 
Brown, Stone and others said the wolf pups would have been helpless to escape or defend themselves 
“When I saw that the other day, I just about puked,” Brown said in an interview Wednesday. “Now that is just f—king sick. That’s what they were doing in the 1920s, the biological survey there at the end, killing the last few wolves.”
Wolves are a native species that humans completely killed off in the Western U.S. by the 1940s thanks to a government eradication campaign that included congressional bounties designed to encourage westward expansion and widespread poisoning.
In 1995, the U.S. government used teams that included Stone and longtime government trapper Carter Niemeyer to capture wolves in Canada and reintroduce them to their native territory of Idaho and Yellowstone National Park.
 Why is killing wolf pups legal in Idaho?

The Idaho Department of Fish and Game has managed wolves in Idaho since wolves were removed from Endangered Species Act protections in 2011. 
The Idaho Legislature has passed several laws, including Senate Bill 1211 in 2021, that expanded the ways and methods wolves can be legally killed, removed the limit on the number of wolf tags hunters could buy each year, legalized trapping year round on private property and allowed the state to enter into contracts with third parties and government agencies to kill wolves.
With a push from the Idaho Legislature and direction from the Idaho Fish and Game Commission, officials with the Idaho Department of Fish and Game have publicly said they are working to reduce the number of wolves in Idaho. 
Widespread hunting and the reimbursement payments are part of that effort. 
Supporters say reducing the wolf population will reduce the amount of livestock and elk that are killed by wolves.
 Why does the state send payments to hunters and trappers who kill wolves?

In the article earlier this month, the Guardian and Public Domain reported the state paid out reimbursements of $2,000 each for 12 wolf pups that were legally killed in Idaho this spring. 
The payments were made through a partnership between the state and the Foundation for Wildlife Management to reimburse hunters who kill a wolf for related expenses such as fuel, ammunition, traps, trail cameras, gear, license fees and even payments for trucks or ATVS used to scout wolves.
Idaho state officials say number of cattle, sheep killed by wolves is decreasing

Opponents of the program call the payments a bounty, and say the practice echoes the tactics that the government used in the early 20th century to kill off nearly every wolf in the western United States. 
Although Idaho Department of Fish and Game officials did not speak to the Sun for this article, Deputy Director Jon Rachael discussed the goals of the reimbursement program in 2025 for the Idaho Capital Sun and Boise State Public Radio’s series Howl.
“Any of the funds that come from the state of Idaho, from the Wolf Depredation Control Board, or, in the past, from the Fish and Game Commission Challenge Grants did require that this money was not just a straight payment of a certain amount, but rather the individual claiming compensation present evidence of their expenses,” Rachael said in the 2025 interview. “And so in that regard, it was compensation for their investment of buying traps or fuel to run a trap line.”
Stone said she confirmed the state made the reimbursement payments for the 12 wolf pups killed earlier this year, after filing a public records request for game management reports, a request she makes regularly. 
Niemeyer, who was part of the government’s wolf reintroduction team in 1995 and 1996, also reviewed the records, Niemeyer told the Idaho Capital Sun. 
 What is being done in response to the killing of wolf pups?

Stone and a coalition of conservationists and wildlife advocates want those wolf pups to be the last ones to be legally killed in Idaho.
Stone said Dallas Gudgell of the International Wildlife Coexistence Network will present the petition during the Idaho Fish and Game Commission’s meeting at 7 p.m. Pacific Time at the Idaho Department of Fish and Game Clearwater Regional Office, 3316 16th St., in Lewiston.
“What we’re asking is that wolves simply be managed as promised, like black bears and mountain lions, that their young and that the mothers are protected until they reach five months of age and that there is no bounty on pups of the year,” Stone said in an interview Thursday, referring to wolf pups born in the spring of the current year. 
“There’s no bounty on black bears, there’s no bounty on mountain lions, and their young are protected,” Stone said. “We’re just asking for the same thing with wolves.”
Idaho Conservation League Wildlife Program Associate Jeff Abrams said the killing of wolf pups should be banned for many reasons, including to maintain consistent policy for managing predators and wildlife. 
Abrams said existing laws and rules prohibit hunters and trappers from going to a bear den and killing newborn bear cubs or killing a sow with cubs present. 
But in Idaho it is legal to kill wolf pups and mother wolves with pups. 
“In the conversations that led up to the delisting of wolves, (Idaho Department of Fish and Game) told Idahoans that they plan to manage wolves as prized big game animals,” Abrams said. “This latest incident plainly shows they’re not doing that. Big game animals like black bears and mountain lions may not be taken weeks into their life cycle. The department needs to be consistent in setting big game management policies.”



Need to get in touch?
Have a news tip?


CONTACT US



Abrams said the state-sanctioned legal killing of wolf pups is giving the state a bad reputation. 
“We may have finally reached a point when this insane persecution of wolves is questioned, even by mainstream sportsmen,” Abrams said. “This was not fair chase. There’s little doubt these pups were killed by blunt force at close range. This violates the North American model of wildlife conservation; we cannot continue to outsource wolf management to a tiny slice of sportsmen that despise native predators, let alone incentivize it with a bounty.”
Brown, the hunter from St. Maries, described himself as a 70-year-old who has hunted all his life but is now getting away from hunting but still enjoys training hounds in the backcountry and tracking animals. 
Brown said wolves have killed multiple hounds of his in the backcountry, but he supports wolves and other predators because he grew up in the mountains and on public lands. 
Brown said he places immense value in an intact ecosystem, and spends a great deal of time, thinking about, reading about and seeking out some of the dwindling few remaining intact ecosystems that are left. 
He also strives to learn how wolves live in order to avoid conflicts.
“It’s in a horrible state, everything is,” Brown said. “I always enjoyed hunting in a pristine environment because that’s where the (mountain) lions and bears were, you know, and that’s where the wolves were.”
Lisa Young, director of the Idaho Chapter of the Sierra Club, said she was disgusted by the killing of wolf pups and the state reimbursement payments.
“The disgraceful practice of paying bounties to slaughter wolf pups in their dens is more reminiscent of the 20th Century wolf extermination than modern wildlife management,” Young said in a written statement. “And this comes at a time when deer, elk and other big game in Idaho are at healthy numbers.”
“This waste of public money is just another example of how ill suited Idaho is to manage these iconic wildlife species,” Young added. “It’s time to end these practices and move into the 21st Century with a sensible wolf management policy that recognizes the important role they play in a functioning ecosystem. Idaho has shown that we have so much further to go in wildlife management, and why states can’t be trusted to manage carnivore species including wolves, grizzly bears and mountain lions.”
The reimbursement payments for hunters or trappers who kill wolves is not new. The state of Idaho paid out $849,750 in such reimbursement payments between 2019 and 2025, the Sun previously reported. 
The government-sanctioned killing of wolf pups is not new either. 
In 2022 some students at Timberline High School spoke out after Wildlife Services officers killed wolf pups from the Timberline wolf pack that the school had symbolically adopted and studied for years. In a 2021 letter to the International Wildlife Coexistence Network, U.S. Department Agriculture officials confirmed that young wolves were killed in 2021 in Idaho as part of an effort to protect livestock and push adult wolves to relocate. 
Stone said that while the petition to end killing wolf pups and mother wolves will be presented Tuesday, the Idaho Fish and Game Commission will actually hear it or respond to it during the following meeting.
“This petition will not be heard until the January meeting, which will be here in Boise, and we hope to turn out as many people as possible,” Stone said. “Wolves only den once a year, so our goal is to stop this before the April denning season.”

text:
States Newsroom graphic illustration New Developments

Saginaw Township and Romulus are among the newest Michigan communities to establish restrictions on data centers, Glenn Hedin reports for Michigan Public. While the Saginaw Township Board of Trustees set standards for the development of any prospective data center, Romulus has approved a 180-day moratorium on data center development.
Summit Township and Napoleon Township in Jackson County have also taken action on data center development, WILX’s Riley Connell reports, with Napoleon Township passing a 12-month moratorium and Summit Township adopting new rules around noise, water use and setbacks.

Updates

Mere weeks after the Lansing Economic Area Partnership and Lighthouse Sustainability announced their plans to pursue public engagement for a potential data center in Delhi Township, the developer has decided to withdraw. According to a news release from the Lansing Economic Area Partnership, Lighthouse Sustainability will seek other opportunities across the country, bringing an end to the proposal.
Following a data center proposal in Howell Township which has since been put on ice, township officials have directed their attorney to draft an ordinance which could ban local officials, staff and contractors from signing nondisclosure agreements, MLive’s Jennifer Eberbach reports.
Saline Township Trustees have reaffirmed a 12-year, 50% tax break for the Oracle and OpenAI data center, and moved to establish an Industrial Development District for the project, despite concerns from residents that trustees had not followed the proper legal pathway for approving the abatement. The Detroit News’ Max Reinhart reports that both measures passed unanimously.
More details have emerged around a large-scale development in Lenox Township that residents fear may be a data center, MLive’s Lucas Smolcic Larson reports. A conceptual plan submitted to township officials shows 10 buildings covering more than 2 million square feet. While a related application to rezone 1,400 acres in the community does not refer to the project as a data center, the company behind the proposal previously sent letters to local officials stating that it was developing a data center campus on the land matching the rezoning request. The township is scheduled to hold a public hearing on the rezoning request tonight.
The University of Michigan is pursuing an archaeological review of its proposed computing center site in Ypsilanti Township, to evaluate the likelihood that Indigenous artifacts or remains could be unearthed at the site, Etai Smotrich-Barr reports for Michigan Public. The review follows a warning from the State Historic Preservation Office that the area surrounding the Huron River, which the project site borders, is “highly archaeologically sensitive.”
Hyperscale Data, the parent company for the Dowagiac data center operated by Alliance Cloud Services, announced that is had sold off its remaining Bitcoin reserves in order to finance the development of its Michigan data center, which is transitioning from Bitcoin mining operations to artificial intelligence computing.
Allen Park has extended its moratorium on data center development, The Detroit News’ Max Bryan reports. The city unanimously agreed to pause development for another six months, after approving its original six-month moratorium on June 9,

News of Note

As a data center developer proposes underwater data centers in Maine and Alaska, Michigan Advance spoke with environmental advocates about the guardrails in place were a developer to pursue a similar proposal in the Great Lakes.
WDIV Local 4’s Brandon Carr reviews Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s plan on data centers, including a moratorium on new data center construction until the state establishes regulations for community transparency and environmental protections.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Doula care aiming to improve maternal health and wellbeing grows in NC’s rural counties.
description: “I just don’t want to die having my baby,” a pregnant woman told her doula, Taya Partin, at their first meeting. Partin shared that memory at a doula training workshop in the Halifax County town of Enfield, where 14 women attended three days of intensive classes offered by N.C. Central University. Fear of death is […]
text:
Participants in N.C. Central University-sponsored doula training  in October 2026 work on recognizing the stages of labor. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)“I just don’t want to die having my baby,” a pregnant woman told her doula, Taya Partin, at their first meeting.
Partin shared that memory at a doula training workshop in the Halifax County town of Enfield, where 14 women attended three days of intensive classes offered by N.C. Central University.
Tara Partin, a doula enrolled in NCCU’s workshop, said she was able to calm a client who feared she would not live through childbirth. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)
Fear of death is a real worry for Black women who are pregnant. In North Carolina, Black women are 1.7 times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes, according to the state Maternal Mortality Review Committee report released last month.
Death rates were highest among women who live in rural areas and in southeastern counties, the report said. Nearly nine in 10 deaths were preventable.
NCCU’s training program was created to help provide doulas to rural counties where it can be hard for pregnant women to find care.
Doulas provide non-medical support during pregnancy, labor, birth, and for a short time after babies are born.
In recent years, efforts to integrate doulas into maternal care have expanded. Research has found that women who have doulas are less likely to have cesarean sections, have lower risks of preterm birth, and are less likely to be given a drug that speeds up labor.
The continuous presence of doulas during labor helps reduce stress. Doulas help women in labor walk or change birthing positions, practices that help shorten labor. Doulas stay in contact with parents in the weeks after they bring their babies home, and can be the first to spot medical problems or signs of postpartum depression.
The NCCU classes convene at the university’s Rural Health Hub headquarters in Enfield. The hub provides services aimed at improving the health of residents in low-wealth counties.
Students in a doula training class sponsored by NC Central University use a small ball inside a balloon to demonstrate how the cervix thins during labor. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)
Undi Hoffler is the doula training program’s director. Inspired by her own experiences as a doula, she worked to add the training to NCCU’s work on rural health.
The NCCU program recruits participants from rural counties in northeastern North Carolina.
That region of the state has a cluster of counties the March of Dimes calls “maternity care deserts.” Those are counties without a medical professional that delivers babies or a birthing center or hospital that offers obstetric care.
Some women in these rural counties may have to travel an hour or more to see an obstetrician or midwife, Hoffler said.
Providing evidence-based information and emotional support to someone who is pregnant is “a tremendous resource,” she said.
NCCU’s training represents one effort to build support systems for pregnant women in the state’s rural counties.
Building community-based support for women’s health in Chatham

A Chatham County nonprofit has similar goals, but is working to build a range of community services for women.
EMBRACe (Equity for Moms and Babies Realized Across Chatham) helps provide doula training for Black women and Latinas, and is helping support a multi-cultural community-based doula cooperative called Abriendo Caminos that hosts bilingual childcare classes.
EMBRACe started as a project of the Chatham County Health Department in response to health disparities. It was focused on bringing institutions together to address inequities, said Casey Hilliard, one of the co-founders.
The organization is now a separate nonprofit that focuses on building and supporting community leaders to transform maternal care.
The healthcare system too often fails when it comes to women’s health, she said.
“We have the data and the experiences to prove that they’re not listening to us, they’re not seeing us,” Hilliard said. “So what we’re trying to do is to find ways to shift the money and the power and the resources into the spaces where care really does exist.”
That means having doulas, community health workers, childbirth education and support groups, and paying birth workers to provide services to everyone who needs them, Hilliard said.
At an EMBRACe retreat in October, some doulas said their own traumatic experiences drew them to the work because they wanted to help make births better for others.
Liliana Nava at the EMBRACe retreat in Chatham County in October 2026. (Photo: Lynn Bonner/NC Newsline)
Liliana Nava, who is in nursing school, said she endured a long, traumatic labor before giving birth to her daughter by C-section four years ago.
Nava was at UNC, where a volunteer doula helped her with massages and encouragement.
“She was able to ground me,” Nava said. “She talked to me in such a voice that I felt like she was soothing me to sleep.”
The doula was able to impart a sense of calm that medical personnel and Nava’s partner could not.
“Being a doula is just making a difference for somebody else and making them feel like they’re not alone,” she said.
Chatham County has a relatively high Latino population. More than half of Siler City’s population is Latino. That makes it important for some pregnant women to find fluent Spanish speakers for support.
Omayra Pumalpa started EMBRACe’s childbirth education classes in Chatham and has attended births as a doula.
“Most of the pregnant women in the immigrant community don’t even want to go to the doctor because they don’t know what they’re going to find,” she said. Federal law requires video interpretation in medical offices and hospitals, but it can be an imperfect solution.
Pumalpa said she has attended births with teenagers and women who would otherwise have been alone. At least once, the family was afraid of ICE and didn’t want to come to the hospital.
Doulas help women advocate for the birth experiences they want, she said.
“When our kids grow up and say, ‘Mom, how was it the day I was born?’ What do we want to tell them?” Pumalpa asked. “Do we want to tell them a horror story?”
Hours in the classroom
NCCU’s program isn’t about shifting money or resources, but to train doulas to, as instructor Tonya Daniel put it, “work alongside health systems to improve outcomes.”
Before the 1930s, most women, attended by midwives, had babies at home. Now, most people give birth in hospitals. Doulas are a bridge connecting community-based care and hospitals, Daniel said.
The first day of class, Daniel took students through history, anatomy, and the phases of labor.
She had students squeeze balloons with small balls inside to demonstrate how contractions change the cervix during labor. She told students when to urge clients to seek immediate medical care. She talked about building trust with clients and giving them the information and confidence they need to advocate for themselves.
“We as a society have conditioned women not to trust our instincts. Especially women of color,” she said.
Most women don’t have comprehensive postpartum medical check-ups until four to six weeks after giving birth, Daniel said. Doulas can be the first to pick up on health complications after parents return home because doulas visit in the two weeks after babies are born.
Supporters say state action can reduce pregnancy-related deaths of Black women in NC

Follow-up sessions supplement the three consecutive days in the classroom.
NCCU pays for materials and all or part of the training. The classes are intended to lead to students’ certification by DONA International. One of the certification requirements is providing continuous support through labor to three people.
Women taking the class said they enrolled because they want to serve their communities.
Partin, who lives in Edgecombe County, said the woman who was afraid of dying was one of her first clients. Partin said enrolled in NCCU’s doula training to have in-person classes to build on her earlier online instruction. The training is also a path to providing services to women insured under Medicaid.
Partin was able to calm the mother-to-be, give her information so she could advocate for herself, and promised she would be with her in the hospital room.
“By the end she was like, ‘I”m ready,’” Partin said. “Now, that made me really happy.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee’s used EV market is growing, but stood at 1.4% of overall market in 2025
description: Tennessee’s used electric vehicle market grew four-fold between 2019 and 2025, but still made up just 1.4% of used vehicle sales in the state in 2025, according to a report recently published by Atlas Public Policy in partnership with the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation’s Office of Energy Programs. Dealers and private sellers registered [...]
text:
Sales of elective vehicles in Tennessee have increased by still lag far behind those of gas-powered autos.  (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee’s used electric vehicle market grew four-fold between 2019 and 2025, but still made up just 1.4% of used vehicle sales in the state in 2025, according to a report recently published by Atlas Public Policy in partnership with the Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation’s Office of Energy Programs.
Dealers and private sellers registered 7,166 used electric vehicles, or EVs, in 2025, according to the report. While that is a small percentage of the 507,000 used vehicles sold that year, it marks a substantial increase from the 1,908 used EVs registered in 2019.
Tennessee aims to build out infrastructure needed to support the adoption of 200,000 EVs by 2028. The state closed a 400-mile loop of electric vehicle charges connecting Nashville, Knoxville, Cookeville and Chattanooga in its Fast Charge TN Network in May 2025, making charges available every 34 miles. The state’s Office of Energy Programs is accepting applications until Nov. 30 for its fourth round of the program, offering up to $600,000 for the buildout of fast charging stations on key roadways.
Tennessee’s used EV market share comes in above some of its Southern neighbors — including Alabama, Kentucky, South Carolina and Mississippi — but is outpaced by Georgia’s 2% share and North Carolina’s 1.7% share. 
“This growth is being driven by a maturing EV market, a growing wave of lease returns, and falling prices that have brought used EVs closer to price parity with comparable gas vehicles,” the report, which was supported by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Energy Efficiency, states.
The report drew from used vehicle sales data from Experian from 2019 through 2025, used EV listing data from early 2026 from Cars.com and loan data from Capital One filings from January 2019 through December 2025. What used EVs are Tennesseans buying?
Tesla vehicles account for about a quarter of all used EV sales in Tennessee during the report’s study period.
But new EVs introduced in the state in 2025 project growing diversity in the future, as EVs reach the end of their first ownership cycle or their lease terms, the report noted.
Cars and SUVs account for 97% of used EV sales in Tennessee, with pickup trucks making up less than 1% (though the report notes that EV pickups weren’t available at “meaningful volumes” until 2023). 
More than half of used EV listings in Tennessee are for vehicles three years old or less, and 34% are listed between $20,000 and $30,000, according to the report.
“These relatively affordable price points reflect in part the faster depreciation EVs have historically experienced compared to gas vehicles, though that gap has nearly closed as battery performance improves and buyer confidence grows,” the report stated.
In 2025, about 65% of the used EVs registered were battery-powered, and the remainder were plug-in hybrids.
Who is buying used EVs in Tennessee?
Used EV buyers in Tennessee are disproportionately concentrated in higher income brackets, loan data from Capital One suggests. The report reviewed data from more than 17,000 used vehicle loan records from January 2019 through December 2025. Of those, about 100 were loans for used EVs.
About 20% of used EV borrowers reported earning $70,000 (Tennessee’s median household income) or less, compared to 44% of borrowers for used gas-powered vehicles, according to the report. More than 60% of used EV borrowers reported earning at least $100,000 annually.
“These figures suggest that lower- and middle-income households are not yet participating in the used EV market at the same rate as higher-income buyers,” the report states.
But the report also notes that lower-income households tend to spend a larger proportion of their income on gasoline, and vehicles powered by electricity are more insulated from global oil market fluctuations that can drive up gas prices. 
“The used EV market in Tennessee is at an inflection point. Supply is growing, prices are falling, and the vehicles available to buyers are becoming more diverse,” the report states. “Whether the benefits of this maturing market reach households across the income spectrum will depend in part on the programs and investments that the State of Tennessee, local governments, utilities, and community partners put in place in the coming years.”
