title: Ohio’s laws make it more difficult to right a wrongful conviction
description: This article was first published by The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system. Sign up for their newsletters, and follow them on Instagram, TikTok, Reddit and Facebook. Tim Montgomery looked down and sighed as he tried to explain why he lied to police decades ago about the 1992 murder […]
text:
Stock photo from Getty Images.This article was first published by The Marshall Project, a nonprofit news organization covering the U.S. criminal justice system. Sign up for their newsletters, and follow them on Instagram, TikTok, Reddit and Facebook.
Tim Montgomery looked down and sighed as he tried to explain why he lied to police decades ago about the 1992 murder of two elderly sisters in Cleveland.
“I was not there. I said that thousands and thousands of times, but nobody will believe me. So I told them what they wanted to hear,” Montgomery testified at a hearing last year.
A prosecutor continued to press him about his past statements implicating him and Terry Ferrell in the home invasion and murders of Mary Mosberger, 82, and Loretta Fallat, 77.
“You want the truth?” Montgomery shot at the prosecutor from the witness stand. “I’m trying to give it to you. Nobody wants to hear the truth.”
Ferrell, stone-faced until then, leaned back in his seat and shot an approving glance at his wife, Jessica, in the gallery of the stuffy Cuyahoga County courtroom.
The hearing was a milestone in Ferrell’s two-decade-long effort to prove his innocence, which still isn’t over. An appeals court will hear Ferrell’s case Tuesday, highlighting the long and difficult road for people in Ohio prisons who say they were wrongfully convicted.
A task force convened by the Ohio Supreme Court studied the state’s drawn-out process for addressing wrongful conviction claims. At the top of its 2022 list of recommendations were changes to state law and procedure that would have sped up new trial requests.
But no one has enacted those reforms.
Instead, judges have continued to ignore or dismiss credible claims of new evidence. Delays in processing new trial requests for defendants who were later exonerated have cost taxpayers millions of additional dollars in wrongful imprisonment settlements.
All the while, people who actually committed crimes have not been brought to justice, and families are in court for decades after losing a loved one.
Across from Ferrell’s wife sat relatives of Mosberger and Fallat, who lived next door to Ferrell and his family on Seymour Avenue in Cleveland.
In December 1992, a relative found the sisters dead in their ransacked home. Cleveland police canvassed the neighborhood. Within days, investigators had Ferrell, 21, in jail. He was fingerprinted, questioned and released without being charged.
No physical evidence tied Ferrell, or anyone, to the crime. The case went cold.
Five years later, detectives finally caught a break after a 12-year-old neighbor led them to Montgomery. They questioned Montgomery but didn’t charge him. Another five years passed until a jailhouse informant who cut a deal to avoid prison time came forward as the state’s star witness.
At the trial in 2003, prosecutors argued that Ferrell and another man, who has never been identified, led Montgomery into the sisters’ home on the night of their murders.
Ferrell’s attorneys questioned the lack of evidence linking their client to the crime, how witnesses waited a decade to speak up, and a timeline for the murders that included hours when Ferrell was at a bar or a friend’s house.
A jury found Ferrell guilty of murder, aggravated burglary and kidnapping. The judge sentenced him to life without the possibility of parole.
Montgomery, who didn’t testify at Ferrell’s trial, pleaded guilty to aggravated burglary and served three years in prison for his alleged role in the crime.
Ferrell exhausted the regular appeals process in 2006. He filed motions from his prison cell to preserve evidence, which Cuyahoga County Judge John J. Russo denied. In 2016, Russo appointed Ferrell an attorney, who successfully pushed for DNA testing. It would take eight years to complete that testing due to crime lab delays and objections from prosecutors. Finally, in 2024, Ferrell’s new legal team convinced Russo to hold evidentiary hearings in pursuit of a new trial.
In several hours-long hearings over the course of six months, Ferrell’s attorneys presented a slew of new evidence: The jailhouse informant who had been the state’s star witness recanted his testimony. Detectives had developed alternative suspects, but they were never discussed at trial. And DNA on the murder weapons didn’t belong to Ferrell or the victims.
Despite all that, Russo denied Ferrell’s request for a new trial in January.
Ferrell appealed Russo’s decision. A panel of judges in Ohio’s Eighth District Court of Appeals is set to hear the case Nov. 10. It could be Ferrell’s best chance to have his conviction overturned.
Defense attorneys and prosecutors declined to comment while the case is ongoing. A relative of Mosberger and Fallat also declined to comment.

It can be difficult to impossible for older prisoners like Ferrell to prove that evidence was withheld in their cases.
The 1963 U.S. Supreme Court case Brady vs. Maryland enshrined the requirement that prosecutors share any evidence that might help a defendant through what is called discovery. The ruling made full disclosure through open discovery the national standard in criminal law. Well into the 2000s, though, many states allowed a less transparent process called closed discovery.
In Ohio, that meant prosecutors didn’t have to share paper copies of witness statements, police reports or other documents. They only had to read the files to defense attorneys in closed-door pre-trial meetings. Prosecutors kept no record of what was — or wasn’t — shared.
After sustained critiques in the press, Cuyahoga County judges unanimously voted in 2008 to adopt open discovery. The Ohio Supreme Court required open discovery statewide in 2010.
More than 1,000 Cuyahoga County defendants, including Ferrell, are still serving time in Ohio prisons after being convicted during the era of closed discovery, according to a Marshall Project review of state corrections department data.
“It was a very dangerous time for the possibility of wrongful convictions taking place because of the opaque nature of how discovery was conducted,” said Mike Donnelly, a former Ohio Supreme Court Justice who was trained to practice closed discovery as an assistant Cuyahoga County prosecutor early in his career.
The attorneys who filed Ferrell’s motion for a new trial have gathered nearly a thousand pages of police reports that included interviews and evidence that were not introduced at the trial. Witnesses had contradicted themselves or the prosecution’s timeline. Police had other suspects, including a man who admitted his involvement after pawning an item stolen from the crime scene.
Ferrell’s original attorneys — Jack Hildebrand and William McGinty, who each had decades of experience in criminal defense — said at the hearings last year that they no longer could remember what was shared with them during closed discovery. That made it harder for Ferrell to prove that prosecutors improperly withheld evidence. But they both testified that they would have used such exculpatory evidence during the trial if they had it.

No one knows how often Ohio prisoners seek new trials. Anecdotally, attorneys say judges often ignore such requests or reject them without ever weighing any evidence.
In 2022, local judges, defense attorneys and the few prosecutors on the Ohio Supreme Court’s task force recommended that state officials address a litany of often insurmountable court procedures that stall efforts to seek new trials.
For four years, neither the legislature nor the Ohio Supreme Court has made those changes.
“There’s a definite need for reform,” said attorney Rachel Troutman with the Exoneration Project, a legal clinic at the University of Chicago Law School that fights to overturn wrongful convictions in Ohio and other states. “A lot of innocent people get turned away by the court for procedural matters.”
To get a new trial, Ohio defendants must prove that they were deprived of a fair trial due to errors beyond their control. The most common of those errors, according to attorneys, is the withholding of evidence that could have helped in their defense. Still, the burden falls on defendants to show that it was not possible for them to uncover that evidence prior to their convictions.
Unlike in other states, credible evidence of a person’s innocence is not grounds for seeking a new trial in Ohio, and only people who pursue new trials while on death row are guaranteed attorneys. Troutman said Illinois offers a better model by ensuring legal counsel in post-conviction hearings and allowing new trial requests based solely on innocence claims.
Ohio prisoners with limited resources are forced to fumble around on their own to uncover new evidence and to fight without an attorney to convince a judge to hear what they may find. Ohio state Rep. Josh Williams, a Toledo-area Republican, reintroduced a bipartisan bill last year that would require judges to act on new trial requests with credible evidence.
“We’ve seen individuals waiting in prison without judges making decisions,” said Williams, who is also an attorney. His bill has not yet moved out of committee and its future is uncertain.
Since 2013, at least 10 people who were convicted in Cuyahoga County have been collectively awarded more than $50 million in settlements for their wrongful imprisonments. Seven of them were initially denied new trial requests before their exonerations.
One of them was Michael Buehner, who was convicted of murder in 2002. Buehner, like Ferrell, fought for about a decade from behind bars before his court-appointed attorneys discovered two exonerating eyewitness statements among 30 previously withheld police reports. Still, for years Buehner was denied motions for an evidentiary hearing and a new trial.
Ultimately, the appellate court reversed those decisions. A new jury found Buehner not guilty. Last year, he was awarded nearly $2 million for his 21 years of wrongful imprisonment.
“Because of all of those years of fighting, that’s more money that they got paid,” said Troutman. “It’s the state costing itself more money by not holding a hearing on the merits.”

In 2024, Ferrell’s new attorney, public defender Cullen Sweeney, motioned the prosecutor’s office to release all the evidence in Ferrell’s case, revealing for the first time the full scope of their investigation into the killings of Mosberger and Fallat.
The records showed that, nearly five years after the murders, a child in the neighborhood pointed police to a potential suspect: Montgomery. The boy told police he saw Montgomery, whom he could not recall by name until questioned again years later, hop a fence the night of the murders. Police took Montgomery in for questioning. He insisted that he wasn’t there.
Thinking he would avoid charges, Montgomery eventually said he followed Ferrell and another man into the home. Then he tried to withdraw that statement, saying he made it up so police would let him go, according to the detective’s summary of the 1997 interrogation.
On the witness stand in the 2025 hearings, Montgomery said that Cleveland Homicide Detective Gary Garisek and an FBI agent who was with him were laser-focused on Ferrell. Montgomery said he tried to tell the truth. “They would not believe the truth when I told them. So I told them what the hell they wanted to hear.”
Garisek died in 2009.
At the hearings last year, the state’s star witness from Ferrell’s trial, jailhouse informant Stephen Lenchak, also recanted.
Lenchak grew up on Seymour Avenue. He knew Ferrell like a “scary uncle” from the neighborhood, he said. In 2002, while awaiting trial on unrelated burglary and theft charges, Lenchak said he was starving, deprived of phone calls and brutalized daily by other men in the county jail.
Detectives told him his way out would be to testify against Ferrell and find others to do the same. Lenchak said Garisek left him alone in a conference room with a phone and the case file, complete with photos of the crime scene.
“If I can call these people and have them come in to talk to this homicide detective, he would bring me out of the dorm every day, feed me, and he would eventually get me out of this hell that I was in,” Lenchak told Judge Russo last year, even after being advised that he could be charged with perjury for recanting his trial testimony.
Lenchak, who got the lightest sentence possible on his own case, was one of three jailhouse informants to cut deals and testify against Ferrell. He also gave Garisek names of people, including Ferrell’s ex-girlfriends, who testified at the trial that Ferrell threatened to kill them like he did the sisters.
But it was all a lie, Lenchak testified. And he’d felt guilty for decades about his role in convicting Ferrell.
Judge Russo took a couple of months to consider whether any of the new evidence would have swayed the jurors who convicted Ferrell. Then, in a 15-page opinion issued in January, he denied Ferrell a new trial after applying “the utmost suspicion” to Lenchak’s recantation and discounting the newly discovered DNA and previously undisclosed records.
Before issuing his decision, Russo said he knew it was likely to be appealed by one side or the other.
Donnelly, the former Supreme Court justice, said he disagreed with Russo’s decision to deny Ferrell a new trial, but credited him for at least holding the evidentiary hearings. Because Ohio law doesn’t mandate it, too many judges simply never hold hearings on new evidence that might exonerate someone, he said.
“Look at any of these anecdotes where people have been exonerated and how long it took them to fight in a system that values finality over the truth,” Donnelly said. “Most of the time, they are fighting not that they’re innocent — it’s just for the opportunity to be heard.”

 Catching Our Eye

• Ground stop. The New York Times’ Karoun Demirjian is reporting, “Ground stop highlights chronic vulnerabilities in air traffic system.”
The ground stop that brought air travel across the country to a halt Friday evening highlighted persistent weaknesses in the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control infrastructure, which has had several disruptive failures in recent months.
Two months ago, a circuit failure and severed fiber optic cable caused crippling ground stops and delays at airports along the East Coast. Smaller outages unfolded in October at Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina and George Bush Intercontinental Airport in Houston, when contractors accidentally cut into fiber line.The Friday ground stop, which was only the third the F.A.A. has issued this century, eclipsed the fallout of previous air traffic communications equipment failures.
• The governor. The Columbus Dispatch’s Laura Bischoff is reporting, “Mike DeWine’s 50 years in Ohio politics comes to a close.”
Whether cutting a ribbon on a renovated highway rest stop or guiding Ohio through a global pandemic, no assignment was too big or too small for Republican Mike DeWine as he served eight years as governor.
Over his nearly 50-year political career, DeWine likely attended more events, held more press conferences, shook more hands and navigated more crises than any politician in Ohio history.
• Congress. Ideastream Public Media is reporting, “Democrats hire independent firm to investigate harassment allegation against Brian Poindexter.”
U.S. House Democrats are investigating a sexual harassment complaint lodged by a campaign staffer against U.S. Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter.
Poindexter defeated incumbent Republican Max Miller to claim the seat for Ohio’s 7th Congressional District.
According to reports from media outlets including CNN and Politico, a campaign aide filed a complaint alleging Poindexter made comments that made her uncomfortable.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Byron and Erika Donalds emphasize ‘accountability’ for public, ‘choice’ schools
description: The incoming Donalds administration will try to put aside the labels for the different systems operating Florida schools and focus instead on the performance of students and institutions, Byron and Erika Donalds said last week. Appearing Friday during an education technology showcase in Hollywood, attended by small vendors and education companies worth billi[...]
text:
Gov.-elect Byron Donalds spoke to education technology companies and investors on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, at a resort in Hollywood. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)The incoming Donalds administration will try to put aside the labels for the different systems operating Florida schools and focus instead on the performance of students and institutions, Byron and Erika Donalds said last week.
Appearing Friday during an education technology showcase in Hollywood, attended by small vendors and education companies worth billions of dollars, the governor-elect and his wife presented their shared vision for Florida classrooms.
“I’m agnostic on the school. I’m much more focused on the outcomes for our students,” Byron Donalds told the room of businesspeople and investors. “So, everything that we’re going to be doing in our state with respect to K-12 education and beyond is about making sure that the students of Florida have the rigor, have the information, have the support that they need in order to be better than any other students in the United States of America.”
Erika Donalds said the “language” used to categorize schools is important.
Erika Donalds speaks to a crowd of education technology investors and business owners during a showcase in Hollywood on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)
“We have to completely change the way that we communicate about schools and students in our state, in a way that is more cohesive as one education freedom economy, of which public, private, charter, and homeschool and modular types of hybrid schooling are all participants,” Erika Donalds said. “So, we have to change the culture and the language that we’re using.
“I think you’ll find in the next administration an effort to align all of those infrastructure pieces — funding, counting students, assessments, accountability, transparency — will go along with that theme, and that’s going to go a long way to bringing that one, publicly-funded education system that does not consist of just one kind of school,” she said. 
Transparency
Private schools bear far less financial accountability than do public schools — many of the former receive state money via vouchers but are not subject to public meeting laws or requirements to publish their budgets. Private school operators are not elected by voters. Public tax dollars aren’t tied to standardized testing scores if taken by private school students.
State education funds are supposed to be allocated per student, wherever he or she attends classes, but a state audit found that records could not establish that was happening in all cases because of fuzzy accounting practices. Public and private schools alike complained to the Legislature that they were not receiving their payments on time, and Sen. Don Gaetz, R-Crestview, observed at one point, “Whatever can go wrong with this system has gone wrong.”
‘Funding did not follow the child’: State audit displays school choice woes

The Legislature punted on addressing the problem during its 2026 session after its two chambers couldn’t agree on a fix.
The Donaldses have a particular interest in education. Erika owns a virtual reality education company and is founder of the Education Freedom Foundation; Byron championed education bills during his time as a state lawmaker.
‘My own silo’
Roberto Alonso, a member of the Miami-Dade School Board present at the showcase, questioned, for example, why healthcare and education approach private and public relationships differently.
“I think across all industries, majority of industries, best practices are shared, and it’s a collaborative effort,” Alonso told the Phoenix — explaining that patients have a choice of which hospital to use, but all hospitals “share medical journals and they share studies.”
“I feel that sometimes at the ground level at the schools, there’s a little bit of, ‘No, I want to work in my own silo because I don’t want to share my competitive advantage with somebody else,’” he added.
If private schools don’t want to share their information, or “be accountable,” “then a parent has something to be concerned with,” Alonso said.
“To what degree the state gets involved, that’s going to be interesting over the next couple years as we look at this model grow further into our educational ecosystem,” he said, referring to the voucher system.
“The most important takeaway,” he said, is that conversations are happening and “people are understanding that some level of accountability has to be put in place.”
What accountability could look like, Alonso continued, “we’re going to see it kind of unfold over the next couple of months.”
Education Commissioner Henry Mack also wants transparency.
“I’m not going to bind [private schools] to anything, other than I’m asking to know how their students are performing,” Mack told the Phoenix.
“It could be an option” to tie a private school’s voucher eligibility to transparency requirements, Mack said, although “I wouldn’t pretend to be a policymaker on this topic,” deferring to the governor-elect and the Legislature to “adjudicate” that matter.
Mack used the same tone as the Donaldses when he took the stage during the showcase.
“If we are going to commit ourselves to the choice agenda, a choice can only mean something if we’re all working, I guess, maybe, from the same accountability handbook,” Mack said. “We can’t compromise choice, but what, as a parent of an 11-year-old and a 9-year-old and a 4-year-old, myself, what does choice mean without insight in the performance of the options that are available to me?”
At the show
The event the Donaldses appeared at featured students pitching startups to investors and at least six companies in search of contracts from school leaders. Some of those companies, for example, leverage newer technologies to teach students math and solve problems in the classroom.
The showcase was hosted by LaunchEd Group, which says it “validates new education technology inside real public, charter, private, and hybrid classrooms before it reaches the wider market.”
“We keep looking for silver bullets. And there are no silver bullets. It’s still good, old-fashioned teachers in classrooms that care about kids. Kids having an experience that they actually want to be a part of,” Jon Hage, CEO of Charter Schools USA, said.
“But I also know that if I don’t have tools that make my teachers feel supported and cared for, then they’re not going to want to stay teachers,” he added.
Rulebook
Florida’s universities and K-12 schools will be subject to a new AI policy in July. Local school boards must require parents to opt-in their children to use AI at school. And those rules must “protect students, parents, and instructional personnel from unlawful, deceptive, unsafe, or unauthorized uses of artificial intelligence systems.”
State colleges, preK-12 schools must implement AI guardrails before July

“My personal belief is that you have to have an adult human being in the classroom,” Byron Donalds said. “There’s not replacing the teacher. People naturally need to learn from another human being, that’s just how we process information as people.”
Technologies such as those being showcased in Hollywood “have their place,” he added, “in terms of efficiencies to help teachers be able to deliver the best academic outcomes for their students.”
Erika Donalds mused about how best to evaluate school-choice options. To officers of LaunchEd, host of the event, she said, “You are actually creating a platform to showcase how school choice can be the laboratories of innovation that then can get fed back into maybe even the traditional public school system.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT voters gave us a mandate. Let’s meet the moment.
description: Here are four things CT Democrats can do to make life better for the people who put their faith in us Nov. 3.
text:
On Nov. 3, Americans frustrated by high costs and anxious about their future gave the Democratic Party a mandate to try and make their lives better.
On Election Night, some pundits strained to explain how voters could swing from Donald Trump to overwhelming Democratic majorities in just two years. The answer is simple: people are stressed — financially, physically and mentally — and they are willing to vote for whoever speaks to that.

Sean Scanlon

And if the party who wins doesn’t act quickly to make their life better, they vote for someone else who they hope will.
If Democrats do not want this seesaw to continue — if we want to retain our large majorities and keep the historic number of seats we won in our state House and Senate — then we need to deliver on making life better for people who put their faith in us on Election Day.
Here’s four big things we can do early next year to make Connecticut more affordable, protect consumers and restore trust in government.
Health care
The new Democratic Congress should reverse Trump’s two worst policies on health care: stopping the Big Beautiful Bill’s Medicaid cuts that will kick an estimated 100,000 people in our state off of their insurance next month, and reinstating the subsidies that helped middle class Connecticut residents purchase health insurance on Access Health exchange.
If they don’t act quickly, we should. We’ve already done that on the subsidies. Last year, the Governor and legislature stepped in to cover one year of the subsidies, and they are right to be doing it again this year.
On Medicaid, mayors like Caroline Simmons and Arunan Arulampulam have done great and important work by standing up localized efforts to assist impacted residents in their cities, and the state is preparing for how we could act if Congress doesn’t. One way we could do this is to create a New Deal-like program that links affected residents with businesses and non-profits in their area where they can satisfy H.R. 1’s work and volunteer requirements.
But reversing the worst decisions of the Trump administration and going back to a status quo that wasn’t working in the first place is not enough. If we really want to lower costs and make things better for the people who voted for us, we need to go further, and we need to go big.
That means passing the Connecticut Option next session.
Put simply, the Connecticut Option is about one thing: giving the people and small businesses dealing with the highest health care costs access to a new, affordable plan that will, in the first year, dramatically lower their costs.
I know first-hand why this matters. I was raised by a single mom who ran a small business. She spent most of my childhood uninsured and struggling to afford the bills, let alone health coverage. Fast forward 30 years, and that coverage is even more unaffordable for people like her. By passing the Connecticut Option, we will change that for the first time in my lifetime.
Property taxes
The only thing more broken than our health care system is our property tax. It stops people from buying their first home, forces people out of their lifetime homes and creates a never-ending doom loop for local elected officials where their only options are the false choices of raising taxes or cutting vital services like police or education. There is another way.
This summer, I worked with 100 randomly selected citizens from all walks of life and political parties at the first-ever Connecticut Citizens’ Assembly.
They came up with ten recommendations that change our broken system and deliver relief to working families. Some of the ideas, like progressive taxation, have been proposed before. But when they’ve been proposed by politicians, a classic response has been to say that the citizens wouldn’t like them.
This time, the ideas are coming from the citizens themselves. And I look forward to working with the citizens and a separate, bipartisan group of mayors and first selectmen to present the legislature with common sense big ideas for how they can lower the biggest tax paid by most residents in this state.
Artificial intelligence and data centers 
Pretty much everyone I talk to is worried about the unchecked growth of artificial intelligence, and I am too. And besides being worried about it generally, they are worried that elected officials either aren’t taking the threat seriously or aren’t moving fast enough to put guardrails in place before it’s too late.
The most efficient place for those guardrails is at the federal level. Yet, so far, the only meaningful regulation has come at the state level. In fact, the President and his allies — at the behest of big tech — have proposed banning states from regulating AI.
This regulation, including great work done here in Connecticut by people like State Sen. James Maroney, is really important. But no state has yet done what should be the centerpiece of any federal reform: regular independent safety evaluations.
Our legislature should consider a bill similar to one currently being debated in Massachusetts that would require independent evaluation of models up to three times per year.
Trust in the companies developing these models is understandably at an all time low. We require the FDA to test drugs to make sure they are safe and the FAA to certify our planes. Artificial intelligence should be no different, and Connecticut should be bold in requiring first-in-the-nation oversight of these powerful companies.
The same goes for data centers. State Sen. Bob Duff is right — there should be a short moratorium until statewide ground rules are put in place. But these centers, for as much as we all worry about them, are important economically and technologically. And if we want to find the balance between their importance and the valid concerns about them, here’s four principles for how we might do it.
Any future data center must: follow all state environmental standards, generate (or pay for) 100% of its energy costs, be built with 100% Connecticut union labor and, most importantly, receive local approval.
Stocks and predictive markets 
You can’t be outraged by the President’s blatant efforts to enrich himself and his family in office and not be equally outraged at the Democrats and Republicans in Congress who trade stocks and crypto based on insider information they have. A recent report from Common Cause showed that Members of Congress made over $600 million in trades in 2025 alone.
Congress should pass the Ban Congressional Stock Trading Act, and Connecticut should pass a similar bill preventing all state elected officials (including me) from doing the same. While we’re at it, it’s totally insane that — right now — I could place a bet using inside information I have as a government official to win a bet on a predictive market like Kalshi or Polymarket. That, too, should be banned.
These four ideas are just that: four ideas. There is so much more we can and must do to make life easier and more affordable.
But the thing that excites me most about having been re-elected to serve this state I love for four more years is this: we are truly at an inflection point as a state. After years of hard work getting our state out of a fiscal crisis, we are finally in a position to do the big things we’ve long wanted to do to make Connecticut better.
Voters entrusted us with a big job, and we won’t do it without big ideas. I look forward to pushing for these big ideas and working with my fellow partners in government to deliver the big change the people of this state expect and need from us.
Sean Scanlon is the Connecticut Comptroller.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT’s gun laws work. Washington is coming for them anyway.
description: After Sandy Hook, Connecticut made a promise: never again. We kept that promise with laws that work. We cannot let Washington break it.
text:
In December 2012, after 20 children and six educators were murdered at Sandy Hook Elementary, Connecticut successfully did something that most states only talk about. Lawmakers came together across the aisle and passed some of the most stringent gun safety laws in the country.
 In Connecticut, there is a ban on military-style assault weapons, limits on high-capacity magazines, and a permitting system that asks a simple, yet rarely asked, question before someone acquires a firearm: should this person have one?
 More than a decade later, that framework is under attack from two different fronts, and Connecticut residents have a right to know what is at stake. 
The first front is the U.S. Supreme Court. This summer, the justices agreed to hear a challenge to Connecticut and Chicago’s assault rifle ban. The version of the ban now before the court was written after Sandy Hook. If the court strikes it down, the consequences don’t stop at Connecticut’s borders, with a dozen other states having similar laws. 
This is a national attack on national gun violence prevention laws. The gun lobby has spent years funneling cases toward this court in hopes of exactly this outcome.
The second front is closer to home. In October, the U.S. Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division opened a new investigation into how Middletown and Waterbury issue firearm permits, suggesting that local police may be “unnecessarily” delaying or denying them. 
Consider what this actually means. The office created during the civil rights movement to protect voting rights, combat housing discrimination, and manage police misconduct is now being turned against local police. These police departments are doing their jobs, carefully screening the people who apply to carry handguns.
The local judgment is the backbone of another important innovation: the Extreme Risk Protection Order (ERPO). In 1999, after a gunman killed four people at the Connecticut Lottery headquarters , Connecticut passed the nation’s first “red flag” law, allowing police to ask a judge to temporarily remove guns from someone who poses an imminent danger. 
In 2021, lawmakers expanded it to allow family members, household members, and medical professionals to petition the court directly. When an order is issued, the person is flagged in the system police use to review permit applications. That’s how these protections fit together: a family raises the alarm, a judge acts, and a local officer reviewing a permit application knows to say no. A federal investigation that pressures police to process permits faster and ask fewer questions threatens every link in that chain.
 It is worth nothing what the DOJ has not said.   It has offered no public evidence or explanation   as to why Waterbury and Middletown were chosen. Its own letters, also, acknowledge it has reached no conclusions. It seems like there is a message being sent: screen too carefully, and federal investigators may come knocking.  
The exact approach being attacked is one that has historically worked in Connecticut. In 2024, Connecticut had the sixth-lowest gun death rate in the country, less than half the national rate. When Johns Hopkins researchers studied the permit-to-purchase law, which requires handgun buyers to get a permit through local police and pass a background check, they found it was associated with a 40 percent drop in gun homicides over the following decade. The local permit review DOJ now wants to second-guess isn’t red tape. It’s one of the most effective tools we have.
 So what can Connecticut do? 
We must hold our congressional delegation accountable. They should demand that DOJ explain the basis for this investigation. Attorney General William Tong deserves our full support as he defends the assault weapons ban before the Supreme Court. Middletown and Waterbury officials should continue to follow state law and should not let federal pressure push them toward rubber-stamping applications. And state lawmakers should be prepared now, whatever the court decides, to protect the strongest possible version of Connecticut’s laws.
 After Sandy Hook, Connecticut made a promise: never again. We kept that promise with laws that work. We cannot let Washington break it. 
Gray West of Middletown writes for Brady United: Team ENOUGH.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: New Haven’s short-term rental ban will hurt renters it’s meant to help
description: We must protect the rights of New Haven renters, especially students, to legally sublet the apartments they actually live in.
text:
New Haven is near and dear to my heart. It will always be home. It’s where I was living when COVID-19 struck and where I did my graduate studies, eventually earning my MBA.
 On October 6, Alders Leland Moore, Frank Douglass, and Mandy Martinelli proposed a ban on short-term rentals in New Haven, and residents are going to pay the price.

Alikiah Barclay

I understand the frustration driving this. The cost of living is simply out of control, with housing costs a chief driver. The Board of Alders would be right to crack down on any corporate hoarding of the housing supply, but are short-term rentals a root cause or a convenient distraction as we avoid tackling the true issues?
The hotel union backing the ban relies solely on a pandemic-era study from Irvine, CA. It found a 3% drop in transacted rent and unchanged asking rent. But it draws conclusions using data from late 2019 through March 2021 when UC-Irvine went virtual and eviction moratoriums were in place.
They ignore economist Alexander Marsella’s 2026 study of nearby New York City finding zero measurable drop in market rents. Median rents in Irvine remain unaffordable and median rents in NYC have risen to record highs of $5,000/month.
 Opportunities to improve the ordinance
As written, the ban would also punish the very people it claims to protect: everyday New Haven renters, students in particular.
It prohibits all residents who haven’t spent over a year at a particular address in New Haven from qualifying as “eligible residents;” practically eliminating students from short-term subletting. Owners maintain the right to rent out rooms, but most tenants lose the ability to sublet their full apartment short-term because the ban defines home-sharing as limited to “bedrooms in a dwelling unit.”
This ordinance is blazing its way from proposal to law in six weeks, all while ignoring best practices seen across the many municipalities that have incorporated common-sense measures that protect the subletting rights of renters.
I urge our leaders to pause and do the analysis required to understand the ban’s impact, taking students and renters into account. With six hours of diverse public testimony, it’s hard to believe that there’s nothing worth further consideration.
Offsetting costs and recouping rent
I don’t come to this issue unbiased. New Haven is also special to me because it’s where I launched my first startup, Reeku, tackling housing affordability.
As a student, I was managing my housing costs by living with several roommates, but I realized I still was leaving rent on the table. Every time I was out of town, I was paying rent for an empty apartment; and as I added up my time away during summer, winter, spring and fall break, I knew there had to be a better way.
It turns out that by short-term subletting while away, a renter can recoup 20–50% of their annual rent. Today Reeku has helped renters in many cities like Boston and SF ease their high rental burden, turn a liability into an asset, and recoup hundreds of thousands in rent.
Across the country, apartment buildings are explicitly allowing tenants to sublet short-term to increase both flexibility and affordability. By recognizing this class of homesharing, New Haven would be defining a novel best practice, one that builds on the city’s momentum.
Maintaining New Haven’s momentum
New Haven is quickly becoming Connecticut’s leading travel hub and is further establishing itself as a premiere destination. No other Connecticut city has a commuter rail to New York City plus a quickly growing public airport. Just marking its five-year anniversary, Avelo Airlines has expanded, bringing direct flights into Tweed-New Haven Airport from 28 cities across the country.
Yet just as the city becomes more accessible, this ban will make it far more expensive to visit. We are poised to increase nightly hotel rates for our limited 1,800 hotel rooms that already struggle to handle peak times like graduation season. Post regulation, hotel prices across New York City skyrocketed, with rooms now costing an eye-watering $500 a night.
Protect renters’ ability to sublet
There is a better way forward. The city’s regulations should explicitly protect primary residents and allow them to sublet short-term on occasion. 
We can and should ban out-of-town investors from operating commercial hotels in residential neighborhoods. But we must protect the rights of New Haven renters, especially students, to legally sublet the apartments they actually live in.
We can craft thoughtful legislation that provides visibility and guardrails for short-term rentals without stripping renters of a key way to offset rising housing costs; the very thing this ban attempts to address.
Alikiah Barclay is a founder of Reeku, a property technology platform that partners with landlords to ensure tenants can safely and legally host their primary residences, recouping rent.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Can News Media In Hawaiʻi Survive AI?
description:
Islanders once had an insatiable appetite for the news, with more than 1,200 newspapers published in the islands before the year 2000. Now the state is a news desert and AI could make things a whole lot worse. 
The post Can News Media In Hawaiʻi Survive AI? appeared first on Honolulu Civil Beat.
text:
For the last few months, Civil Beat editors have been getting an increasing barrage of AI-generated emails, offering everything from an off-shore builder eager to be a future source (clearly autogenerated by a story about a kauhale) to a marketing firm that wants to automatically post stories on our site and a “news” site that wants to repost all of ours — for free!
But the one that caught our eye the most had this subject line: “Honolulu could have a daily paper.”
Putting aside the fact that Honolulu already has a daily paper — albeit one with fewer and fewer pages each year — we were intrigued by what the email was pitching: a national effort to bring a “daily local paper back to towns that lost theirs.”
How might one do this? By becoming the editor-in-chief or publisher of an AI-powered local news site for the starting price of $299. No journalism experience required. (We emailed the company behind the pitch hoping to learn more about how AI “News Agents” could help bolster the dwindling power of the Fourth Estate but have not heard back.)
While the Star-Advertiser is thankfully still plugging along, the truth is that Hawaiʻi has become one of the nation’s many news deserts. 
It’s a fact made all the more heartbreaking by Hawaiʻi’s storied media legacy. 
The Hawaiian Kingdom had one of the highest literacy rates in the world, and — despite Hawaiʻi’s geographic isolation — in the mid-1800s, people here were more versed in global affairs than residents in many parts of the United States. Hundreds of ships a year docked at harbors in Honolulu and Lahaina, and local publishers were eager to get their hands on whatever news those ships carried with them. 
“Little rowboats would go out and pick up the newspapers they had collected from around the world,” local historian Anita Manning told Civil Beat in 2019. It was “like the Twitter of its day.”
U.S. President Abraham Lincoln’s assassination was front-page news when it reached Hawaii on 11 May 1865.  (Papakilo Hawaiian Newspaper Database)
The appetite for news was seemingly insatiable. 
Between the mid-19th century and the start of the millennium, more than 1,200 different newspapers were printed in the islands. More than 100 were in ʻŌlelo Hawaiʻi, and the collection of surviving Hawaiian language newspapers is “one of the largest repositories of Indigenous language material” in the world. 
Some of the reporters and editors in our newsroom entered this field long after the precipitous decline of newspapers that came with the internet age. Others remember an era when newsrooms were in heavy competition with each other, even smaller regional newspapers had the budget to send reporters far afield to chase a scoop. Fifty years ago this week, back when Hawaiʻi had two major daily newspapers, the Sunday edition for just one of them clocked in at 266 pages. 
When Civil Beat transitioned to a nonprofit a decade ago, sites like ours were seen as a bright spot in an otherwise dreary landscape. In 2015, there were roughly 200 nonprofit newsrooms in the U.S. Last year there were more than 400 digital-first nonprofit newsrooms. 
But even nonprofit news sites are facing another major media transformation, one that could be as disruptive as the entry of the World Wide Web: the age of AI. 
Rose and James used to read the headlines on The Garden Island’s website. Alas, the program has been cancelled. (Screenshot/2024)
Some of the early forays of AI into journalism were humorous (anyone remember when The Garden Island debuted two AI avatars reading the news.) But AI is becoming increasingly hard to spot, and at the same time, its incursions are becoming too pervasive to ignore. It’s by no means a scientific study, but this bit of research from a San Francisco marketing company merits real concern and further investigation: “AI Now Writes as Many Online Articles as Humans.”
A company called Hoodline that operates a Honolulu news site publishes several stories a day about Hawaiʻi. One from a few days ago about health insurance hikes by HMSA and other local insurers says it was written by Marc Suzuki. There is, however, no Marc Suzuki. 
Hoodline’s story has a little “ai” symbol next to Suzuki’s byline, but it takes some real research to figure out that button means Suzuki is a fictitious persona, with a Japanese surname chosen perhaps make him seem local and create trust with the local community. (Hoodline’s CEO has said that names are chosen at random by AI and not meant to ethnically mirror local communities, but in 2024 Nieman Lab found a notable trend in how the names shifted based on local demographics.) 
AI is changing how news is produced and it’s also changing how people find news. Algorithms on social, search settings, chatbots. It’s hard to tell how and where people will be getting their news in the decades to come. 
So where does that leave us? In the same place journalists have been for the last several decades: Needing to adapt and be nimble. 
Civil Beat launched a new website last week — not because of AI specifically, though we hope that our transition will protect our site from crippling bot attacks, which, surprise!, tend to originate from cities with large data centers, which are being rapidly built to accommodate the voracious needs of AI. Our new site still has some kinks, but it will also give us new tools to help us be flexible in the next few years. We’ll be able to get information up faster, embed videos directly on our homepage, add bite-sized takeaways to stories, and more easily include content from Civil Beat archives that are relevant to issues today. 
And though we are cautious about AI, we’re leaning on it for what we think is its current best use here: sorting through thousands of hours of government meetings to make sure that anyone can hone in on exactly what our elected officials are doing during the legislative session in every hearing — and share links to the exact moment they said something so that you can get directly to the source of information, too. (You can read more about Digital Democracy and find our full AI policy here.) 
And rather than generating avatars with ethnic-sounding names tailored to Hawaiʻi, we’re continuing to invest in our pipeline program to nurture the next generation of local journalists: people from here who will be deeply committed to being the watchdogs for their community and reporting stories that can often only be told by creating deep human connections. 
These future reporters, like the ones currently in our newsroom, will have to enjoy a challenge. It’s sort of essential in our line of business. 
The future of news is a little scary. But it’s definitely not boring. 
— Jessica Terrell, Civil Beat Managing Editor 
Go deeper: 
Hawaiʻi Supreme Court Says Current Rules Are Enough To Prevent AI AbusesDespite lawyers citing fake, AI-generated citations in court documents, a new report finds existing rules provide adequate safeguards.Artificial Intelligence Is Here To Stay. Are Hawaiʻi Schools Ready?From preschoolers to high school seniors, Hawaiʻi students share how artificial intelligence is shaping their learning and plans for the future.
Schatz Pushes AI Oversight As Tech Goes Rogue: ‘Humans In Control’In an interview with Civil Beat, Hawaiʻi’s senior senator explains why Congress needs to set up AI safety rules now before something “horrifying” happens.
How We’re Thinking About AI At Civil BeatFrom typewriters onward, newsrooms have benefited from technological advances. Artificial intelligence, however, offers particular challenges.
Spotting AI: ‘It’s The Hair’ 
Courtney Teague, our director of audience at Civil Beat, became known this election season as something of a whiz when it came to identifying AI-generated photos. When her eagle eyes spotted something amiss, there would occasionally be a groan in the newsroom (no one wants to hear at the end of the day that the only photo we have for a political candidate might need to be pulled from publication) but we came to rely on her as AI-generated photos became a more common occurrence. 

Courtney Teague, our directory of audience, is a whiz at picking hair products — and spotting fake photos based on hairstyles.  (Kawika Lopez)

Courtney, a UH grad who first joined Civil Beat as an intern in 2016, worked at several news operations in California before returning to us to head newsletters and then our overall audience strategy. She says the 2026 campaign cycle was the first where she recalls spotting so many — at least a dozen by her estimation — AI-generated photos from political candidates. She found it particularly disheartening to see seasoned politicians shopping around fake images of themselves. 
So what’s her secret for ferreting out the fakery? It’s all about the hair. 
“It just looks like a cartoon,” Courtney says. Basically, it’s too perfect. 
Courtney’s got a bit of an obsession with hairstyles — and a full Pinterest board to prove it — and she usually has the best-coiffed hair in the office. But even with her vast knowledge and strong opinions on hair products, she’s got a few stray wisps and some frizz on even the best day. Not so on many of the AI photos she’s been spotting. “It all just looks like one piece if you zoom in on it,” she says. 
The problem is AI is getting better at making things like hair seem a little more realistic, adding in some imperfections as needed. So what’s the takeaway? 
“I hope that this isn’t too cynical, but I would just say assume it’s fake unless you know where it’s coming from,” Courtney says. “I myself am stumped by stuff in my own feed all the time, and I feel like I have a pretty good eye for it.”
Can you spot what’s real? 
The decline in the number of journalists nationally over the last few decades has been paired with a remarkable growth in the number of public relations professionals. We don’t dislike PR folks — reporters rely on them daily for critical information and many government spokespeople were once our colleagues. But it’s alarming that even as there are fewer watchdogs tracking what local officials are doing, there are more people tasked with promoting them. 
The amount of money the state spent publicizing the work of the no-bid contractor building homeless villages in Hawaiʻi actually raised some serious eyebrows in a recent Legislative hearing. 
“Oh god, the public relations,” State Sen. Joy San Buenaventura said.  “I mean why do we even need to publicize a homeless initiative?”
Lawmakers were also concerned about other more questionable expenses that HomeAid was reimbursed for by the state, costs that had little to do with housing the homeless. Take our quiz to see if you can spot which expenses the state reimbursed HomeAid for.

text:
The Delaware Department of Education will host the Zoom session from 6 to 7:30 p.m. to explain its proposed School Performance and Support Framework, answer questions and hear public feedback.
Virtual meeting offers residents a chance to ask about student progress, school spending and leadership responsibilities before comments close Nov. 20
DOVER, Del. — Delaware families can ask how the state plans to help struggling schools — and what should happen when students continue falling behind — during a virtual town hall Tuesday, Nov. 17.
The Delaware Department of Education will host the Zoom session from 6 to 7:30 p.m. to explain its proposed School Performance and Support Framework, answer questions and hear public feedback.
The meeting comes three days before the Nov. 20 deadline for written comments. The framework remains a draft, with DOE seeking input before developing final recommendations. Delaware Department of Education
What accountability means for families
For parents, the accountability debate begins with practical questions: Is my child learning to read? How will I know whether the school is improving? If a district spends more on an improvement strategy, what evidence should show that it works? And who must act when progress stalls?
Those questions connect student learning with public reporting, spending decisions and the responsibilities of school leaders, local boards and the state.
The draft would consider achievement, student growth, literacy screening and other indicators. No single measure would determine a school’s placement.
It proposes plain-language school profiles explaining support, progress, review dates and consequences if improvement does not occur.
Spending and leadership responsibilities
On spending, the proposal directs resources toward demonstrated needs and evidence-based strategies. It does not establish a simple funding bonus for schools that raise scores.
Superintendent and principal performance goals would connect to student outcomes. More intensive intervention could include principal reassignment or leadership replacement; the draft does not establish automatic superintendent dismissal when scores fail to rise.
At the highest level, persistent underperformance could lead to state receivership. Some provisions would require legislative or regulatory action. education.delaware.gov
A central issue for residents to consider is how to balance timely help with clear expectations: What progress should schools demonstrate, how long should they have and what should change if the approach is not working?
Understanding what changes in your district
For parents, a school’s overall performance is only part of the picture. Families can also ask how their own child’s progress is measured, what additional instruction is available and how they will be told whether that help is working.
When reviewing district reports or attending school board meetings, parents can ask about improvement plans, spending priorities and the goals used to evaluate leadership.
First State Educate’s Knowledge Hub helps families and community members follow what their school boards are discussing and understand how district decisions are made. They can read school board meeting summaries, use guides to district budgets and public comment, and share questions with others across Delaware as they prepare to talk with their own boards.
In October, First State Educate brought school board members together for two discussions on Delaware’s draft School Performance and Support Framework. According to the organization, the sessions gave board members space to ask questions, share what the proposal could mean for their districts and hear how their peers were thinking about it.
How to submit feedback
Residents can review the proposal and submit comments through DOE’s website. They do not need to answer every feedback question. DOE asks for specific concerns and suggested changes where possible.
The department says comments submitted through its online form become part of its documented review, including feedback residents have discussed at stakeholder meetings. education.delaware.gov
To Go Box

When: Tuesday, Nov. 17, 6 to 7:30 p.m.
Where: Zoom. Visit DOE’s framework page for participation information and proposal materials.
Written comment deadline: Nov. 20, 2026.
Submit feedback: DOE’s online comment form.
Resources for families: First State Educate Knowledge Hub.
