title: New Mexico House Democrats retain leadership
description: The Democratic caucus for the New Mexico House of Representatives kept its leadership in place, according to a news release on Saturday. Among other positions, the caucus retained state Rep. Javier Martínez (D-Albuquerque) as speaker, a position he has held since 2022, pending an official vote by the full house on opening day of the 2027 session on Jan. 19.
text:
NM House Speaker Rep. Javier Martínez (D-Albuquerque) acknowledges members of the Democratic caucus during a press conference on House Floor following the close of the 30-day legislative session on Feb. 19,  2026. (Danielle Prokop/Source NM)The Democratic caucus for the New Mexico House of Representatives will keep its leadership in place for next year’s legislative session, according to a news release on Saturday.
The caucus retained state Rep. Javier Martínez (D-Albuquerque) as speaker, a position he has held since 2022, pending an official vote by the full House on opening day of the 2027 session on Jan. 19.
“As the son of hardworking, blue-collar immigrants, I could not be more grateful for the opportunity to continue fighting for New Mexico’s working families from the Speaker’s Chair, alongside the incredible leaders in this caucus,” Martínez said in a statement. “We’re heading into session energized and with an ambitious agenda to continue to deliver real results for New Mexicans, while providing the blueprint for the rest of the nation.”
The caucus also retained Majority Floor Leader Reena Szczepanski (D-Santa Fe), House Majority Whip Dayan Hochman-Vigil and Raymundo “Ray” Lara (D-Chamberino) in their positions.
New Mexico House Democrats have eight newly elected members following the Nov. 3 election, and unseated four incumbent Republicans. As a result, Democrats will hold 47 of 70 House seats when the new legislative session begins on Jan. 19 for a 60-day session. Democrats also kept their 10-seat majority in the state Senate. New Mexico is one of six states whose legislatures have at least 50% women following the midterm elections.
New Mexico House Republicans last week also named their leadership team for the upcoming session, reelecting Rep. Gail Armstrong (R-Magdalena) as minority floor leader.

name: VTDigger
title: Wolk makes Vermont history as first independent elected to state Senate
description:
Dave Wolk returns to the Senate chamber where he served more than three decades ago as a Democrat.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Wolk makes Vermont history as first independent elected to state Senate.
text:
The Senate chamber at the Statehouse in Montpelier on Tuesday, Feb. 26, 2019. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Katy Savage was first published in the Mountain Times on Nov. 11, 2026.
In May, Dave Wolk returned to a workplace he hadn’t seen in over 30 years, and it felt like a homecoming.
He visited the Senate chamber, where he served 34 years ago, after dropping off the signatures needed to get his name on the November ballot at the secretary of state’s office.
Much of the chamber looked as he remembered it, from the furniture and decor to the desk where he once sat. Inside, Wolk found his son’s signature, written there when his son was just 8 years old.
“They allow you to have your kids write their names inside the desk, and my son is now 46, so he was 8 years old then,” Wolk recalled. “I sat there and I felt like I was at home.”
At the time, Wolk didn’t know whether voters would send him back to Montpelier.
Six months later, they did.
Wolk, 73, made Vermont political history on Election Day, becoming the first independent candidate elected to the state Senate. The former Democratic senator, who served from 1988 to 1992, defeated Republican incumbent Terry Williams to claim one of Rutland County’s three Senate seats, finishing second in the four-way race with 14,259 votes.
Williams finished fourth with 11,190 votes. Days before the election, Williams was arrested and charged with domestic assault after allegedly striking a relative in the face during an argument over chores at his Poultney home.
Wolk will serve with Republican Brian Collamore, who led the field with 15,755 votes, and Republican David Weeks, who finished third with 13,319 votes. 
Wolk’s return to the Statehouse will be different this time. He’s heading back without a political party behind him — and that’s exactly how he wants it.
“You don’t want to be beholden to anyone except for voters,” he said.
Wolk ran an unconventional campaign. He refused contributions from political action committees, lobbyists and lawyers who represent lobbyists. He also never directly asked anyone for a donation.
Instead, individuals contributed $23,214 to his campaign.
“I was grateful that a lot of people sent enough money in to run a campaign,” he said.
For Wolk, running as an independent was about more than campaign financing. He said he wanted the freedom to vote according to his constituents’ interests rather than the demands of party leadership.
Wolk said conversations with Republican and Democratic lawmakers reinforced that decision. Some told him they had felt pressured to support legislation favored by party leaders, even when they personally disagreed.
Wolk also said he has grown frustrated with the increasingly confrontational tone of politics.
“I have felt it more acutely in the last few years that I’ve seen more people try to lift themselves up by tearing other people down, and it doesn’t work,” he said.
Running without a party affiliation, he said, has been liberating.
“I know who I’m beholden to, and it’s not a political party, and it’s not a political action committee, it’s not a lobbyist, not a lawyer. It’s for the people I represent,” he said.
Wolk’s election marks another chapter in a public service career spanning more than five decades and all three branches of Vermont government.
Wolk is a Middlebury College graduate. He began his career in education in the 1970s as a teacher and guidance counselor at Mount St. Joseph Academy in Rutland.
He later earned a master’s degree from the University of Vermont and pursued graduate studies at Harvard before returning to Vermont, where he became principal of Barstow Memorial School in Chittenden.
In 1988, he was elected to the Vermont Senate as a Democrat, serving two terms before running for lieutenant governor in 1992. He lost that race to Republican Barbara Snelling.
Wolk then returned to education, serving as principal of Rutland High School and later as superintendent. He went on to become Vermont’s commissioner of education for two years. He then spent 16 years as president of what is now Castleton University.
During his tenure he ushered in a $25.7 million initiative that included the multipurpose Spartan Stadium — now named Dave Wolk Stadium. That investment in athletics increased participation rates fivefold and increased the offerings to 28 varsity programs.
Most recently, he served as an assistant judge in Rutland County.
Even after leaving those positions, Wolk has remained involved in public service. He has operated a leadership coaching business and served as a guardian ad litem, a court-appointed advocate who represents children’s interests in legal proceedings.
He admits that stepping away from work has never been easy.
“I failed retirement,” he joked.
Wolk said he doesn’t have hobbies outside of public service.
“I’m sort of addicted to public service,” he said. “I love it. I feel a kind of sense of purpose.”
During his campaign, Wolk met with local boards and heard concerns about deteriorating roads and bridges and rising education and property taxes.
Wolk said public safety was among the issues that came up most frequently, particularly concerns about repeat offenders who commit property crimes and fail to appear in court.
Wolk wants to change Vermont law to give judges additional tools to address repeat offenders who consistently miss court appearances.
Wolk said the goal is to address what he sees as a revolving door for people repeatedly accused of misdemeanor property crimes, including thefts from stores and break-ins involving homes and vehicles.
He said the issue affects the quality of life in communities.
When Wolk returns to the Senate in January, he’ll be entering a chamber that looks much as it did more than three decades ago. But he’s less certain about how much the political atmosphere has changed.
During his first two terms, Wolk remembers lawmakers from opposing parties working together despite their disagreements. He hopes to find that same spirit of cooperation when he returns.
“The decorum back then was bipartisan or nonpartisan, and it was collegial, friendly, civil,” Wolk said. “I’m not saying it’s not that way now, but I’m going to be curious about that.”

name: VTDigger
title: Saving pennies, saving a planet
description:
The Chittenden Energy Fair celebrated the highlights of the Rutland County town’s Energy Challenge and introduced the next chapter of the community’s energy goals.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Saving pennies, saving a planet.
text:
Maddy Murray, project manager with Green Mountain Power, answers questions at the Chittenden Energy Fair in Chittenden on Thursday, November 12, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell, VTDigger
CHITTENDEN — Sue Priest’s freshly mowed grass has recently found a new purpose: feeding her family’s cattle.
Priest and her husband participated in the Chittenden Energy Challenge, which called on residents of the small town in Rutland County to participate in 500 creative sustainable actions over the past year. 
In addition to sustainability measures they’ve taken in the past, the couple decided to mow their lawn less, repurpose the grass and embrace bike commuting, including on trips to the grocery store.
“We’ll carry back 20 to 40 pounds worth of groceries, and so save a car trip that way,” Priest said.
A fair held Thursday at Mountain Top Resort marked the end of the challenge. But the event wasn’t simply an ending. At a community dinner after the fair, a “Menu of Ideas” placed on dining tables at the resort served up inspiration for future projects.
The challenge and corresponding fair were intended to enhance community awareness and excitement for saving energy and the environment. There were learning opportunities throughout the challenge that incorporated experts in eco-friendly transportation, renewable energy transitions and invasive species, among other things.
But the project was about more than enthusiasm for sustainability. It was designed, as many other energy fairs across Vermont are, to bridge the gap between affordability and green energy investments.
“This isn’t just for the wealthy,” said Melanie Paskevich, chair of the Chittenden Energy and Climate Committee. “This isn’t just for, maybe the low income either. We can all do this.”
The fair featured giveaways of everything from travel mugs to weather-proofing supplies. Energy experts set up tables in an event room at the resort and answered community members’ questions.

Bekah Kuster of Efficiency Vermont, left, speaks with Robert Baird at the Chittenden Energy Fair in Chittenden on Thursday, November 12, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell, VTDigger

Bekah Kuster, community engagement manager at Efficiency Vermont, fielded questions from residents about their personal energy goals and ways to make them happen through rebates and other cost-saving measures. Efficiency Vermont, a statewide energy efficiency utility designed to help Vermonters reduce their energy consumption, provides a variety of rebates, advice and financial assistance for renewable energy projects.
Awareness is a crucial part of the puzzle when encouraging residents to go green, Kuster said. It’s important to help people find economic resources to implement measures like heat pumps and weatherization, Kuster said, and educate them about smaller measures that people can take.
These conversations become increasingly important when households are preparing for worsening winter weather, Kuster said. And people are especially concerned this year, she added, due to rising prices for energy and other everyday essentials. 
“My hope is just to make people aware of the ways that they can save energy this winter and be more comfortable with rising energy costs,” Kuster said.
Priest has taken advantage of rebates in the past when updating appliances to energy-efficient alternatives, she said.
“We always look before we buy something to see if there’s a rebate available to help with the cost,” Priest said.
John and Ellen Bodin, residents of North Chittenden and relatives of Priest, attended the event. They have had a long interest in sustainability, investing in solar panels and heat pumps and replacing their appliances with higher-efficiency models. For this year’s challenge, they decided to carpool more, hang laundry outside to dry and cut their lawn less.
The Chittenden Energy Fair is one of many energy fairs that have sprouted across Vermont to encourage community involvement in conservation. There’s also an annual Waterbury LEAP Fair in April focused on educating residents on saving energy and costs. Another event, the Net Zero Energy Festival in Burlington, centers on electrification and reducing fossil fuel use.The festival was in August this year.

Robert Harness, left, speaks with Paige Prouty of Downvalley Bike and Apparel at the Chittenden Energy Fair in Chittenden on Thursday, November 12, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell, VTDigger

Last week’s event in Chittenden was somewhat unusual because of the series of workshops and community events that spanned a year leading up to it, according to Sean Beatty, a regional planner with the Rutland Regional Planning Commission who worked one of the event tables.
“It’s a real chance to educate people,” Beatty said. “And especially on a smaller scale, where this is really only Chittenden residents, where we can get pretty specific to some of the problems that Chittenden residents might have.”
The challenge’s goal was to record 500 actions taken by community members during the year, Paskevich said. 
Chittenden exceeded expectations and recorded 624 actions.
The “Menu of Ideas” featured different options for energy-saving actions. Options ranged from individual community support, including home energy visits and a community firewood lot for residents in need of heat assistance, to townwide actions such as a rideshare system.
People who attended the event voted on the possible actions to implement. The most popular was safer walking and biking routes. As for community energy support, the favorites were volunteer weatherization/project help and home energy supply kits.
John Bodin said going green is a matter of “individuals coming together to make it happen.” He highlighted the efforts of the energy committee for organizing the project.
“It exposes more people to it,” Bodin said, “so that they’re aware of what opportunities there are and what kind of financial rebates there are, which makes it a little less scary when, if you’re thinking in dollars and cents, which we often are these days.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Scott Colom’s win in the midterm election ends years of job security for a senator from Mississippi
description: Democratic Sen. James Eastland, right, unseated one of Mississippi's U.S. senators in 1942 and was the last to do so until Democrat Scott Colom defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith in 2026. In this photo from Aug. 10, 1967, Eastland confers with Sen. Edward M. Kennedy, D-Mass., before announcing that the Senate Judiciary Committee would meet in a closed[...]
text:
For years, winning a United States Senate seat in Mississippi has provided hands-down, lead-pipe cinch job security.
The Senate became almost a nursing home as age and health issues caught up with most of Mississippi’s senators, but they kept getting reelected.
Incumbent Mississippi senators just did not get beat – until this past week when Democratic challenger Scott Colom’s improbable victory over Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith.
A week after the Nov 3 general election, Colom, a district attorney in the Lowndes County area in north Mississippi, was declared the winner of the closely contested campaign. Around the time that The Associated Press called the race for Colom, Hyde-Smith, still the only woman elected to federal office in Mississippi, graciously conceded.
Colom’s victory is historic for numerous reasons. He is the first Black person elected through popular vote to the Senate from Mississippi and, for that matter, the first Black person elected to any statewide office in this state since Reconstruction.
Colom is also the first challenger to unseat a U.S. senator from Mississippi since 1942, when James. O. Eastland defeated Wall Doxey. “Big Jim” Eastland, as he was called, went on to serve until he retired in 1978.
U.S. Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during his election celebration at Tougaloo College in Jackson on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The junior senator from Missisisppi during Eastland’s tenure was John Stennis, who served from 1947 until 1989.
After winning the office, Eastland and Stennis faced few serious challenges. Republican maverick Gil Carmichael of Meridian ran an aggressive campaign against Eastland in 1972, but in the end the incumbent won with 58% of the vote – a nail-biter historically speaking  by Senate campaign standards in Mississippi.
When Eastland opted to step down in 1978, Republican U.S. Rep. Thad Cochran won the post with a plurality of the vote. Six years later, he faced Democrat William Winter.
Winter, who was finishing his gubernatorial tenure, wavered on whether he wanted to challenge Cochran, who was a friend, or try to become chancellor of University of Mississippi. In the end, Winter garnered only 39% of the vote in the Senate race and was not named chancellor.
For all practical purposes, Cochran did not face another serious challenge until 2014, when state Sen. Chris McDaniel, a Tea Party favorite, nearly upset him in the Republican primary.
When Stennis, the last Democrat before Colom to win a Senate election in Mississippi, opted not to seek reelection in 1988, Republican U.S. Rep. Trent Lott defeated Democratic U.S. Rep. Wayne Dowdy in a relatively close election.
Lott was never seriously challenged during his tenure that ended when he retired in 2007.
Republican U.S. Rep. Roger Wicker was appointed by then-Gov. Haley Barbour to succeed Lott. Wicker defeated Democratic former Gov. Ronnie Musgrove in a 2008 special election and has enjoyed relatively comfortable reelection efforts since then.
Such has not been the case for Hyde-Smith.
Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith speaks to supporters during her watch party held at the Sheraton Flowood The Refuge Hotel & Conference Center, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Flowood. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Hyde-Smith, a former Democratic state senator from Brookhaven, was in her second term as a Republican state agriculture and commerce commissioner when she was appointed by then-Gov. Phil Bryant to succeed Cochran, who also retired before his term ended.
As she was appointed, some, including many Washington insiders, questioned whether Bryant had chosen the strongest Republican, electorally speaking, to the important post.
She endured a tough battle in a nominally nonpartisan special election against McDaniel and Democratic former U.S. Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy. Mississippi does not have runoffs in regular elections for full six-year terms in the U.S. Senate, but it does have them for special elections to fill unexpired terms. In a runoff, Hyde-Smith defeated Espy 53.6% to 46.4% in what was then the closest nonpartisan Senate race in the state’s modern era.
In 2020 with her political protector – Donald Trump – on the ballot, Hyde Smith garnered 54% of the vote against Espy in a tough rematch.
Going into the 2026 election, Hyde-Smith had to be thinking she would finally have an easy race. In fairness, Hyde-Smith’s loss might be as much a referendum on President Trump as it was on her. After all, he told people to vote like he was on the ballot.
Perhaps, other candidates could have defeated her this year. It has been a tough midterm election cycle for Republicans, even in normally ruby-red Mississippi.
But the fact remains, had it not been for Hyde-Smith single-handedly blocking Colom’s nomination to the federal judiciary by President Joe Biden, Colom would have been presiding as a judge in a lifetime appointment and would have never run for the Senate.
Now, based on Mississippi history, Colom may have a lifetime job as a United States senator.

name: Delaware
title: University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens Earn Sixth Straight Homecoming Victory
description: The University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens (5-5, 3-3 CUSA) defeated the FIU Panthers (4-6, 2-4 CUSA), 24-16, Saturday evening and are now a win away from becoming eligible for a bowl game.   NEWARK, Del. — FIU quarterback JJ Kohl dropped back and looked left where the Panthers sent three receivers out on routes. Kohl found a receiver open ... Read More
text:
The University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens run out to the field for their game against FIU. Photo Credit: Dave Reeder
The University of Delaware Fightin’ Blue Hens (5-5, 3-3 CUSA) defeated the FIU Panthers (4-6, 2-4 CUSA), 24-16, Saturday evening and are now a win away from becoming eligible for a bowl game.
 
NEWARK, Del. — FIU quarterback JJ Kohl dropped back and looked left where the Panthers sent three receivers out on routes. Kohl found a receiver open near the back left pylon, but his pass was behind his intended receiver, Maguire Anderson. Anderson adjusted to make the catch, but neither him nor Kohl accounted for first-year safety Kevin Moore. 
Moore trailed Anderson on the route and flew in front of the redshirt junior when the ball went spiraling through the air. Moore completed the catch and raced down the left sideline with the time ticking down in the second quarter. Moore’s return was stopped at Delaware’s 46-yard line with two seconds remaining in the half. A failed hail mary attempt followed, but Moore’s play kept the score tied, 7-7, going into halftime.
The Blue Hens scored 17 points in the second half to defeat the FIU Panthers, 24-16, Saturday evening in their annual homecoming game. Delaware is now 53-19 in homecoming games.
Moore’s defensive play was a bookend for a fantastic defensive effort from the Delaware defense in the first half. Senior Jawarren Corbin kicked off the strong play with an interception on the game’s first drive. Corbin’s interception came on a tipped pass by Kshawn Cox Jr. that required Corbin to dive to secure the pick. 
The Blue Hens offense rewarded the defense’s effort driving 68 yards down the field in six plays for the game’s opening touchdown. All six plays were passes and the final throw was an 11-yard pitch and catch from Nick Minicucci to tight end Elijah Sessoms along the right side of the endzone.
The Panthers answered the scoring drive with one of their own during their next possession and the two teams finished the first quarter tied, 7-7. The score held that way through the second quarter due to Moore’s interception and the defense’s ability to be resilient in the red zone. The Panthers held the ball for over 11 minutes in the second quarter, drove into the red zone twice and walked away without points each time. 
“I think staying the course was really the way they had to do it,” head coach Ryan Carty said about the defense. “When the field kind of shrunk, when, you know, they might have given up some chunk plays to get down there, when the field shrunk, I thought they did a really nice job.”
Delaware started the second half with an 11 play drive that took over six and a half minutes of gametime — two more minutes than UD held the ball for in the entire second quarter — but ended with a 22-yard field goal from Tucker Smack. 
Smack’s field goal came after a four yard loss on a read option play that was disjointed from the very beginning. The play before the read option it appeared that running back Viron Ellison Jr. broke the goal-line, but he was ruled down at the half yard line. Carty tried to call a timeout before the read option play but wasn’t seen by the officiating crew in time. The play went on and Minicucci was tackled in the backfield without any time to react. 
The Panthers tied the game early in the fourth quarter after a third down stop from the Delaware defense prevented a touchdown. Bryson Graves returned the kick-off to the Delaware 40-yard line and the Blue Hens took advantage of the short field, scoring on a seven-yard touchdown throw from Minicucci to Ellison. 
The Panthers answered with a similar looking drive, but came up short on the extra point try due to the left elbow of defensive lineman Trace Scott III. Scott leaped into the air on Robert Czeremcha’s PAT attempt and blocked the kick. The rejection preserved UD’s lead, but it may not have happened if it hadn’t been for fifth year defensive tackle Dominick Brogna getting Scott lined up correctly.
“First off, I got to give credit to Dom Brogna for putting me in the right position on that blocked field goal, because I was not lined up correctly,” Scott said smiling. 
Delaware’s offense trotted on the field for their next possession, now clinging to a one-point lead with just under six minutes remaining in the game. Following the initial three plays of the drive, Carty and the Blue Hens faced a crucial fourth down decision. The Blue Hens needed a yard for a first down, but were on their own 37-yard line. If UD didn’t convert the Panthers would already be in field goal range. Carty decided to go for it.
“We needed the ball and we needed to go finish the game. That’s how that works,” Carty said postgame. “I’m never gonna sit there and wonder if we went for it on fourth and one, if we would have had a chance to win the game. I’m just not gonna do it.”
Minicucci took the snap from the shotgun with all his receivers out wide and ran through the right side of the offensive line. Minicucci escaped the front line of defenders and had nothing but grass in front of him. He ran the ball 62 yards — the most by a UD quarterback since Andy Hall rushed for an 85-yard touchdown in 2003 — and celebrated the rush with a nod to the knee brace surrounding his right knee. 
“I was referencing that even though I got a knee brace on, I’m still running, still gonna out run you,” Minicucci said. 
The fourth year signal caller did make light of the fact that he technically didn’t out run the defense because he was tackled a yard short of scoring, but said it was fine because he was able to punch it in on the next play for a one-yard score. Minicucci finished the game with 230 passing yards, 69 rushing yards and three total touchdowns. He completed all but three of his 30 pass attempts.
The Blue Hen defense did its part to close out the game by forcing an errant pass from Kohl on fourth and eight, allowing the offense to kneel out the final minutes of the game. The Delaware defense finished the game with six tackles for loss, seven quarterback hurries and two turnovers. The Blue Hens held FIU to three third down conversions on 11 attempts.
“The defense did a really good job at doing their job,” Scott said. “We started off a little sloppy, cleaned it up real quick, and I think everybody played their hearts out. I loved it.”
UD’s win is the program’s sixth straight on homecoming and puts them one win away from becoming bowl eligible for the second straight season. The Blue Hens remain in the race for a chance to play in the CUSA championship game with the win, though the hopes of that are slim. UD would need multiple factors to swing its way for that to become a reality.
Delaware has two more games on its schedule, starting with a road matchup against the New Mexico State Aggies. That game will be played on Saturday, November 21, at 3:00 p.m. The game will be televised on ESPN+.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Commentary: Arkansas Republicans confront their party’s Trump dilemma after midterms
description: If you want to see the divide Republicans face on how to move forward after a midterm election that saw them suffer historic losses in Washington and around the country, look no further than Arkansas’ current and former GOP governors. The day after the election, former Gov. Asa Hutchinson said the results showed his party […]
text:
Arkansas Governor and former Trump Administration Press Secretary Sarah Huckabee Sanders speaks ahead of a town hall with former President Donald Trump in Flint, Mich. on Sept. 17, 2024. (Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)If you want to see the divide Republicans face on how to move forward after a midterm election that saw them suffer historic losses in Washington and around the country, look no further than Arkansas’ current and former GOP governors.
The day after the election, former Gov. Asa Hutchinson said the results showed his party needs to understand voters’ concerns and move on from the “chaos” President Donald Trump is sowing. Instead of focusing on things that matter like diesel prices, the president was fixated on the Lincoln Reflecting Pool and building a new arch in the nation’s capital.
“When President Trump is right on policies such as securing the border, he ought to be supported on it,” Hutchinson told the Advocate. “But, you know, the chaos and the concentration on issues that are not important to average Americans has consequences, and that’s what we see in the election results.”
But Hutchinson’s successor, Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, wasn’t willing to blame the president for whom she worked.
“I think each race has to be looked at independently, and the president, while he still remains the most influential voice in all of Republican politics − frankly, in all of politics − his name wasn’t on the ballot,” Sanders told USA Today in an interview to promote her new book.
Sanders made the statement even though Trump in the final weeks of the midterm campaign told voters to pretend that he was on the ballot.



Let us know what you think...


 


The split between the two isn’t that surprising. Hutchinson left office frustrated with Trump’s brand of politics and mounted an unsuccessful bid against him for the Republican presidential nomination in 2024. Sanders’ ascendance as Hutchinson’s successor owed much to the national profile she gained as White House press secretary during Trump’s first term.
The sharp contrast between the two highlights the challenges Republicans in Arkansas face in navigating Trump.
Sanders launched her book tour days after the election with a victory lap of sorts as a Republican who managed to win reelection by double digits in a difficult political environment for her party. It’s also a soft launch of what could be her 2028 presidential campaign.
But the margin of Sanders’ win belies the setbacks she was dealt in an election where Trump’s unpopularity and concerns about his leadership were a drag. Republicans lost the 75-vote supermajority in the House they needed to pass most budget bills, which complicates Sanders’ legislative agenda next year. 
Despite those setbacks, Sanders is clearly testing out a path to the White House as a defender of the president. Her book regularly praises Trump’s leadership and policies on issues like immigration. Appearing on ABC’s “The View” last week, she defended Pete Hegseth as the Defense secretary faced calls for his impeachment.
Sanders is trying to win the pro-Trump lane as other GOP figures are distancing themselves from the president. That includes Vice President JD Vance, who’s blamed the administration’s war in Iran for Republicans’ midterm losses. 
One of the few areas where Sanders has split with the president is her book’s call for guardrails on artificial intelligence. Trump has resisted the push for such controls but Sanders’ stance indicates she understands the bipartisan reservations about AI and data centers.
Arkansas governor embraces Trump, calls for AI guardrails in new book

Other Arkansas Republicans are also calculating how much space to put between themselves and Trump.
The most prominent example is Republican U.S. Rep. French Hill, who barely survived a reelection challenge from Democrat Chris Jones in central Arkansas.
Days after his race was called, Hill was noncommittal about whether he’d support an impeachment effort against Hegseth. Hill ultimately voted with the state’s other Republican congressmen to effectively table the effort, but made clear he’s not happy with the progress of the Iran war.
“The question is: Are we leading at the Pentagon in the right way or not the right way? That’s very separate from whether or not somebody’s committed an impeachable offense,” Hill said on CBS’ “Face the Nation.”
Hill faces an especially precarious situation after his razor-thin victory. His district had long been eyed by Democrats who believed it was flippable, and last week’s results will encourage the party to focus even more attention on it when the next election rolls around in two years. But Hill also has to manage Trump’s unfavorability in a district while also guarding against primary challenges from the right of his own party.
The divide could also play out in other races in Arkansas in two years, especially if Republican Sen. John Boozman seeks another term. Boozman will lose his chairmanship of the Senate Agriculture Committee with the new Democratic majority in Congress and has also been targeted by primary challengers who have tried to paint him as insufficiently pro-Trump.
The midterm election revealed the limits of the president’s pull in even the Trumpiest of states, but how Arkansas Republicans position themselves in the coming months for 2028 could define the party for even longer.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Insufficient wellness funding is a common hurdle in supporting Native students, researchers find
description: The need for mental health and other wellness services among Native American students outpaces what’s available with existing funding, according to data collected earlier this year and presented recently to South Dakota educators. Dorothy Aguilera-Black Bear and Brooke Rumper, of the Central Comprehensive Center, asked South Dakota principals whose schools h[...]
text:
Dorothy Aguilera-Black Bear speaks to attendees during a breakout session at the annual Indian Education Summit in Pierre, South Dakota, on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight)https://southdakotasearchlight.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/111226-Building-from-Strengths-web.mp3
 Listen to an audio version of this story by reporter Meghan O’Brien. Broadcasters: See below for a downloadable version with a host intro script.
The need for mental health and other wellness services among Native American students outpaces what’s available with existing funding, according to data collected earlier this year and presented recently to South Dakota educators.
Dorothy Aguilera-Black Bear and Brooke Rumper, of the Central Comprehensive Center, asked South Dakota principals whose schools have at least one Native American student to identify the needs and available resources for those students. Of the 673 asked to participate in the survey, Aguilera-Black Bear and Rumper got responses from 157.
The pair shared their findings Thursday at the annual Indian Education Summit in Pierre. Federal grants helped fund the research, and the project is in partnership with the state Department of Tribal Relations and state Office of Indian Education.
“The capacity for schools to have those consistent needs be supported is really difficult,” said Aguilera-Black Bear.
‘We can do it’: A rural school near two Native American reservations nearly doubles its attendance

They’re bringing their findings to tribal education directors to dig deeper into the data, “because they’re very close to what’s going on in the schools that serve their tribal citizens,” said Aguilera-Black Bear. With the feedback from Thursday’s presentation, her team is hoping to help educators create action plans to address their students’ needs.
Nearly 60% of the survey respondents said their schools don’t have enough funding to provide the mental health and reproductive health education and access that students need. Some respondents also mentioned a lack of student access to community elders and knowledge keepers, and a struggle to hire staff with culturally relevant or trauma-informed training.
The survey also showed that many Native students in South Dakota lack access to secure housing, reliable food sources outside of school, and clothing and hygiene products.
Martina Moves Camp is a transition specialist at Crazy Horse School in Wanblee, on the Pine Ridge Reservation. She said her students experience challenges that are reflected in the data, including struggles with basic needs like food and clothing, but seeing the collaboration of researchers and educators gives her hope for finding solutions.
“We’re meeting that need, but we aren’t where a lot of other schools are,” Moves Camp said. “And I can’t wait for the day for our school to be where we are creating those culture-bearers, where they are able to be teachers to their next generation.”
